description: STRIDE threat model for the GenAI Intelligent Document Processing Accelerator (unified architecture: Pipeline + BDA modes). Generated from the Markdown corpus by scripts/build_threat_model.py — do not edit by hand.

threats.title: SQL Injection via Natural Language
threats.description: The Analytics Agent writes its own SQL from the user's natural-language question, so the statement Athena receives is model output. A crafted question, or injected text in data the agent has already read, could steer it toward a statement that writes, changes the catalog, runs a function or reads outside the reporting database
threats.attackVector: User submits a question designed to make the agent generate a write or code-running statement (e.g. "show me all data; DROP TABLE documents--", an `UNLOAD`, a `USING EXTERNAL FUNCTION` clause or a `"lambda:<function>"` catalog)
threats.impact: Unauthorized data access, data deletion, exposure of all processed document data
threats.affectedComponents: Analytics Agent (`run_athena_query` in `idp_common/agents/analytics/tools/athena_tool.py`), Amazon Athena, S3 Reporting Bucket, `AgentChatProcessorFunction`, `ChatStreamProcessorFunction`, `AgentProcessorFunction`
threats.mitigations: `run_athena_query` passes every statement through `validate_read_only_query` (`idp_common/agents/analytics/query_validation.py`) before calling Athena, and a refused statement returns `state: NOT_RUN` without a `StartQueryExecution` call. The check accepts exactly one `SELECT` (optionally opening with `WITH` or a parenthesis), `SHOW` or `DESCRIBE` statement and refuses: more than one statement; any `REFUSED_KEYWORDS` entry outside literals, quoted identifiers and comments (DDL, DML, `UNLOAD`, `INTO`, `PREPARE`/`EXECUTE`, `CALL`, `EXTERNAL`, `FUNCTION`, table functions); a quoted `lambda:` catalog; a backslash in `SHOW`/`DESCRIBE`; and anything it cannot tokenize. The roles that run the agent hold `athena:StartQueryExecution`/`GetQueryExecution`/`GetQueryResults` on the `primary` workgroup and the data catalog only, read-only Glue actions on the reporting database and its tables, `S3ReadPolicy` on the reporting bucket, and `s3:PutObject` on its `athena-results/` prefix alone. `return_full_query_results` inlines at most `MAX_ROWS_TO_RETURN_DIRECTLY` rows; larger results stay in S3. Each query is logged by `analytics_logger.log_query` to the function's log group
threats.residualRisk: The statement check is lexical, not a full SQL parse, and refuses what it recognises rather than proving a statement harmless. The stack does not configure the `primary` workgroup, so no per-query data-scanned limit or enforced result location is set by this solution.

threats.title: Arbitrary Code Execution via AgentCore
threats.description: The Analytics Agent generates Python and runs it in an AWS-managed AgentCore Code Interpreter session to chart or summarise query results. AI-generated code could contain unintended operations if a question or the data it reads carries a prompt injection
threats.attackVector: Prompt injection via user query or data content that manipulates the AI into generating Python that imports networking or process modules, reads other files, or sends query data elsewhere
threats.impact: Code execution within the managed session, which holds no AWS credentials and has no public internet access but can reach Amazon S3 in its Region; query results could be processed or written somewhere unintended
threats.affectedComponents: Analytics Agent (`CodeInterpreterTools` in `idp_common/agents/analytics/tools/code_interpreter_tools.py`), Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter
threats.mitigations: `execute_python` runs `check_sandbox_code` (`idp_common/agents/analytics/sandbox_code_checks.py`) on the exact text it will send and returns an error instead of running code that does not parse, imports a module outside `IMPORTABLE_MODULES` (a data, charting and computation set with no networking, HTTP, AWS SDK, `os` or process modules), uses a dynamic-lookup built-in or an attribute starting with `_`, names a refused module or file-helper submodule as an attribute, holds a `://` literal, or opens or writes a file other than by a direct call on a bare literal file name. `write_query_results_to_code_sandbox` takes no arguments: it copies only the result of the agent's last successful `run_athena_query`, at the location Athena reported, as `query_results.csv`. The session runs in the AWS-managed interpreter (no AWS credentials; no public internet access; reaches Amazon S3 in its Region and an instance metadata service that lists no role), and the roles hold the Code Interpreter actions on the managed `code-interpreter/*` ARN pattern only
threats.residualRisk: `check_sandbox_code` reads the code's text and syntax tree and is not a boundary: a construction it does not recognise still runs. Code running in a session can write data, including the result of the query the agent ran, to Amazon S3 in the session's Region. No execution-time or output-size limit is set by this solution beyond what the managed interpreter applies. `make stacktest-sandbox-network` measures the session's network reach.

threats.title: Agent Routing Manipulation
threats.description: The orchestrator agent decides which sub-agent answers a turn. Prompt injection in the question, in conversation memory or in a sub-agent's result could steer it to an agent or tool the user did not intend, including one that sends the query outside the deployment
threats.attackVector: Crafted user queries, or injected content returned by a data agent, that trick the orchestrator into invoking a more powerful agent or a sensitive tool
threats.impact: Unauthorized access to analytics data, code execution, or data sent to external systems
threats.affectedComponents: Orchestrator Agent (`idp_common/agents/orchestrator/agent.py`), agent registry (`idp_common/agents/factory/registry.py`), all sub-agents, both agent chat processors
threats.mitigations: The orchestrator is built per turn only with the agents the caller may use: `select_orchestrator_agent_ids` (`idp_common/chat_session_agents.py`) leaves out each opt-in kind the request did not opt in to and every opt-in agent once the session holds data-agent results, and `SessionAgentGate` makes an opt-in agent already built into the turn answer `UNAVAILABLE_MESSAGE` instead of running after a data agent returns. The Quick Start agent is never in the orchestrator. Agent Chat itself requires Admin, Author or Viewer (`_enforce_agent_chat_groups` in the processor, the same check in `agent_chat_resolver`, and `_enforce_groups_or_403` on the streaming route), and is Admin-only when `unscoped_is_denied()` holds (`TenantIsolationMode=Strict` or an external `TenantGrantSource`). Each sub-agent holds only its own tools, and the analytics tools check what they run (AGT.T01, AGT.T02). Agent invocations are logged to CloudWatch
threats.residualRisk: Routing among the agents the turn was built with remains a model decision; the controls bound which agents exist in the turn, not which one the model picks.

threats.title: Conversation History Poisoning
threats.description: Conversation memory (up to `MAX_CONVERSATION_TURNS` turns, default 20) is loaded into the agent's context on each turn. If an earlier turn contains injected content, it could influence subsequent agent responses and tool calls
threats.attackVector: Multi-turn attack where early messages, or a data agent's result quoting document-derived text, inject context that activates in later turns when combined with agent tool calls
threats.impact: Persistent prompt injection across conversation, manipulated agent behavior
threats.mitigations: Memory is keyed `conversation#<sub>#<sessionId>` on the caller's verified Cognito `sub`, so a conversation can only be poisoned by its own owner's turns and the results those turns produced; a provider with no user, or a user id containing the key separator, is refused. The session id is registered to its owner in `ChatSessionOwnersTable` before memory is built, and another user's session is refused (CHAT.T02, CHAT.T03). Memory items carry `ExpiresAfter` at `DataRetentionInDays` after their last write, and an item past it is neither loaded nor appended to. History is bounded by `MAX_CONVERSATION_TURNS` and the per-turn context by `DropAndSlideConversationManager`. A new conversation starts from empty memory
threats.residualRisk: Content in memory is not sanitized or tagged as untrusted before it re-enters the prompt, so a user's own earlier turns and the results they produced still shape later turns of that conversation.

threats.title: Cross-User Data Leakage via Athena
threats.description: Every user with agent access queries the same reporting database. The Analytics Agent's queries are not filtered by the caller's configuration-profile scope (`allowedConfigVersions`), so a scoped user can retrieve results from documents processed under profiles outside their scope, or uploaded by other users
threats.attackVector: User asks the agent for processing results of documents they did not upload, or of profiles outside their scope
threats.impact: Cross-user and cross-profile information disclosure of processed document data
threats.affectedComponents: Amazon Athena, S3 Reporting Bucket, Analytics Agent, both agent chat processors
threats.mitigations: Agent Chat requires Admin, Author or Viewer (Reviewer and Annotator are refused) on both chat paths (`_enforce_agent_chat_groups`, `_enforce_groups_or_403`). Under `TenantIsolationMode=Strict` or an external `TenantGrantSource`, Agent Chat and agent queries are Admin-only, and the web UI is given no streaming URL (`VITE_STREAM_URL` is empty under `DeniesUnscopedCaller`). Deploying one stack per environment or data owner keeps the reporting database single-tenant
threats.residualRisk: Outside tenant isolation, profile scope does not bound what the Analytics Agent returns (stated in the RBAC page's Known Limitations). A deployment that relies on `allowedConfigVersions` to separate users should not grant those users Agent Chat.

threats.title: Deployment Data Sent Outside the Deployment by an Opt-in Agent
threats.description: The Code Intelligence Agent sends its query to a public DeepWiki endpoint (`DEEPWIKI_MCP_URL`), and each External MCP agent sends its query to a server named in `ExternalMCPAgentsSecret`. The orchestrator composes that query from the conversation, so results from the data agents (Analytics, Error Analyzer), which hold document-derived data, logs and execution records, could be forwarded to a third party if both kinds of agent served one conversation
threats.attackVector: A user, or injected text in a data agent's result, leads the orchestrator to pass reporting data or error details to an opt-in agent in the same conversation
threats.impact: Disclosure of processed document data or operational detail to a service outside the deployment
threats.affectedComponents: Code Intelligence Agent (`idp_common/agents/code_intelligence/agent.py`), External MCP agents (`idp_common/agents/external_mcp/`), `idp_common/chat_session_agents.py`, `idp_common/chat_session_owner.py`, both agent chat processors, `ChatSessionOwnersTable`
threats.mitigations: Both opt-in kinds are off unless the request opts in for that conversation (`enableCodeIntelligence`, `enableExternalMcpAgents`, `StrictBool`, default `false`, on the REST resolver, the streaming route and the API schema); a non-boolean does not opt in. The first data-agent result in a session is recorded on its `ChatSessionOwnersTable` row (`record_data_results`, attribute `dataResultsAt`), and from then on no opt-in agent is built into that session's orchestrator. Within the turn that produced the result, `SessionAgentGate` makes an already-built opt-in agent answer `UNAVAILABLE_MESSAGE`, and it re-reads the flag before an opt-in agent runs so a concurrent turn's result also closes it. A failed read or write of the flag leaves the opt-in agents out. A request that opts in on a flagged session is moved to a new session with empty memory (`needs_new_session`). The flag lives as long as the owner row, which outlives the session's memory
threats.residualRisk: Before any data-agent result exists in a conversation, an opt-in agent receives whatever the orchestrator puts in its query, including text the user typed or pasted. The External MCP servers are chosen by whoever writes the secret, and what they do with a query is outside this solution.

threats.title: Privilege Escalation via Group Manipulation
threats.description: If Cognito user group assignments are not properly protected, a user could add themselves to higher-privilege groups (e.g., Viewer → Admin)
threats.attackVector: Direct Cognito API calls to modify group membership using stolen admin credentials, or exploiting misconfigured Cognito permissions
threats.impact: Unauthorized access to configuration, processing, and admin functions
threats.mitigations: IAM policies restricting Cognito admin operations, no self-service group management, Cognito user pool advanced security features, CloudTrail logging of Cognito API calls. User Management (`Admin` only) assigns exactly the group of the persona it records; before v0.6.13 its sync mapped every non-Admin persona to `Reviewer` on a persona change, so a deployment upgrading from v0.6.12 should review the groups of users whose persona was changed there.

threats.title: JWT Token Theft/Replay
threats.description: JWT tokens stored in browser (localStorage/sessionStorage) or SDK client could be stolen via XSS, malicious browser extensions, or network interception, then replayed for unauthorized access
threats.attackVector: XSS attack on web UI extracts JWT from storage; or man-in-the-middle (unlikely with TLS) captures token
threats.impact: Attacker gains authenticated access with victim's role permissions
threats.affectedComponents: Web UI, SDK/CLI, API Gateway REST API
threats.mitigations: Short-lived access tokens (1 hour default), secure token storage practices, Content Security Policy headers, XSS prevention in React app, HTTPS-only

threats.title: Insufficient Authorization Granularity
threats.description: The API Gateway authorizer only authenticates, so authorization depends on checks behind it. Any operation whose group check is missing or wrong lets a lower-privilege authenticated user perform a restricted operation by calling `POST /op/{field}` directly, and a newly added operation is open unless a check is declared for it.
threats.attackVector: Call the REST API `POST /op/{field}` directly with a valid low-privilege JWT, targeting operations whose resolver omits (or misconfigures) the `cognito:groups` check — bypassing all UI-level restrictions.
threats.impact: Unauthorized configuration changes, document access, or processing operations
threats.mitigations: **The dispatcher denies by default.** `http_api_dispatcher/authz.py` checks the caller's groups — read from the verified JWT claim, never the request body — against `api_rbac_manifest.json` before routing, and a field with **no entry** is refused with 403: an operation whose required groups were never declared is closed rather than open, so a forgotten resolver check on a **group-scoped** operation is not an open endpoint. ⚠️ **This does not cover every operation.** 8 of the 181 declared operations are declared `ANY` — the dispatcher enforces authentication but not group membership for those — so a forgotten resolver check on one of the 8 is still reachable by any authenticated caller, including a caller in no group at all where self-signup is enabled (`AllowedSignUpEmailDomain`, see AUTH.T04). They are `getMyProfile`, `listChatSessions`, `getLatestPublishedVersion`, the two fine-tuning job reads and the three feature-platform reads, and each entry in `scripts/api_rbac_expectations.yaml` records why `ANY` is the intended policy for **that operation** rather than for the section it sits in. A reason written for a set ("see `listChatSessions` — same decision") is read for whether it holds broadly, not for whether it holds of the one operation carrying it, and the mechanism it points at can differ: `listChatSessions` bounds its read with a DynamoDB key condition on the caller's own partition, while `getChatMessages` reads by session id and layers a separate ownership check (AUTH.T09). 171 require a group: 144 name a subset of roles and 27 are declared **`ANY_GROUP`** — any group `template.yaml` creates, so what those 27 **operations** refuse is precisely the self-registered caller whose `cognito:groups` claim is empty. The remaining 2 are `IAM_ONLY`, which is not a group requirement at all: they reject every Cognito caller irrespective of group. The `ANY_GROUP` set is every document read (`getDocument`, `listDocuments`, `listDocumentsByDateRange`, `getDocumentCount`, `listDocumentsDateHour`, `listDocumentsDateShard`, `listDocumentVersions`, `getDocumentVersion`, `compareDocumentVersions`, `getStepFunctionExecution`, `getFileContents`, `getFilePresignedUrl`, `getFilePresignedUrls`, `queryKnowledgeBase`), the chat transcript read `getChatMessages`, the processing-breaker badge `getCircuitBreakerStatus`, and `deleteAgentJob`, `deleteChatSession` and `sendChatDocumentMessage`, and the eight Inbox operations (`listInboxMessages`, `getInboxUnreadCount`, `getInboxPreferences`, `markInboxMessages`, `markAllInboxMessagesRead`, `deleteInboxMessages`, `clearReadInboxMessages`, `updateInboxPreferences`), each self-scoped to the caller's verified identity; the sentinel is resolved against the `AWS::Cognito::UserPoolGroup` resources at build time, so a group added to the template joins the set without an edit per operation. The document reads in that set include ones that return no extracted value themselves — object keys, a run's section and page URIs, the list of extracted attribute names, a model-written description of the page contents, the workflow execution input and step history — because together they compose into one chain to the content. `getChatMessages` is in it because its ownership check can be switched off (`ENFORCE_CHAT_SESSION_OWNERSHIP=false`), and `getCircuitBreakerStatus` because its `lastError` field carries `Manual pause by <administrator email>: <reason>` after any manual pause. ⚠️ Three things the group floor does not itself decide. Item (1) is an open residual; items (2) and (3) are closed, and (3) is what makes this floor a control on the document bytes rather than only on the API. **(1)** A group check is not a **per-document** check, and the per-document check that exists runs on the configuration-profile axis rather than on ownership: `document_scope` resolves the document owning an Input- or Output-bucket key from the tracking table and matches its `ConfigVersion` against the caller's `allowedConfigVersions` (UI.T06). ⚠️ **State this per caller shape, not per group.** For a **scoped** caller it is a real refusal — a document stamped with a profile outside their scope is denied before S3 is touched, and so are a key no tracked document owns and a document carrying no `ConfigVersion`, both fail-closed. For an **unscoped** caller — a UsersTable row that sets no scope, or no row at all — under the default `TenantIsolationMode=Off` with `TenantGrantSource=Manual` it is deliberately a no-op, because scoping is opt-in per user, so a caller holding any group may still read any document's bytes through the resolver, which is precisely the reach `listDocuments` already gives them; under `Strict` or an external grant source an unscoped non-Admin resolves to a scope no profile matches and is refused (TEN.T01). "Any document that group can see" remains the wrong frame for the same reason it always was: it is true of an unscoped caller, for whom a document's visibility really is a group question, and false of a scoped one, for whom the entire point of `allowedConfigVersions` or `allowedTestSets` is content their group must NOT see. The object-read path enforces the two **per-user** axes on the key as well — a scoped Author cannot read another configuration profile's revision bodies from the Configuration bucket, and a scoped Annotator cannot read another test set's source documents or ground truth from the Test Set bucket. What stays open is per-**document** scope in the sense of ownership, which the product does not define: no record says which user a document belongs to, so there is no such axis for a key check to consult. A tenant is a set of profiles and Input prefixes, so the profile check is also the tenant check. **(2)** The dispatcher's floor gates the **REST route**; `POST /chat/document` on the chat Function URL reaches the same processor as `sendChatDocumentMessage` and applies the same `ANY_GROUP` floor itself, from the Cognito ID token it verifies (`_require_a_group_or_403` in `chat_stream_processor/app.py`), so a groupless caller is refused on both paths (AUTH.T14; check S9 compares the two). **(3) The floor gates the API, and the buckets are behind the API.** `CognitoIdentityPoolSetRole` attaches a **single** `authenticated` role with **no `RoleMappings`**, so group membership plays no part in which role a signed-in user assumes: whatever that role can read, every signed-in user can read, groupless included, with no resolver in the path to apply any check. `CognitoAuthorizedRole` therefore grants **nothing** on the Input and Output buckets, **no** `s3:GetObject`, `s3:GetObjectVersion` or `s3:ListBucket` on any bucket, and **no** KMS action; its two inline policies are `lambda:InvokeFunction` on the chat-streaming Function URL and `ssm:GetParameter` on the settings parameter ([#1033](https://github.com/aws-solutions-library-samples/accelerated-intelligent-document-processing-on-aws/issues/1033)). A self-registered caller in no group who runs `cognito-identity get-id` and `get-credentials-for-identity` with their own ID token and assumes that role fails at `s3api get-object`, because the vended credentials can read no bucket. The UI asks `getFileContents`, `getFilePresignedUrl` or `getFilePresignedUrls` for every document byte it displays, including the file viewer, the page thumbnails, the page-image viewer and the document export, so the **fetch** needs an API operation exactly as the **key discovery** does, and each of those operations is declared `ANY_GROUP` — which is what puts this floor in front of the asset. Two further controls run in the same choke point (`_parse_and_validate_one`): the bucket allow-list, and the per-document and per-user key scopes described in residual (1). The option that was not taken — group-scoped Identity Pool `RoleMappings` — and the obstacles each shape ran into (the Annotator's per-object `allowedTestSets` scope has no IAM expression, four UI surfaces signed in the browser, and the dispatcher's 6 MiB response cap is why `getFilePresignedUrl` exists alongside `getFileContents`) are set out in [Identity Pool group scoping](../../../docs/planning/identity-pool-group-scoping-plan.md). ⚠️ **The two per-user-partitioned buckets must stay off this role.** A browser grant on the **Configuration bucket** would make the configuration-revision store — `config_revisions/<profile>/<nnnnnn>.json.gz`, every profile's recorded prompts and few-shot examples — readable by any authenticated user, defeating `allowedConfigVersions` with no API call to detect; neither it nor the Test Set bucket is on the role, so both axes are reachable only through the three object-read operations, where the key check applies. `scripts/tests/test_browser_s3_grants.py` pins this role's policy set in both directions, so an S3 statement cannot come back under any policy name without the gate saying so. **An `identity` carried on the event is not authoritative** ([#978](https://github.com/aws-solutions-library-samples/accelerated-intelligent-document-processing-on-aws/issues/978)): a principal holding `lambda:InvokeFunction` on the dispatcher could otherwise state its own `cognito:groups` in an invocation event and have this check made against its own claim. `idp_common.api_adapter.normalize_event` builds the identity from the authorizer's verified claims, refuses an asserted identity that contradicts them, and refuses one presented with no verified claims at all; the one shape still passed through is an explicitly null `identity`, which is this repository's marker for a service-to-service invocation gated by IAM on the function ARN and asserts no groups. A guard drives the dispatcher end to end with an operation and required groups read from the manifest at test time, and a second one discovers every consumer of the adapter by parsing the tree and fails if one lets the refusal escape as a 5xx instead of a 403. The manifest is generated from `scripts/api_rbac_expectations.yaml` (`scripts/sdlc/generate_api_rbac_manifest.py`), the same file the static scan and the live harness already assert against, so there is no second list to keep in step; it fails closed if unreadable. Resolver-level authorization for every operation remains in place on top of it — the dispatcher enforces the field-level floor, the resolver enforces per-object scope. Plus **automated per-operation authorization testing** — a static scan (including a manifest drift guard) and a live multi-role harness (`make api-test`, see §5) that fail on any missing/incorrect check and track known gaps; security review of new operations. **Not a control:** the `@aws_cognito_user_pools` directives in `schema.graphql` are **not** defense-in-depth here — nothing enforces them at runtime, so they carry no enforcement weight at all. They are retained as the input for the dispatcher's shape validation and as documentation of intent, and they are read by the static scan as one of the things it checks *for drift against the code*. Reading them as a second layer is exactly the mistake AUTH.T08 describes.

threats.title: Cognito User Pool Misconfiguration
threats.description: Misconfigured Cognito user pool settings (e.g., self-signup enabled, weak password policies, unverified email) could allow unauthorized account creation or account takeover
threats.attackVector: Self-register accounts if self-signup is enabled, or exploit weak password requirements
threats.impact: Unauthorized system access, even at Viewer level provides access to document processing results
threats.mitigations: Self-signup is disabled by default (`AllowAdminCreateUserOnly: true`, admin-created accounts only). Setting `AllowedSignUpEmailDomain` deliberately enables it, restricted to the named email domains and enforced by the `CognitoUserPoolEmailDomainVerifyFunction` PreSignUp/PreAuthentication trigger — anyone holding an address at those domains can then create their own account, so treat the domain list as the trust boundary (it also widens who can reach AUTH.T13). Strong password policy enforcement, MFA option, email verification required, Cognito advanced security features (compromised credential detection).

threats.title: Refresh Token Abuse
threats.description: Cognito refresh tokens have longer lifetime than access tokens and can be used to obtain new access tokens. Stolen refresh tokens provide persistent access
threats.attackVector: Steal refresh token from browser storage or SDK client, use to continuously obtain fresh access tokens
threats.impact: Persistent unauthorized access beyond access token lifetime
threats.affectedComponents: Cognito User Pool, Web UI, SDK/CLI
threats.mitigations: Configurable refresh token expiration: the `RefreshTokenValidityHours` parameter (default 720, 30 days) sets the web UI client's lifetime, and the client is left unmodified at the default (`HasCustomRefreshTokenValidity` in `template.yaml`). Token revocation capabilities, Cognito advanced security (anomaly detection), secure token storage, session monitoring

threats.title: Cross-Tenant Data Access (Multi-Stack)
threats.description: Organizations may deploy one stack per tenant or environment. If users have access to multiple stacks' Cognito pools, they could access data across environments. Several tenants sharing **one** stack is a different boundary, inside the deployment, and is modelled separately as TEN.T01–T05 in [`tenant-isolation.md`](tenant-isolation.md)
threats.attackVector: User with credentials for multiple stacks accesses data from an environment they shouldn't have access to
threats.impact: Cross-environment data access
threats.affectedComponents: Cognito User Pools (per stack), S3 buckets, DynamoDB tables
threats.mitigations: Separate Cognito User Pools per stack (default), IAM resource policies scoped to individual stacks, organizational controls on user provisioning

threats.title: Config-Version Scope Bypass (Fail-Open Scope Lookup)
threats.description: Non-admin users can be restricted to specific named configuration versions via an `allowedConfigVersions` list in the UsersTable. The scope is resolved by reading the caller's UsersTable row, and a lookup written carelessly **fails open** — treats the caller as *unrestricted* — on two distinct paths. (a) If the **lookup key** is derived from a fallback chain (`email` claim, else `identity.username`, else `cognito:username`, else `sub`) put to a single email-keyed index, a substituted identifier does not find the row by another route — it matches **no** row, and an empty page is indistinguishable from "this user has no restriction". Any verified claims set lacking an `email` claim then resolves to *unrestricted*, with **no AWS fault required**. The same arithmetic makes **email itself** an unsafe sole join: an address that diverges from the one on the row (a case difference, an external-IdP attribute remap, a self-service change on a mutable pool) also reads as "no row", and so lifts the restriction with no attacker action at all; and because Cognito does not make `email` unique, two accounts can share an address and so a row. (b) If a **failed query** (a missing `dynamodb:Query` grant, a wrong index name, a throttle) is caught and read the same way, scope enforcement switches itself off precisely on the wiring drift it exists to survive.
threats.attackVector: A config-version-scoped caller invokes a scoped operation (`getConfigVersion`, `getConfigVersions`, the five revision operations, `reprocessDocument`, `syncBdaIdp`, `getStepFunctionExecution`, both document lists, `getDocumentCount`, document chat, class, policy and multi-document discovery, `autoDetectSections`, the test-set operations that take a profile, `sendToReview`, `bulkSkipAllReviews`) for a version outside their allowed set, under verified claims from which the lookup key cannot be derived, or while the scope query is failing. The lookup returns "no restriction" and the request is allowed. Two further routes need no unresolvable caller at all: an operation that checks scope only on a caller-supplied `version` argument (as `reprocessDocument` would if it checked nothing else) acts on any named document when the argument is omitted; and an operation that chooses a profile without checking it (`uploadDocument`, `uploadSampleDocument`, a discovery run naming a target profile) places a document, or a discovered class or rule, into another scoped user's profile. **Config prefix mappings widen that route rather than adding a new threat**, because they introduce a second way to choose a profile which is not the `version` argument at all — the destination key prefix — so a check written against the *request* would miss it; and because an S3 key prefix is now part of what decides the partition, whoever may write a mapping decides which scoped users can see the documents landing under it.
threats.impact: Cross-scope disclosure of configuration (prompts, model settings, pricing) and of documents and their processing detail that a tenant/team was meant to be walled off from; and, for `reprocessDocument`/`syncBdaIdp`, mutation under a profile outside the caller's scope.
threats.affectedComponents: `configuration_resolver`, `reprocess_document_resolver`, `upload_resolver`, `discovery_upload_resolver`, `test_set_resolver`, `process_changes_resolver`, `bulk_review_resolver`, `sync_bda_idp_resolver`, `get_stepfunction_execution_resolver`, `list_documents_gsi_resolver`, `list_documents_range_resolver`, `chat_with_document_processor`, `user_management` (own-profile lookup), the PII-anonymizer feature API, UsersTable `EmailIndex`, `idp_common/config/prefix_mappings.py` and the `ConfigPrefixMap#__index` item on the ConfigurationTable, resolver IAM roles
threats.mitigations: **One fail-closed lookup, shared.** `resolve_allowed_config_versions` in `idp_common/config_scope.py` is the single implementation, and it reads **two disjoint key spaces** on the UsersTable: the immutable Cognito `sub`, via a `SUB#<sub>` pointer item holding the row's `userId`, tried first; and the `email` claim, via the `EmailIndex` GSI, tried second. Each identifier goes only to the key space that indexes it, and neither is a fallback for the other — a `sub` is never put to an email-keyed condition. Preferring the `sub` is what stops a diverged address lifting the restriction. No UsersTable wired / neither key present / any failed read on **either** key space raises `ScopeLookupError`, which every consumer turns into a refusal; so does a caller presenting only a `sub` that no pointer records, because their row may predate the pointer writer and there is no second key to try. The pointer reuses the table's existing `PK`/`SK` key schema rather than adding a GSI, so **no deployment takes a table update** and there is no index-backfill window in which a fail-closed lookup would deny every scoped caller; `dynamodb:GetItem` was already granted to every consumer alongside `Query`. A pointer carries no `email` attribute, so it is absent from `EmailIndex` and cannot be returned by an email query in place of the row. `src/lambda/user_management` is the writer: `createUser` records the `sub` Cognito assigns, `updateUser` writes the pointer when a scope is set and deletes it when one is removed, `deleteUser` deletes it, and the Cognito sync that runs on every Admin `listUsers` records the `sub` and maintains the pointer on each row it can match — which is the workflow an administrator must use to apply a scope at all. That sync matches a Cognito account to its row on the recorded `sub`, then the exact address, then the **case-folded** address, and leaves a row that another account still in the user pool records bound to that account: matching on the exact address alone is what writes a *duplicate* row for a user whose address has changed, and a duplicate carries no scope. **A pointer exists only for a row that carries `allowedConfigVersions`**, which is what makes the preferred leg incapable of *widening* a scope: an unscoped row answers "unrestricted" through either key, so a pointer for one would pin that answer ahead of whatever the email join would have found — including ahead of the scoped row a duplicate was created beside. The reader enforces the same invariant from its side, treating a pointer that resolves an unscoped row as stale and falling back to the email join. **The reader binds the record to the account's Cognito `sub`.** Cognito does not make `email` unique, so the email join reads every row for the address and uses the one recording the caller's `sub`, then one recording none, then any other; a record naming another `sub`, reached by either leg, denies the caller wherever an unscoped caller is denied (strict isolation, `TenantGrantSource` `IdpClaim` or `Api`), and under `Manual` with isolation off its scope is applied, where it can only narrow access. The per-container cache holds the row's raw scope and that flag, so a cached answer is judged against the mode in force at each call. An **empty page still means unrestricted**, deliberately — scoping is opt-in per user, and denying there would lock every ordinary user out. The two document-list resolvers and the two artifacts that ship without an `idp_common` layer (`user_management`, the PII-anonymizer feature API) carry the rule verbatim rather than a variant of it. **Both directions are checked, not just the argument.** `reprocessDocument` resolves the profile each named document was last processed under and refuses any outside the caller's scope, so the control does not stand down when the caller omits `version`; a document whose profile cannot be established (no tracking row, no `ConfigVersion`, a failed read) is refused, and a batch is refused whole rather than part-processed. **`uploadDocument` and `uploadSampleDocument` enforce the same scope, and on the *resolved* profile rather than the requested one** — the only form that covers both routes to choosing a profile, since naming one in upload metadata and choosing a destination prefix a mapping governs are different requests with the same effect. A non-canonical key cannot evade a mapping: `find_match` canonicalizes the object key itself — collapsing leading and repeated slashes and `.` segments — so `finance/x.pdf`, `/finance/x.pdf`, `finance//x.pdf` and `finance/./x.pdf` all resolve to the same mapping, and a `reject` rule on that prefix fires for every spelling. `..` is matched literally rather than resolved, because an S3 key has no parent directory and resolving it would claim a key the bucket serves from elsewhere. The upload site canonicalizes too, which is what makes the stored key agree with the mapping prefix recorded against the document rather than being a second line of defence. **Prefix-mapping CRUD is `Admin` only** (`listConfigPrefixMappings`, `putConfigPrefixMapping`, `deleteConfigPrefixMapping`), which is an authorization decision rather than a convenience one: an Author who could write a mapping could route documents into, or out of, another scoped user's partition, which puts it on the same side of the line as minting a profile rather than editing one's content. The listing is deliberately **not** scope-filtered for the same reason it is Admin-only — a partially-hidden view of a longest-prefix rule cannot tell you which mapping wins. The read-only dry run `resolveConfigPrefixMapping` is open to **Admin and Author** — the two roles that can upload, which is what it serves — and is **scope-filtered over every profile the answer could disclose**, not merely the one it selected: a refusal resolves to no profile while its reason names the mapped one, and metadata precedence resolves to the caller's own in-scope profile while its reason explains that it beat the mapping's, so a guard predicated on the selected profile would leak through both. It withholds the matched **prefix** as well, because the caller supplies a key and the governing prefix is a refinement of it that locates the boundary a probe at a time. **Discovery and test-set operations hold a named profile to the caller's scope.** `discovery_upload_resolver` checks the target profile (`_assert_profile_in_scope`, which with no profile named checks the active one) and the source documents (`_assert_source_in_scope`) for class, policy and multi-document discovery and `autoDetectSections`, and refuses **Replace** on the active profile (`_assert_replace_allowed`); discovered classes and rules are stored as plain text with URLs, images and HTML removed (`idp_common/discovery/discovered_text.py`). `generateDraftLabels`, `reextractTestSetDocument` and `estimateReviewEffort` refuse a named profile outside the caller's scope, as `startTestRun` does. ⚠️ **All of this gates the API, not the bucket:** a principal holding `s3:PutObject` on the Input bucket picks its own prefix and its own `x-amz-meta-config-version` with no API call in the path, which is the bucket-side residual UI.T06 carries; bound it with IAM on whatever writes there. **The class is gated, not just the instances:** `scripts/tests/test_scope_lookup_fail_closed.py` walks every module under `nested/api-resolvers/src/lambda`, `src/lambda` and `feature-platform` that reads the UsersTable — recognised by the **table**, not by an index name, since naming the index wrongly is itself one of the ways this failed, and counting a `get_item` as well as a `query`, because the `sub` key space names no index at all — and fails if any derives a key from another claim, puts one key space's identifier to the other's (rule **SCOPE4**, which is the `SubIndex` shape this threat is named after), or handles a lookup failure with anything but a refusal (including a suppressing context manager, a conditional raise that falls through, and a success-shaped payload). Per-site unit suites assert the three outcomes (no `email` claim denies without querying; a DynamoDB error denies; an empty page stays unrestricted). Static check **S4** of `make api-test-static` reads only the code an operation can *reach* — its dispatch branch bodies and their call closure — so a declaration the reachable code does not honour fails; check **S10** fails when an operation whose arguments name a profile, a document or a session declares no scope for it (`scope_checked`, `scope_filtered`, `document_scope_checked`, `testset_checked` or `ownership`). Every scope-enforcing resolver holds `dynamodb:Query`/`GetItem` on the UsersTable and its `/index/*`; a failed lookup is logged at ERROR and denies. The **live scope suite in `make api-test`** seeds a scoped user and asserts an out-of-scope version is denied and that Admins are unaffected. **Residual:** (1) the `sub` join closes the email-divergence route only for a row that **records** a `sub`, and the back-fill cannot reach every row. It matches on the recorded `sub`, the exact address, or the case-folded address, so a user whose address was re-mapped or changed *beyond case* before this code ever ran matches none of them: the sync writes them a fresh unscoped row, as it always has, and their original scoped row keeps the email-only exposure indefinitely. (The scoped-rows-only pointer invariant keeps that from widening anything — the duplicate gets no pointer, so correcting the address still restores the scope.) The back-fill also runs only when an Admin opens User Management. `docs/rbac.md` carries a one-line `attribute_not_exists(cognitoSub)` scan that lists the rows still in that state, which is the only way to find them. Neither the writer, the back-fill nor the two-key read has been exercised against a live deployment — every statement about them is inferred from the code and from moto-backed suites; (2) nothing asserts at the adapter which *kind* of Cognito token produced the claims, so which token types can reach these operations is a property of the API Gateway authorizer configuration rather than of this code. **Measured on a live deployment 2026-09-20: an access token is refused.** The `COGNITO_USER_POOLS` authorizer on `POST /op/{field}` declares no `authorizationScopes`, and a Cognito **access** token — which decodes cleanly and even carries `cognito:groups` — is rejected **401 at the gateway, before any Lambda runs**, while the ID token from the same session succeeds. So the substituted-identifier path this residual describes is not reachable by presenting an access token to this API. It remains a property of the authorizer rather than of the code, so a future authorizer change could reopen it, and nothing in the tree asserts the token type; (3) the class gate checks **key provenance and failure handling only** — it has no rule about the *matcher*, so a divergent `scope_allows` restatement in an artifact that ships without the shared layer would not be caught (only the two byte-identical vendored copies are held to the letter, by a file-comparison test), and `lib/idp_common_pkg` is outside its scan roots, which leaves `idp_common/testset_scope.py` — a further `EmailIndex` consumer, for the independent `allowedTestSets` axis — unpoliced; its polarity is inverted, so the shapes are not live there; (4) one consumer the gate discovers is **suppressed** rather than enforced: `idp_common/testset_scope.py`, which resolves the independent `allowedTestSets` axis from the same `EmailIndex` with an `or`-chain key and a caught query failure — both shapes this gate exists to forbid. Its polarity is inverted (`assert_can_access_test_set` requires an *explicit* scope, so an unresolvable Annotator is denied), which makes those shapes an availability defect rather than one that widens access, and it has no `sub` join at all, so an Annotator whose address diverges is locked out of their queue. It is carried in `PENDING_FIX` with its two rules named, so any *other* rule firing on it still fails the gate and `test_the_pending_exemption_is_still_needed` deletes the entry the moment those two stop firing.

threats.title: Silently-Ignored Schema Authorization Directives
threats.description: The GraphQL schema carries authorization directives (`@aws_cognito_user_pools(...)`, and the `@aws_auth(cognito_groups: [...])` form that a multi-auth API **silently ignores**), and nothing enforces either at runtime: the REST dispatcher fronts the resolvers and reads the schema only for input-shape validation. A developer who relies on a schema directive alone — without a server-side check in the resolver — ships an unprotected operation that *looks* protected in the schema.
threats.attackVector: Add/keep an operation whose only "protection" is a schema directive; a low-privilege caller invokes `POST /op/{field}` and is authorized because no resolver-side check runs.
threats.impact: Operations appear group-restricted but are open to any authenticated user.
threats.mitigations: Server-side group checks are the source of truth; schema directives carry no enforcement. Since the dispatcher **denies by default** (AUTH.T03), an operation protected by a directive alone is not open: with no entry in the generated required-groups manifest it is refused for every caller, so the failure mode is a visible 403 rather than a silent bypass. The **static scan in `make api-test-static`** flags `@aws_auth`-only / directive-vs-code drift and fails when an operation lacks a documented server-side check; new operations must add a resolver check plus an expectations entry. The feature-platform ops declare `@aws_cognito_user_pools(cognito_groups:["Admin"])` matching their resolver enforcement, so no operation relies on `@aws_auth`.

threats.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR / BOLA)
threats.description: User-owned resources (chat sessions, agent jobs) are addressed by an id supplied in the request. If a resolver keys the record by the supplied id alone — without also constraining to the caller's own identity — one authenticated user (User B) can read or modify another user's (User A's) data by guessing/replaying the id. This is the "broken object-level authorization" class the RBAC group matrix does NOT catch (both users are the same *role*).
threats.attackVector: User B calls `getChatMessages`/`deleteChatSession`/`sendAgentChatMessage`/`sendChatDocumentMessage`/`getAgentJobStatus`/`deleteAgentJob`, or a chat streaming route, with User A's `sessionId`/`jobId`; or a Reviewer calls `getBulkReviewJob`/`cancelBulkReviewJob`/`deleteBulkReviewJob` with another user's `jobId`.
threats.impact: Cross-user disclosure, extension or destruction of chat history, agent conversation memory or job data within the same deployment.
threats.mitigations: Ownership is enforced by construction where the key allows it (agent-job ops derive the DynamoDB partition key from the caller identity, so a foreign id resolves under the caller's own empty partition; `listChatSessions` reads the caller's own partition). For chat, whose messages are keyed by session id alone, `ChatSessionOwnersTable` records each session id's owner — the Cognito `sub` from verified claims — with a conditional write, so the first user of an id owns it (`idp_common/chat_session_owner.py`, vendored byte-identical into the resolvers without the layer). Every path that writes a turn (both REST send operations and both streaming routes) registers or checks the owner before any processing; `getChatMessages` and `deleteChatSession` check it and never register a fresh id; a session written before the registry is claimed only by the caller holding older evidence of using it. Agent conversation memory is keyed on the verified `sub`. `getChatMessages`'s check is on by default (`ENFORCE_CHAT_SESSION_OWNERSHIP`) and denies when its tables are unconfigured. Bulk review jobs are readable and changeable only by their requester (`RequesterKey` from verified claims) or an Admin; another user's job reads as not found. The **live IDOR suite in `make api-test`** seeds a session owned by User A and asserts User B is denied/empty for that id while the owner retains access — catching a regression that dropped the ownership check.

threats.title: Token Lifecycle — Post-Logout Token Reuse (Stateless JWT)
threats.description: Cognito ID/access tokens are stateless JWTs validated by the API Gateway authorizer against signature + `exp`. A global sign-out (`admin-user-global-sign-out`) revokes **refresh** tokens, but a still-valid **access/ID** token continues to be accepted until it expires unless the API additionally checks token revocation. So a token captured before logout remains usable for the remainder of its lifetime.
threats.attackVector: An attacker who captured a valid token continues calling `POST /op/{field}` after the user logs out, until the token's `exp`.
threats.impact: Session does not truly end at logout; a leaked token is usable for up to its (short) TTL after sign-out.
threats.affectedComponents: Cognito User Pool app client, API Gateway Cognito authorizer
threats.mitigations: Keep token TTL short (the web UI client sets 1-hour ID and access token validity, with token revocation enabled) so the post-logout window is bounded; expired tokens ARE rejected (verified by the token-negative + expiry suites in `make api-test`). The **logout suite in `make api-test`** performs a global sign-out and re-tests the token, surfacing continued acceptance as a documented gap (**GAP-SEC-LOGOUT**, WARN) so the accepted-risk is visible. Full revocation would require an authorizer-side revocation check (Cognito token revocation / a deny-list) — tracked as a follow-up, not yet implemented.

threats.title: Weak Transport Security (TLS downgrade / cleartext)
threats.description: If the API endpoint negotiates obsolete TLS (1.0/1.1) or answers over plaintext HTTP, tokens and document data in transit are exposed to downgrade/interception attacks.
threats.attackVector: A man-in-the-middle forces a TLS 1.0/1.1 handshake or intercepts a cleartext request.
threats.impact: Disclosure/tampering of bearer tokens and document content in transit.
threats.affectedComponents: API Gateway (execute-api) domain / CloudFront distribution TLS policy
threats.mitigations: API Gateway `execute-api` enforces TLS 1.2+ and does not serve on port 80; CloudFront uses a TLS 1.2+ minimum-protocol security policy. The **TLS suite in `make api-test`** actively attempts TLS 1.0/1.1 handshakes and a plaintext HTTP request against the live endpoint and asserts they are refused while TLS 1.2 succeeds.

threats.title: Missing Input-Shape Validation (Type Confusion via Lost Schema Validation)
threats.description: The REST dispatcher receives `event["arguments"]` as arbitrary JSON. Without validation against the schema, a caller can send an object/array where a scalar is expected, an unknown argument, or omit a required one — reaching resolver code that indexes into the shape untyped. Depending on the resolver that means silent acceptance or an uncaught 500, and a wider surface for type-confusion / NoSQL-style injection payloads flowing into DynamoDB expressions or LLM prompts.
threats.attackVector: A caller posts `POST /op/{field}` with a malformed `arguments` object (e.g. `{"ObjectKey": {"$ne": null}}` where a `String!` is expected) that the resolver was not written to defend against.
threats.impact: Type-confusion / unexpected-shape handling in resolvers; denial of service via uncaught 500s; loss of the boundary that constrained input before business logic.
threats.mitigations: **Central schema-shape validation in the dispatcher** (`validation.py` + build-time `api_validation_spec.json` generated from `schema.graphql`) rejects unknown args, missing non-null args, wrong scalar types, and bad enum values with HTTP 400 before routing, for every operation at once. The validator is conservative (type-only, shallow input-objects) and fails open on its own errors so it can't 500 the API. A drift guard (`generate_api_validation_spec.py --check` + unit test) keeps the spec in sync with the schema. The **input-validation suite in `make api-test`** exercises malformed payloads per op (strict mode asserts a clean 4xx).

threats.title: Group Assignment From a User-Writable Attribute (External IdP Mapping)
threats.description: With external IdP federation and `ExternalIdPGroupAttributeName` configured, Cognito maps the IdP's group claim onto the `custom:idp_groups` User Pool attribute, and the `ExternalIdPGroupMappingFunction` pre-token-generation trigger turns that attribute into Cognito group membership — including `Admin`. The attribute is `Mutable: true`, and because Cognito applies IdP attribute mapping *as the app client*, a mapped attribute must also be writable by that client. Nothing in the stored value records which principal wrote it, so a trigger that reads it without establishing provenance treats a value of any origin as the IdP's assertion.
threats.attackVector: A low-privilege user of the pool (or, where `AllowedSignUpEmailDomain` permits self-registration, anyone with an address at an allowed domain) writes the group value corresponding to `ExternalIdPAdminGroupName` to their own attribute, then obtains a fresh token so the trigger reads it.
threats.impact: Application Admin: configuration and user management, and every configuration version. The trigger writes group membership with `AdminAddUserToGroup`, so the effect outlives the attribute value that caused it.
threats.likelihood: Low (requires federation *and* group mapping to be configured, and knowledge of the deployment-specific admin group string)
threats.affectedComponents: `ExternalIdPGroupMappingFunction` (inline handler in `template.yaml`; standalone copy `src/lambda/external_idp_group_mapping/index.py`), `UserPool` schema (`idp_groups`), `UserPoolClient` attribute permissions
threats.mitigations: **Provenance:** the trigger reads the Cognito-managed `identities` attribute via `AdminGetUser` — a field no client can write — and honours `custom:idp_groups` only for a user linked to the provider named by `EXTERNAL_IDP_NAME`. A native user who writes the attribute themselves gains nothing. **Freshness:** only fresh sign-in trigger sources are honoured, never `TokenGeneration_RefreshTokens`, so a value written after sign-in cannot be picked up by refreshing; at a fresh federated sign-in Cognito has just rewritten the attribute from the assertion. Both checks fail closed. **Attribute permissions:** `UserPoolClient` now declares an explicit `WriteAttributes` naming only the IdP-mapped attributes, so every other attribute is read-only to end users (an attempt returns `NotAuthorizedException`). `scripts/sdlc/tests/test_userpool_attribute_permissions.py` pins that list between its two failure modes. **Tests:** `src/lambda/external_idp_group_mapping/test_index.py` asserts that a user-written attribute and a token refresh both grant nothing, and re-runs those assertions against the InlineCode copy extracted from `template.yaml` so the deployed handler cannot drift from the tested one. `scripts/security/live_checks/verify_idp_group_mapping.py` runs the same scenarios against a real pool, provider and federated identity. **Residual:** a user already federated through the trusted provider can self-set the attribute, and if their IdP omits the group claim on a later fresh sign-in Cognito may leave that value in place — assert the group attribute for all federated users in the IdP (documented in `docs/external-idp.md`).

threats.title: Alternate Entry Path Bypassing an Operation's Group Check (Streaming Function URL)
threats.description: Agent Chat and Chat-with-Document are reachable by **two** entry paths. Besides `POST /op/sendAgentChatMessage` and `POST /op/sendChatDocumentMessage` on the REST dispatcher, token deltas are streamed from a Lambda **Function URL** (`AuthType=AWS_IAM`, `InvokeMode=RESPONSE_STREAM`) whose FastAPI app (`chat_stream_processor`) drives `agent_chat_processor` and `chat_with_document_processor` directly, without passing through the dispatcher or the resolvers. IAM authentication of that transport proves only that the caller holds the Identity Pool's authenticated role, which carries no Cognito group. An operation whose group, scope or ownership check lives only in the resolver is therefore enforced on one path and not the other, and a route that takes the caller's identity from the request body lets the client decide whose session and history a turn is written against.
threats.attackVector: An authenticated principal invokes a streaming route for an operation whose group restriction is implemented only in the resolver; supplies a caller identity in the request body that differs from the verified one; or names another user's session id.
threats.impact: The Agent Chat group restriction (Admin/Author/Viewer; Reviewer excluded), the `ANY_GROUP` floor on document chat, the Chat-with-Document profile scope or session ownership not applied on the streaming path, and chat history or memory keyed to an identity other than the verified caller.
threats.likelihood: Low (both paths require an authenticated principal of this deployment's pool; the streaming path additionally requires `lambda:InvokeFunction` on the URL, granted to the authenticated Identity Pool role)
threats.mitigations: **The transport carries verified claims.** The browser sends its Cognito ID token in `x-idp-id-token`, and both routes verify it (`_verified_caller`) and answer 401 without a valid one; nothing identity-like is read from the request body, and a body `callerSub` is ignored. **Checks in the route, before the response is committed.** `/chat/agent` applies the Agent Chat groups, and the Admin-only rule under tenant isolation, synchronously (`_enforce_groups_or_403`); `/chat/document` applies the `ANY_GROUP` floor (`_require_a_group_or_403`); both register or check the session id against its owner in `ChatSessionOwnersTable` (`_claim_session_or_403`) before the stream opens, so a refusal is an HTTP 403 rather than an error frame on a 200. **Enforcement at the worker as well.** `agent_chat_processor` applies the same group check before any agent or Bedrock call, outside its error-to-stream conversion, on the group claim either path forwards, and keys conversation memory on the verified `sub`; `chat_with_document_processor` applies the `allowedConfigVersions` scope from the verified email and `sub`. A unit test plus a both-directions static check assert that the resolver's and the processor's group lists cannot drift apart. **Input shape:** both routes declare Pydantic request models, so a malformed body is rejected with a 422 and every string the processors consume is length-bounded. **Coverage:** `make api-test-static` checks S6–S9 discover every `AWS::Lambda::Url` and its routes from the template, require each route to be declared in `scripts/api_rbac_expectations.yaml` with its authorization, and fail when a route prefers a client-supplied identity, omits the conflict refusal, or reaches a handler with no group check; a test drives the scanner over a defective fixture tree, and an unrecognised policy key is a hard failure. Under tenant isolation or an external `TenantGrantSource` the web UI is built without the stream URL (`DeniesUnscopedCaller`) and uses the REST path; the transport exists in the commercial partition only, and on GovCloud the UI uses the REST dispatcher plus polling.

threats.title: Authentication Material in Resolver Logs (Name-Based Redaction Denylist)
threats.description: `idp_common.utils.log_sanitizer` holds the canonical denylist of key substrings whose values must never be written to logs (credential, token, key and password spellings). Resolvers log request payloads and DynamoDB items through it, so whether a credential-shaped value reaches CloudWatch Logs depends on that one list naming the key it arrives under. A resolver carrying its own hand-copied subset of that list can fall behind it — missing, say, the underscore and concatenated forms of access key, secret key and private key, `passwd` or the API-key header name — and log a payload carrying one of those keys with its value intact (issue #921).
threats.attackVector: Not an attack step so much as an exposure: any operation whose logged payload contains one of the missed key spellings writes the value to its log group, where it persists for the retention period.
threats.impact: Credential or token material readable by principals granted CloudWatch Logs access, which is a broader and less-reviewed population than the operation's own group allow-list.
threats.affectedComponents: `lib/idp_common_pkg/idp_common/utils/log_sanitizer.py`, the byte-identical copies vendored into the resolver Lambdas that carry no `idp_common` layer, every resolver that logs its event, CloudWatch Logs
threats.mitigations: **One denylist.** Every resolver under `nested/api-resolvers/src/lambda/` calls the canonical `sanitize_event_for_logging`: those with an `idp_common` layer import it, and the eight without one carry a byte-identical copy synced by `scripts/sync_resolver_log_sanitizer.sh`. `scripts/tests/test_resolver_log_sanitizer.py` fails if a copy differs, if the effective denylist differs from the canonical one, or if any file in that tree defines a local key list again; the same rule now covers the logged invocation events under `src/lambda`. Adding a key to the canonical list therefore protects every resolver. **Log storage.** Log groups are retention-bounded, and every log group declared across `template.yaml`, `nested/api-resolvers/template.yaml` and `patterns/unified/template.yaml` except two sets `KmsKeyId` to the stack's customer-managed key, including `HttpApiDispatcherLogGroup`, the group every UI API request passes through. The two that do not are the `StacknameCheckFunction` and `ReadPreviousIDPPatternFunction` custom-resource groups, which handle no request data and carry a recorded `cfn_nag`/`checkov` suppression. `scripts/tests/test_log_group_encryption.py` fails if any log group in these templates drops `KmsKeyId` or `RetentionInDays`, including through an `Fn::If` branch that resolves to `AWS::NoValue`. The optional feature-platform, sample hook and scaffolding stacks declare further log groups without `KmsKeyId`, tracked in **issue #972**.
threats.residualRisk: The denylist matches key **names**, not values: a token carried in free text, or under a key the list does not name, is logged as it is. Two custom-resource log groups use the default log-group encryption rather than the stack key.

threats.title: Per-Object Authorization Is Opt-In Per Resolver (Default Deny Covers the Group Floor Only)
threats.description: AUTH.T03 covers a resolver whose group check is *wrong*. This covers the structural reason that is easy to do: beyond the field-level group floor, nothing requires a check to exist. The dispatcher now **denies by default** — `http_api_dispatcher/authz.py` refuses any field with no entry in the generated `api_rbac_manifest.json`, so an operation whose groups were never declared is closed — but that floor decides only *which groups may call an operation*. Every narrower decision is still hand-written inside the resolver that does the work: the configuration-profile scope (`allowedConfigVersions`), the test-set scope (`allowedTestSets`), session and job ownership, review-queue eligibility and assignee-only writes (HITL.T02), and bulk-job requester checks (HITL.T05). A resolver that omits one of those is reachable by every caller the floor admits, and it fails *open*. The shape to watch for is several operations sharing one group policy, such as `[Admin, Reviewer, Annotator]`, where one of them is given the group list without the per-object half, so a scoped Annotator is confined by nothing but the floor. Eight operations are declared `ANY`, where the floor checks authentication only and the resolver is the whole check. Separately, whether a resolver's denial becomes an HTTP 403 still depends partly on **message text**: the dispatcher maps `PermissionError`/`AuthorizationError` by class name *or* a message beginning `Unauthorized`/`Forbidden` (`index.py`), so a reworded denial raised as a bare `Exception` becomes a 500.
threats.attackVector: A caller holding a group the floor admits invokes `POST /op/{field}` naming an object outside their scope — another profile's document, another test set, another user's session, a queue they are not eligible for — on an operation whose resolver was shipped without that object's check. No UI path is involved.
threats.impact: A missing per-object check exposes, to every caller the operation's group list admits, the objects the scope or ownership rule was meant to confine; for an `ANY` operation, to every authenticated caller including one in no group.
threats.likelihood: Medium (the failure mode is omission during development, not an attack step, and it has recurred)
threats.mitigations: **Default deny at the dispatcher** (`authz.py`, from `api_rbac_manifest.json`, generated from `scripts/api_rbac_expectations.yaml` and failing closed when unreadable): an undeclared operation is refused with 403 and the message does not distinguish an unknown field from an undeclared one. **The manifest-plus-scan pair** declares the required groups for all 181 operations, and `make api-test-static` (both CI systems) fails when an operation drifts from the manifest or its `enforced_in` file carries no enforcement pattern — including, for an operation declared `scope_checked` or `scope_filtered`, no scope check in the code that operation's dispatch branch can reach. Check **S10** works in the other direction: an operation whose arguments name a configuration profile, a stored object or a session (decided by the words of the argument's name) must declare how that object is scoped — `scope_checked`/`scope_filtered`, `document_scope_checked`, `testset_checked` or `ownership` — and S10 then requires the matching entry point in the code it reaches; an op callable only by Admin or IAM needs none. MCP tools are held to the same table by checks M1–M5, which fail when a tool admits a role its equivalent REST operation does not. `make api-test` re-tests the matrix live with one user per group, and `object_scoped_roles` lets a cell assert a refusal that the group floor did **not** produce (`authzControl` ≠ `api-group-floor`), which is the only automated assertion that a per-object control exists rather than that the floor is right. Every 403 carries `errors[0].authzControl` (`api-group-floor`, `resource`, `resolver`, `unverified-identity`), so a per-object refusal is distinguishable in telemetry from a group refusal. An unexpected error answers a generic 500 `InternalError` with a request id and logs the detail server-side, so a reworded denial that falls through to 500 returns no internal text to the caller.
threats.residualRisk: **Per-object checks are not enforced by construction.** The static scan verifies that an enforcement *pattern* exists in a named file — for scope, one reachable from the operation's dispatch branch; for a declared `ownership`, an owner check that can refuse — but it cannot verify that the check matches the right object; S10 decides which operations must declare a scope from argument names, so an operation that reads scoped objects without naming one in its arguments is outside it; and the scan has no rule at all for review-queue eligibility. The live harness asserts a per-object refusal only for operations carrying `object_scoped_roles`. The message-prefix arm of the 403 mapping remains, so a denial raised as a bare `Exception` with reworded text becomes a 500 (now generic, so the effect is a lost 403 in denial telemetry rather than a disclosure). The eight `ANY` operations each carry a reason bounded to that operation in the expectations file.

threats.title: BDA Service Opacity
threats.description: BDA is a managed service with limited visibility into internal processing. Unlike Pipeline mode, customers cannot inspect intermediate OCR results, model prompts, or processing logic
threats.attackVector: Not directly exploitable; represents a visibility/auditability gap
threats.impact: Difficulty diagnosing processing errors, limited ability to detect adversarial document manipulation, reduced forensic capability
threats.mitigations: BDA output validation, comparison with Pipeline mode results for critical documents, evaluation framework, CloudWatch metrics monitoring

threats.title: BDA Output Format Mapping Errors
threats.description: The normalization layer that maps BDA output to standard pipeline format could introduce data loss, misrepresentation, or injection if BDA returns unexpected output structures
threats.attackVector: BDA returns malformed or unexpected output that exploits mapping logic
threats.impact: Data corruption in downstream processing, incorrect extraction results passed to shared tail
threats.mitigations: Strict output schema validation after mapping, defensive parsing, error handling with fallback to error state

threats.title: BDA Project Configuration Tampering
threats.description: Modification of BDA project configuration (blueprints, extraction schemas) could alter processing behavior for all BDA-mode documents. Historically amplified by project sharing: before v0.6.1 the BDA-as-OCR project was account-global under a hardcoded name, so a change made by (or a compromise of) **any** stack in the account altered every other stack's processing — a cross-stack tampering path that bypassed per-stack RBAC entirely.
threats.attackVector: Compromised admin account or direct AWS API access to modify BDA project settings
threats.impact: Systematic misprocessing of documents, data extraction to wrong schemas
threats.affectedComponents: Amazon BDA project, BDA Invoke Lambda
threats.mitigations: IAM policies restricting BDA project modification, RBAC (Admin only), CloudTrail logging of BDA API calls, BDA project versioning. **Per-stack project isolation (v0.6.1)**: the BDA-as-OCR project is now a stack-owned `Custom::BDAOCRProject` resource named `<stackname>_OCR_StdOutput`, created and deleted with the stack, so tampering is confined to the stack whose IAM boundary the actor already holds — cross-stack interference via a shared account-global project is eliminated.

threats.title: BDA Service Availability
threats.description: BDA service throttling, outage, or quota exhaustion stops all document processing when in BDA mode
threats.attackVector: Volume-based attacks exceeding BDA service limits, regional service disruption
threats.impact: Complete processing stoppage for BDA-mode deployments
threats.mitigations: SQS retry with DLQ, CloudWatch alarms on BDA errors, capacity planning, ability to switch to Pipeline mode via configuration

threats.title: S3 Cross-Access via BDA
threats.description: BDA reads documents directly from S3 using service-linked roles. Misconfigured S3 bucket policies could allow BDA to access unintended objects
threats.attackVector: Overly permissive S3 bucket policies or IAM roles granting BDA access beyond intended scope
threats.impact: BDA processes unintended documents, potential data exposure
threats.affectedComponents: S3 Input Bucket, BDA service IAM role
threats.mitigations: Scoped S3 bucket policies, prefix-based access restrictions, IAM policy condition keys limiting BDA access

threats.title: Prompt Injection via Chat Messages
threats.description: User chat messages, and document text in Chat-with-Document, are included directly in prompts to Bedrock models. Malicious content could manipulate the model's behavior, override system instructions, trigger unintended tool calls, or shape a response that leaks data when the browser renders it
threats.attackVector: User sends messages containing prompt injection payloads (e.g., "Ignore previous instructions and..."), or chats with a document whose text carries one
threats.impact: System prompt bypass, unauthorized tool invocation, data exfiltration via model response
threats.affectedComponents: Chat Stream Processor, Agent Chat Processor, Chat-with-Document processor, Amazon Bedrock, web UI markdown rendering
threats.mitigations: When the stack is deployed with `BedrockGuardrailId`, `GUARDRAIL_ID_AND_VERSION` is set on every Lambda that invokes a model and the guardrail is applied to the agents' Strands models (`strands_guardrail_kwargs` in `idp_common/agents/common/strands_bedrock_model.py`), to Chat-with-Document's direct `converse_stream` call (`guardrail_config_from_env` in `idp_common/bedrock/guardrail.py`), and to `BedrockClient` calls. Tool-level authorization bounds what an injected instruction can reach: the analytics tools check every statement and every piece of Python (AGT.T01, AGT.T02), opt-in external agents are absent from sessions holding data results (AGT.T06), and the Agent Chat group check applies on both transports. Model output reaches the page only through `SafeMarkdown`, whose policy (`src/ui/src/components/common/safe-markdown-policy.ts`) loads images only from the app's own origins, shows any other image as a link and drops embedded `<style>` blocks, and the web UI's content policy names specific sources for every fetch directive
threats.residualRisk: The guardrail applies only when `BedrockGuardrailId` is set, and OpenAI GPT-5.x models reached through the Responses route do not receive it (a warning is logged). Neither a guardrail nor the tool checks can establish that a model ignored an injected instruction.

threats.title: Conversation Session Hijacking
threats.description: Session ids are chosen by the browser and arrive in the request body, and `ChatMessagesTable` is keyed by session id alone. If a session id were not bound to its owner, a user who learned or guessed another user's id could read, add to or delete that conversation
threats.attackVector: Call `getAgentChatMessages`, `deleteAgentChatSession`, `sendAgentChatMessage` or `sendChatDocumentMessage` with another user's `sessionId`
threats.impact: Access to another user's chat history, including potentially sensitive document-related queries and agent responses; misattributed turns in their conversation
threats.mitigations: UUID session ids. Every path that writes a turn registers the session id to the caller's Cognito `sub` in `ChatSessionOwnersTable` with a conditional write before it stores anything, and refuses an id another user owns (`claim_chat_session`, vendored into each resolver as `chat_session_owner.py` and kept identical by a test). `getChatMessages` and `deleteChatSession` accept only the recorded owner and never register a fresh id, so asking about an unused id cannot reserve it; a `ChatSessionsTable` row the caller holds counts only for an id nobody owns yet that has history from before the registry. The checks fail closed: an unconfigured owner table or a DynamoDB error denies. A signed-in caller cannot store an assistant-method message. The streaming routes apply the same registry (CHAT.T03). See AUTH.T09
threats.residualRisk: Deleting a session from the list does not remove its owner row or its memory, which expire with `DataRetentionInDays`; this keeps the id bound to its owner for that period.

threats.title: Chat Streaming Function URL — Missing Group and Session-Ownership Enforcement
threats.description: The UI's default chat transport is a **public Lambda Function URL** (`ChatStreamProcessorUrl`, `AuthType=AWS_IAM`, `InvokeMode=RESPONSE_STREAM`) that the browser calls directly with SigV4 credentials from the Cognito Identity Pool. It does not traverse API Gateway, the Cognito authorizer, the WAF or the `http_api_dispatcher`, so every authorization decision on it has to be made in the function. IAM alone cannot make them: `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` is granted to `CognitoAuthorizedRole`, the single authenticated role shared by every Cognito group, and the transport forwards no Cognito claims. Without checks in the function, a Reviewer could use Agent Chat, a caller in no group could use Chat-with-Document, a scoped caller could chat with a document outside their profiles, and a caller supplying another user's `sessionId` could have that user's memory loaded into the stream
threats.attackVector: An authenticated user (any group) obtains Identity Pool credentials — the SPA does this normally — and `POST`s a SigV4-signed request to the Function URL with another user's `sessionId`, from a group the REST path refuses, or for a document outside their profile scope
threats.impact: Cross-user disclosure of chat conversation content (which may quote document contents, PII, and analytics results); use of the agent fleet — including Athena and AgentCore tool access — by a role that policy excludes from Agent Chat
threats.likelihood: Medium (requires an authenticated account and a target `sessionId`; the SPA already mints the necessary credentials, and `sessionId`s are exposed to their owner)
threats.mitigations: **Authentication is enforced**: `AuthType=AWS_IAM` means an unauthenticated or non-SigV4 request is rejected by Lambda before any code runs. **Every chat route also verifies the caller's Cognito ID token**, which the browser sends in the `x-idp-id-token` header: `_verified_caller` calls `idp_common.cognito_id_token.verify_id_token`, which checks the signature against the user pool's key set, the issuer, the web UI's app client as audience, `token_use` and expiry, and the route answers 401 without a valid token. **Groups are enforced from the verified claims** before the stream opens: `/chat/agent` applies the Admin/Author/Viewer check (and Admin-only under tenant isolation) via `_enforce_groups_or_403`, and `/chat/document` refuses a caller in no group (`_require_a_group_or_403`). **Session ownership is enforced**: `_claim_session_or_403` registers the session id to the caller's verified `sub` in `ChatSessionOwnersTable`, or answers 403 when another user owns it, and fails closed; the agent processor checks again before it builds the orchestrator, and memory is keyed `conversation#<sub>#<sessionId>`. **Profile scope applies to Chat-with-Document**: the route forwards the verified `email` and `sub`, and the processor's `allowedConfigVersions` check runs as on the REST path. Every refusal is raised before `StreamingResponse` is returned, so it is a real HTTP status. CORS is safe (`AllowCredentials: false`, no cookies). Chat tables are KMS-encrypted with TTL
threats.residualRisk: The `make api-test` cells for this transport (`run_chat_session_idor_suite` in `scripts/api_security_cases.py`) are tested offline; no live run against a deployment is cited here. WAF and API Gateway throttling do not cover the Function URL (CHAT.T05).

threats.title: Conversation History Data Exposure
threats.description: Conversation history and agent memory persisted in DynamoDB may contain sensitive information from document analysis, including PII, financial data, or classified content discussed in agent interactions
threats.attackVector: Direct DynamoDB access via compromised credentials, or backup/export of conversation data
