threats.impact: Exposure of sensitive business data discussed in chat sessions
threats.mitigations: Every chat table is encrypted with the stack's customer-managed KMS key (`SSEType: KMS`). Messages, session rows and memory items carry `ExpiresAfter` at `DataRetentionInDays`; memory past its expiry is skipped on load before DynamoDB deletes it, and the owner row's expiry is kept past the messages it governs. Memory is keyed per user (`conversation#<sub>#<sessionId>`). Users have no direct DynamoDB access; the tables are reached only through the chat functions and resolvers
threats.residualRisk: Point-in-time recovery is enabled on these tables, so a restore can bring back items for up to the recovery window after their TTL deletion. IAM scope of each function on these tables is not re-measured here.

threats.title: Streaming Response Denial of Service
threats.description: Long-running agent conversations with complex tool use chains could consume excessive Lambda execution time and Bedrock tokens, impacting system availability and cost
threats.attackVector: Repeatedly submit complex queries that trigger expensive agent operations (multi-tool chains, large Athena queries, Quick Start document generation)
threats.impact: Lambda concurrency exhaustion, elevated Bedrock costs, degraded system performance
threats.affectedComponents: Chat Stream Processor, Agent Chat Processor, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Athena
threats.mitigations: Lambda timeout limits (`ChatStreamProcessorFunction` 900 s, `AgentChatProcessorFunction` 600 s), per-request Bedrock token limits, conversation history bounded by `MAX_CONVERSATION_TURNS` and context trimmed by `DropAndSlideConversationManager`, Pydantic length limits on the streaming request fields (`prompt` up to 100,000 characters). The REST path is covered by API Gateway stage throttling and, when enabled, the WAF
threats.residualRisk: Rate limiting on the **streaming transport** is weaker than on the REST transport: a Function URL has no API Gateway stage throttling and is **not** covered by the WebACL, which is associated with the REST API stage only. The chat functions declare no reserved concurrency, so the account's regional Lambda concurrency is the effective bound, shared with the rest of the stack. Cost-amplification abuse via `/chat/agent` is therefore cheaper to mount than via `/op`.

threats.title: Client-Supplied Caller Identity on the Agent Streaming Route
threats.description: On the streaming transport the only identity signals are the request body, which the client controls, and the SigV4 request context, which names the assumed role and its session name. Under the Cognito Identity Pool enhanced flow that session name is chosen by Cognito and is the same for every user of the pool (measured as the literal `CognitoIdentityCredentials` in every CloudTrail `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` record of a reference deployment; AWS publishes no commitment to that string), and Function URLs do not populate `requestContext.authorizer.iam.cognitoIdentity`. A route that took its caller from either signal would accept a caller-chosen identity, or one that does not distinguish users, as the key for session lists, ownership and memory
threats.attackVector: `POST /chat/agent` with `{"sessionId": "...", "prompt": "...", "callerSub": "<another-users-sub>"}`, or any other identity-like body field
threats.impact: Turns written into another user's session list, ownership and memory decisions made on the wrong principal, and log records naming the wrong user
threats.mitigations: Neither route reads an identity from the request body or from the SigV4 context: the Pydantic request models declare no identity field, so a `callerSub` sent by an older UI build is an unknown key and is dropped, and every identity the routes use comes from the verified ID token (`_verified_caller`). The session list is filed under the token's `email` (then `cognito:username`, then `sub`), the same value the REST resolvers use, and ownership and memory under its `sub`. Only the groups, `email` and `sub` claims are forwarded to the processors
threats.residualRisk: None identified beyond CHAT.T03's. The route-level identity checks are also asserted structurally by the static scan (`scripts/sdlc/scan_api_rbac.py`). This transport is commercial-partition only; GovCloud uses the REST path, where the Cognito authorizer supplies the verified subject.

threats.title: Feature UI Bundle Executes Unsandboxed in the Host Origin
threats.stride: Tampering, Information Disclosure, Elevation of Privilege
threats.description: An installed feature's `ui-bundle.js` is loaded via `document.createElement('script')` from the **host's own origin** and executes with the full privileges of the host SPA in the visiting user's browser. It is not isolated by an iframe, a worker, a separate origin, or CSP: both hosting modes send a policy with `default-src 'self'` and `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/` (UI.T07), and the bundle is same-origin, so `'self'` admits it regardless of how narrow the other directives are. The bundle can read the DOM and any in-memory/session-storage tokens, call `POST /op/{field}` as the user via the host-provided `IdpFeatureHost.generateClient`, and reach any origin the CSP `connect-src` allows. Installing a feature therefore grants that feature's code the **effective privilege of every user who loads the UI**, including Admins.
threats.attackVector: (a) A malicious or backdoored third-party feature is installed by an Admin who evaluated its *documented* behavior, not its bundle contents. (b) A legitimate feature's build/supply chain is compromised upstream, and the published bundle differs from what was reviewed. (c) An attacker who obtains write access to the feature's prefix in the Web UI bucket (or to the ui-deployer's role) replaces the bundle.
threats.impact: Full compromise of the Web UI session for every user: exfiltration of document content and extracted PII via authorized API calls, silent configuration tampering (which redirects all subsequent document processing — PM.T06), privilege abuse as an Admin visitor, credential/token theft.
threats.likelihood: Low (requires an Admin install decision or a supply-chain compromise)
threats.affectedComponents: `FeatureLoader.tsx`, `feature-host-globals.ts`, S3 Web UI Bucket, feature ui-deployer roles, `listInstalledFeatures`
threats.mitigations: **Install is a privileged, deliberate, out-of-band act**: a feature is a CloudFormation stack an Admin deploys with their own credentials — it cannot be installed through the UI by a lower-privileged user, and `subscribeFeature`/`unsubscribeFeature`/`getFeatureLaunchUrl` are **Admin-only** (server-side enforced; `scripts/api_rbac_expectations.yaml`). Each shipped feature template scopes its ui-deployer's S3 write to `features/${FeatureId}/*` in the Web UI bucket, so one feature cannot overwrite another's bundle or the host SPA's own assets; a feature can overwrite any of its own versions. Bundles are served same-origin (no third-party CDN in the trust path) with `Cache-Control: max-age=300`, so a malicious version can be replaced and propagate within minutes rather than being pinned for a year. The pipeline-hooks dispatcher role may invoke only same-account, same-Region functions tagged `idp:feature-id` or named `GENAIIDP-*` (HOOK.T06). Features are distributed with source in-repo for the bundled ones.
threats.residualRisk: **No integrity verification occurs at load time** — there is no Subresource Integrity (SRI) hash, no signature, and no version pinning check against a manifest digest (`expectedVersion` only produces a warning; loading proceeds regardless). Recommended, in order: (1) record a SHA-384 digest of the bundle in the feature registry at install time and set `script.integrity` from it in `FeatureLoader` — this is a small change that converts (b) and (c) from silent to blocked; (2) document the trust decision explicitly in the install flow ("installing a feature grants it your users' UI privileges"); (3) longer term, consider rendering third-party feature UIs in a sandboxed iframe on a distinct origin with a narrow `postMessage` API instead of `window` globals. Treat FEAT.T01 as **accepted-with-compensating-controls for first-party/bundled features and open for third-party features**.

threats.title: Feature Registry Enumeration by Any Authenticated User
threats.description: `listInstalledFeatures`, `listCatalogFeatures`, and `checkFeatureEntitlement` are readable by **any authenticated user** (`groups: ANY`). They disclose which extensions are installed, their versions, and their `uiBundlePath`s.
threats.attackVector: A low-privileged authenticated user calls `listInstalledFeatures` to inventory the deployment's extensions and versions.
threats.impact: Reconnaissance: an attacker learns which features (and versions) are present, enabling targeting of a known-vulnerable feature version. Low direct impact — no document data is exposed.
threats.mitigations: Necessarily readable by all roles — the host SPA must render the Extensions nav for every user, so this is a **design requirement**, not an oversight. No secrets, credentials, or document data are returned. Version information is also inferable from the loaded bundle paths. Install/modify operations are Admin-only.

threats.title: Feature Stack IAM Privilege and Host Resource Access
threats.description: A feature stack creates its own IAM roles and is granted access to host resources it imports (e.g. `${MainStackName}-InputBucketName`, `-WebUIBucketName`, `-UsersTableName`). A feature can therefore read/write host data directly from its own Lambdas, independent of the host's API authorization. A hook feature additionally receives full document content in-band.
threats.attackVector: A malicious or over-permissioned feature template grants its own role broader host access than its function requires, then reads document content or writes configuration outside the host's RBAC controls.
threats.impact: Data exfiltration or tampering that bypasses the host's resolver-side authorization entirely, because it operates at the AWS API layer rather than through `POST /op/{field}`.
threats.affectedComponents: Feature templates, feature Lambda execution roles, host `Fn::ImportValue` exports
threats.mitigations: Features declare their host imports explicitly in their template, so the grant surface is **reviewable in the IaC before install**. `PermissionsBoundaryArn` is forwarded to the feature-platform nested stack and attached to the roles it creates, and a static test asserts that every deployed-stack template attaches the boundary to every role it creates and that every nested stack forwards the parameter — so an SCP-enforced account can bound a feature's maximum privilege centrally. Feature-owned data (e.g. the PII mapping table) lives in the feature's own stack, encrypted, rather than in host tables. Install requires CloudFormation privileges.
threats.residualRisk: The permissions boundary is the real control here and is only as tight as the account's boundary policy. In accounts with no boundary, a feature stack's roles are bounded only by the installing principal's own privileges. Recommend requiring `PermissionsBoundaryArn` for deployments that install third-party features.

threats.title: Stale or Downgraded Feature Bundle Served to Users
threats.description: The host loads whatever bundle exists at the registry's `uiBundlePath`. If a security fix is published under the **same** feature version, browsers and CDN edges may continue serving the old bytes; conversely, a rollback to a known-vulnerable version is not detected.
threats.attackVector: A feature hotfix is republished at the same version; users continue running the vulnerable bundle from cache. Or an attacker with the feature's S3 prefix write access reverts the bundle to an older vulnerable build.
threats.impact: A patched client-side vulnerability remains exploitable for the cache lifetime; version-based assurance is unreliable.
threats.affectedComponents: Feature ui-deployers, S3 Web UI Bucket, CloudFront TTL, `FeatureLoader` version check
threats.mitigations: Feature ui-deployers set `Cache-Control: public,max-age=300`, matching the CloudFront TTL — so an update propagates within minutes. The module-level registry loads a given feature's script once per page load, so a mid-session swap does not take effect until reload. `expectedVersion` mismatches are logged.
threats.residualRisk: The `expectedVersion` check **warns but still loads**, and there is no digest pinning (see FEAT.T01 recommendation 1, which also closes this). Prefer publishing security fixes under a **new version** so the registry path itself changes.

threats.title: Test Set Generator's Model-Written HTML Reaches the Network While Rendering
threats.description: The Test Set Generator extension (`feature-platform/idp-data-generator`) runs SEED (`seed-data`) in an AgentCore runtime created in `PUBLIC` network mode. Its document-generator model writes HTML that is rendered to a PDF. A renderer that fetches the `http(s)` images, stylesheets, `@import`s and fonts the HTML references would let the model's output cause outbound requests from the runtime, and the model's context holds the document class schema, the scenario text, the data it generates, and any file it reads with `editor`.
threats.attackVector: Instructions in a class description, scenario or file the model reads lead it to write HTML whose resource URLs carry context data to an external host, or pull external content into a generated test document. A change in SEED's tools or default PDF backend between releases adds a tool that takes a URL or runs a command.
threats.impact: Disclosure of schema and generated data to an external host; test documents carrying externally supplied content.
threats.mitigations: The image pins `seed-data[augment]==0.0.7` and `xhtml2pdf==0.2.28`, so the tool set the models hold changes only with a pin change. The adapter names the `xhtml2pdf` backend explicitly, which keeps SEED's `shell` tool (given only with its `reportlab` backend) out of the set, and replaces that backend with one that renders under `ResourceAccessPolicy(allow_remote=False)`: a remote reference is logged and left out of the PDF. With that policy no tool the models hold takes a URL or makes a network request, and no tool calls an AWS API; the runtime role's S3 and DynamoDB permissions are used only by the runtime handler and the adapter. The extension's README records the per-agent tool inventory for the pinned release.
threats.residualRisk: If the installed `xhtml2pdf` lacks `xhtml2pdf.config.resources`, or SEED stops keeping its backends in `seed_data.tools._HTML_RENDERERS`, the adapter logs `Render fetch policy not applied` and SEED's own renderer runs, which fetches remote references; the pin is what keeps that from happening. Inline `data:` resources and files in the runtime user's home directory still load. `file_write` and `editor` read and write any path the image's `appuser` can, so anything that user can read can enter the model's context. The runtime keeps outbound internet access, and VPC network mode is not offered; an account that requires no internet route should not install the extension.

threats.title: Queue Listings Show Items Outside the Caller's Profile Scope
threats.description: Queues are system-wide, so one queue holds items of several configuration profiles, and an Annotator's access to an item is bounded by two things: queue eligibility and profile scope (`allowedConfigVersions`). A queue reference carries no profile, so a check made at the queue level cannot apply profile scope; it has to be made against each item's own profile. A listing that applies only eligibility shows a scoped Annotator the items of every profile in the queues they work. A listed item carries the document's object key, its profile, the fields that raised confidence alerts with their scores, and the holder's email.
threats.attackVector: An Annotator with `allowedConfigVersions` set, eligible for a queue that also holds other profiles' items, calls `listReviewQueueItems`, `getMyReviewQueues`, `listMyReviewWork` or `claimNextReviewItem`.
threats.impact: Disclosure of review-item metadata — document names, profile names, alert fields and scores, holder identity — across the profile boundary. Not document content, drafts or the work itself, which the per-item operations refuse.
threats.mitigations: Every per-item operation and every listing decides profile scope by the **item's own profile**: `ReviewQueueService._sees`, which uses `idp_common.config_scope.scope_allows` — the same comparison the rest of the API uses (AUTH.T07) — and so admits an item with no profile to no scoped caller. It applies to `listReviewQueueItems` (one queue or all of the caller's), `getMyReviewQueues`, `listMyReviewWork` and `claimNextReviewItem`; a listing that leaves items out still pages forward, and Claim next reads past them up to `CLAIM_NEXT_MAX_PAGES` pages of a queue. `QueueDirectory.in_scope`, which admits an empty profile, is used only for a queue reference, never for an item. `lib/idp_common_pkg/tests/unit/review_queues/test_listing_profile_scope.py` covers each listing for a scoped caller, an unscoped caller and an Admin. Admins and unscoped Annotators see every profile by design.
threats.residualRisk: A queue's counts (depth, unclaimed, oldest item) are filtered for a **scoped** caller item by item, in one projected pass per queue (`ReviewQueueService` in `idp_common/review_queues/service.py`), so they count only the items the caller's scope admits; Admins and callers whose scope is unrestricted get whole-queue counts, which match what they are shown. The static RBAC rule (`make api-test-static`) checks that a scope lookup is reachable from a `scope_filtered` operation, not that its result is applied to each returned item, so a regression of this class is caught by the unit tests above rather than by that gate. The behaviour has not been exercised against a live deployment.

threats.title: Reviewer-Controlled Drafts Become the Document's Final Output
threats.description: Review exists to let a person change what the pipeline produced, so the threat is a holder who changes it wrongly — deliberately, or because their account is compromised. A draft is any JSON object up to 2,000,000 bytes and nesting depth 64; it is not validated against the class schema or restricted to the extracted values, and on completion the finalize execution copies each section's latest draft verbatim over that section's extraction result. The holder can also regroup pages, and the finalize run reprocesses with the new grouping. An Admin can complete or reject an item someone else holds, take one over, or **remove** a document from review, which completes it with its unreviewed machine output. **Send to review** widens which documents can reach that path: an Admin or Reviewer can put any finished production document in their profile scope into the Default queue, not only one that raised confidence alerts, then claim and complete it like a routed item. Downstream consumers — the post-processing hooks, reporting, evaluation against a baseline, and any external reader of `status.json` — receive the result as reviewed.
threats.attackVector: An eligible Annotator or a Reviewer claims an item and saves a draft that alters values or the section structure, then completes it; a Reviewer sends an already-finished document to review and then works it the same way; or an Admin removes a document from review to release machine output that should have been checked.
threats.impact: Falsified final extraction results presented as human-reviewed, reaching every downstream consumer of the document.
threats.mitigations: Only the holder can save, complete or reject: each write is a transactional `Put` conditioned on the item's version **and** on `Status = CLAIMED AND OwnerKey = <caller>` (with the lease unexpired), so a stale or concurrent writer is refused by DynamoDB rather than by a read-then-check. Supervisor operations (take over, assign, unassign, move, remove, force release) are `Admin` only at the dispatcher and again in the service, and a take-over tells the former holder in their Inbox. The finalize message body is built server-side from the tracking row, so no request argument reaches the workflow input; the finalize token is validated by shape and becomes the execution name, so a resent finalize does not start a second run. The item records its review activity, field edits and disposition; `status.json` and the `document_reviews` reporting table record the reviewer and disposition. Legacy review operations and `uploadDocument` refuse a document a queue manages, so there is one write path while it is in review. `sendToReview` is `Admin` and `Reviewer` only at the dispatcher and in `bulk_review_resolver`; it checks each document against the caller's scope by the document's own profile (`review_skip.in_scope`, `scope_allows`), refuses a Test Studio document, one not `COMPLETED` and one already in a review, and makes the tracking row the commit point with a conditional update (`attribute_not_exists(TestSetId)`, finished, not in review), so a concurrent run or a second send cannot overwrite it. The item records `origin=manual` and a `sent_to_review` history entry naming the sender, the reason (from a fixed list) and the note. `processChanges` requires a caller who is not an Admin to hold the document's open review and to have the document's profile in scope, and refuses section and page changes to a document whose pinned revision routes it to BDA.
threats.residualRisk: The review history lives in `HITLTable`, which several Lambda roles in the stack hold write grants on, so it is an operational record rather than a tamper-evident one. A draft is not checked against the section's schema; validating it there would bound a draft to the fields the class declares and keep a malformed body out of the consumers that render it (UI.T01). Remove-from-review is a supervisor decision with no second approver, recorded only as a disposition. A Reviewer can both send a document to review and complete it, so one person can replace any finished in-scope document's output with a reviewed-looking result; the send and the completion are recorded on the item, but nothing requires a second person.

threats.title: Review Metadata Reaches Readers Beyond the Queue's Audience
threats.description: Three channels carry review metadata further than a queue's eligible Annotators. **(1) Inbox announcements.** The "items waiting" message for a queue is addressed to the queue's member groups, which every queue definition returns as `Annotator`, `Reviewer` and `Admin` (`queue_defs.member_groups`), so it reaches every Annotator in the pool whether or not they are eligible for that queue; messages carry the queue and test-set ids, the profile name, the assigning user's email and the document's file name. **(2) `review/status.json`.** It records the reviewer's email and, for a rejection, the free-text reject note, and it sits under the document's prefix in the Output bucket, where the generic object reads serve it to any caller whose scope covers the document. **(3) Output-bucket EventBridge.** Every object event in the Output bucket — not only `status.json` — now goes to the account's default event bus, carrying object keys (document names) to any rule another workload in the account defines. The `document_reviews` reporting table also records reviewer identity, so it is queryable wherever Athena reporting is (AGT.T05).
threats.attackVector: An Annotator reads announcements for queues they cannot work; a caller with document read scope fetches a document's `status.json`; a principal in the same account subscribes a rule to the default bus.
threats.impact: Disclosure of queue activity, profile names, document names and reviewer identities beyond the queue's audience; no document content.
threats.mitigations: No API operation posts a message, so Inbox content comes only from platform code; a bulk Skip All Reviews job's completion notice goes to its requester only and carries counts, not document names. Reading, marking and deleting are keyed on the caller's verified identity and take no user argument, and the Inbox operations require an assigned group. A message's link must be an in-app route: the server refuses a scheme, a host or a protocol-relative form, and the UI repeats the check before rendering it as a hash route. Message bodies are rendered through `SafeMarkdown` (`rehype-sanitize`), not raw HTML, and skip notes are never put into a message. `NotificationsTable` is encrypted with the stack CMK, expires rows by TTL and has point-in-time recovery. EventBridge delivery from S3 carries object metadata, not object content.
threats.residualRisk: Address the waiting-work announcement to the queue's eligible Annotators rather than to the whole `Annotator` group. Message bodies interpolate the uploader's file name and are rendered as sanitized markdown. The sanitizer removes script, event handlers and `<style>`, loads an image only from the app's own origins or the deployment's buckets (any other image is shown as a link), and keeps a `style` attribute only for layout and typography properties with no URL-capable value (`safe-markdown-policy.ts`); it still admits external `http(s)` links, so a file name is rendered as markup — emphasis, a link — in another user's Inbox rather than as text. Rendering the interpolated name as plain text would remove that class. Whether every Output-bucket event needs to reach the default bus, rather than only the `status.json` key, is a deployment decision; a rule filtering on the key suffix bounds what a consumer receives but not what the bus carries.

threats.title: Resolvers Serving Annotator Operations Hold Write Grants on Authorization and Workflow State
threats.description: The review resolvers are reachable by the `Annotator` and `Reviewer` groups and carry grants wider than any one of their operations needs. `TestSetResolverFunction`, which serves `claimTestSetDocument` and the test-set draft and save operations to Annotators, can now `PutItem` and `UpdateItem` on the **UsersTable** — the table `allowedTestSets` and `allowedConfigVersions` live in — because the Admin-only `assignTestSetDocuments` writes the assignee's `allowedTestSets`. `ReviewQueuesResolverFunction` can `UpdateItem` anywhere in the TrackingTable, read every object in the Output bucket, write the Working bucket, and send to `DocumentQueue`, which starts a workflow execution. `BulkReviewResolverFunction`, which serves `sendToReview` and `bulkSkipAllReviews` to Reviewers, and `BulkReviewWorkerFunction`, which runs a Reviewer's job with its own role, can each read and write any `HITLTable` item, `UpdateItem` any tracking row, read every Output-bucket object and write its `*/review/*` keys, write the Working bucket, send to `DocumentQueue`, and write `NotificationsTable`. `ReviewQueueSweeperFunction` and `TestRunSweeperFunction` can update any tracking row.
threats.attackVector: A defect in one of those resolvers' Annotator- or Reviewer-callable paths — an argument used as a key without the per-object check, a missing branch guard — is steered by the caller into a write the operation was not meant to make, such as widening a user's scope, re-queueing a document, or finishing another profile's review.
threats.impact: A scope change on any user row, or a document re-run or status change, made with the resolver's role rather than the caller's authority.
threats.mitigations: The dispatcher's group floor admits `assignTestSetDocuments` to `Admin` only, and the resolver checks again. Every grant is scoped to a named table, bucket, prefix or queue of this stack; the only `*` resources are `cloudwatch:PutMetricData` statements conditioned on the namespace. `states:StopExecution` on the queue processor and `states:DescribeExecution` on the sweeper are scoped to this stack's processing state machine. The finalize message is built server-side from the tracking row (HITL.T02). The bulk resolver takes the caller only from verified claims (`_caller_context`), its scope lookup fails closed, and it never reads a key, profile or job id it was given without the per-document or requester check of HITL.T05. `BulkReviewJobQueue` and its dead-letter queue are encrypted with the stack key, and their queue policies deny non-TLS access.
threats.residualRisk: IAM cannot express "this item" or "this user's own row", so a resolver's per-object correctness is the only bound on these writes (AUTH.T16). Moving the `allowedTestSets` write behind the user-management function, which already owns UsersTable writes, would take UsersTable write off a role Annotators reach.

threats.title: Bulk Skip All Reviews Releases Unreviewed Output at Scale
threats.description: `bulkSkipAllReviews` finishes up to `MAX_JOB_DOCS` pending production reviews in one request, each completing with its unreviewed machine output, and by default resubmits each for Summarization, Evaluation and the post-processing hook. A by-profile request reaches every pending review of a profile in a submitted-date range without naming any document. So one Admin or Reviewer can release, in one action, the output review was meant to check across a whole profile, and downstream consumers receive it as finished. A large job runs in the background under the requester's recorded identity for as long as it takes, and only one job runs at a time per stack.
threats.attackVector: A Reviewer, or a compromised Reviewer account, submits a by-profile bulk skip over a profile in their scope with resubmission on; or submits a series of large jobs that hold the per-stack job lock and keep `DocumentQueue` busy with resubmissions.
threats.impact: Many documents completed without the human check their configuration asked for, reaching every downstream consumer; delayed review work and processing for other users while a large job runs.
threats.mitigations: **Who.** `bulkSkipAllReviews`, the four job operations and `sendToReview` are `Admin` and `Reviewer` only, at the dispatcher and again in `bulk_review_resolver` (`_FIELD_GROUPS`) before any work, the same roles that may skip one review (`skipAllSectionsReview`). **What.** A by-profile request is refused unless the profile is in the caller's `allowedConfigVersions`, before any document is read (`_enforce_scope`, `assert_profile_in_scope`); a selection is classified per document (`review_skip.classify`): a document outside the caller's scope or unknown is `NOT_PERMITTED`, a Test Studio document is excluded, a queue item claimed by someone else or a legacy review owned by someone else is `HELD_BY_OTHER` for a non-Admin, and one still processing or already finalizing is left alone. The dry run uses the same classification, so its counts match the run. **While it runs.** A background step rebuilds the requester from the job row and intersects the scope recorded at submission with the requester's current scope, looked up by the recorded Cognito `sub` (`BulkSkipService._caller_for`, the worker's `_scope_resolver`); a by-profile job whose profile has left that scope fails as `scope_revoked`, and a failed lookup fails the step rather than widening it. Retried pages neither skip nor count a document twice (conditional per-document result puts). **Accountability.** A reason from a fixed list is required, each document's skip goes through the queue's finalize path with the `skipped` disposition or the legacy skip, both recorded in review history, `BulkReviewOutcomes` counts every outcome, and the requester is told in their Inbox when the job ends. A Reviewer reads, cancels and deletes only the jobs they requested (`RequesterKey` from verified claims); another user's job reads as not found, and an active job cannot be deleted. **Volume.** One job runs at a time per stack (a lock row), the worker's event source mapping has a maximum concurrency of two, and a job advances one page per step, paced against `DocumentQueue` depth.
threats.residualRisk: A Reviewer can skip every pending review of any profile in their scope in one action with no second approver; the reason and the requester are recorded, but nothing prevents it. A background job keeps the requester's groups as recorded at submission, so a Reviewer removed from the group mid-job does not stop it, while a scope narrowed mid-job does; an Admin can cancel any job. Because one job runs at a time per stack, a large job delays every other requester's job.

threats.title: Malicious Customer Code Execution
threats.description: Customer-managed Lambda hooks execute arbitrary code within the customer's AWS account. Malicious or compromised hook code could abuse its position in the processing pipeline
threats.attackVector: Deploy malicious Lambda function as inference or post-processing hook that exploits its access to document data and AWS resources
threats.impact: Data exfiltration, modification of processing results, abuse of IAM permissions, lateral movement within AWS account
threats.mitigations: Customer responsibility for hook security, documentation of security best practices, hook Lambda runs with customer-managed IAM role (separate from platform roles), platform only has invoke permission on hook

threats.title: Data Exfiltration via Post-Processing Hook
threats.description: Post-processing hooks receive complete decompressed processing results including all extracted data, PII, and document content. This data could be sent to unauthorized external destinations
threats.attackVector: Post-processing hook sends full document results to unauthorized endpoint
threats.impact: Complete exfiltration of all processed document data
threats.mitigations: Customer-managed VPC with egress controls on hook Lambda, security review of hook code, network-level monitoring, data loss prevention policies

threats.title: Inference Hook Result Tampering
threats.description: Inference hooks return results that feed into the downstream pipeline. A compromised hook could return manipulated extraction results
threats.attackVector: Inference hook returns carefully crafted false extraction data that passes validation but contains incorrect or malicious content
threats.impact: Corrupted processing results, incorrect business decisions based on tampered data
threats.affectedComponents: Inference Hook Lambda, downstream pipeline steps
threats.mitigations: Output schema validation in platform code, assessment step as verification layer, evaluation framework to detect accuracy degradation, human review for critical documents

threats.title: Hook Lambda Timeout/Failure Cascade
threats.description: Customer hook Lambdas that timeout, fail, or hang can block the processing pipeline, especially if retry policies are aggressive
threats.attackVector: Hook Lambda with infinite loop, external dependency timeout, or resource exhaustion
threats.impact: Pipeline processing blocked for affected documents, Step Functions execution stuck
threats.mitigations: Step Functions timeout configuration on hook invocation states, error handling with fallback states, CloudWatch alarms on hook failures, DLQ for failed processing

threats.title: Privilege Escalation via Hook IAM Role
threats.description: If the hook Lambda's IAM role has excessive permissions, compromised hook code could access platform resources beyond its intended scope
threats.attackVector: Hook Lambda with over-permissioned IAM role accesses platform S3 buckets, DynamoDB tables, or other resources
threats.impact: Unauthorized access to platform data and resources
threats.affectedComponents: Hook Lambda IAM role, platform resources
threats.mitigations: Documentation emphasizing least-privilege IAM for hooks, platform resources use resource-based policies that don't grant hook roles access, clear boundary between platform and customer IAM roles

threats.title: Preprocessing Hook Operates on the Raw Source Document and Can Halt or Replace It
threats.stride: Tampering, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service
threats.description: The `preprocessing` hook point (v0.6.2) is materially more powerful than the post-step `postHook` lists this document originally covered. It runs **first** — before BDA/pipeline routing — so it fires in **both** processing modes and even when OCR is disabled, and it operates on the **source document itself** rather than on derived results. It may return `halt: true` to end the execution outright, and it can write replacement documents back to the Input bucket. A preprocessing hook therefore sees every document in its most sensitive, un-redacted form and can suppress, substitute, or mutate any document before any processing occurs.
threats.attackVector: A malicious or compromised preprocessing hook (a) exfiltrates raw source documents including all PII, (b) silently substitutes a benign document for a sensitive one, or (c) returns `halt: true` for targeted documents so they are never processed — a **silent, targeted denial of processing** that is harder to notice than an outright failure.
threats.impact: Complete pre-pipeline compromise: exfiltration of raw documents, undetected substitution of content that all downstream results are then derived from, or selective suppression of documents.
threats.likelihood: Low (requires registering a hostile hook, which is an Admin/config action)
threats.affectedComponents: Pipeline hooks dispatcher, `preprocessing` config section, S3 Input Bucket, workflow state machine
threats.mitigations: Registration is a **configuration action** requiring the Admin/Author group and is config-versioned, attributable, and reversible (PM.T06 controls). The hook is a **separate customer/feature-managed Lambda** with its own IAM role — the platform holds only `lambda:InvokeFunction` on it (HOOK.T01/T05 controls apply unchanged). The dispatcher role (`PipelineHooksDispatcherFunctionRole` in `patterns/unified/template.yaml`) may invoke only a same-account, same-Region function that carries an `idp:feature-id` tag (`aws:ResourceTag/idp:feature-id` condition) **or** whose name starts with `GENAIIDP-`; an ARN outside both is refused by IAM with `AccessDenied`. The hook config is a deliberately **generic** `arn` + key/value `args` shape with no feature-specific fields, limiting the platform's own attack surface. `onError: fail` is **terminal** (fail-closed — no fall-through to processing the un-preprocessed original). The distinct, visible **`PREPROCESSING`** document status (abortable like other in-flight statuses) makes a hook that hangs or halts observable in the UI rather than silent, and it is a no-op when no hook is registered (backward-compatible default).
threats.residualRisk: A `halt: true` return is a legitimate, expected outcome (the PII feature uses it after spawning a replacement document), so a *malicious* halt is not distinguishable from a *correct* one by the platform alone — detection depends on operators noticing documents that never produce results. Recommend monitoring the rate of halted executions and alerting on anomalies. See [PII Anonymization](pii-anonymization.md) for the reference consumer's own threats (PII.T01–T05).

threats.title: `onError: fail` Does Not Halt the Workflow at Six of Seven Hook Points
threats.description: A hook declares `onError: fail` to mean "if I cannot run, do not continue processing this document". The dispatcher (`patterns/unified/src/pipeline_hooks_function/index.py`) raises `HookFatalError` when such a hook returns not-ok, and whether the document then stops depends entirely on how the hook state's `Catch` blocks in the Step Functions definition route that error. A catcher that matched `States.ALL` before `HookFatalError` and routed to the next processing step would turn a gate into advice: the document would complete normally and be indistinguishable, in its results, from one whose hook succeeded. This matters most where a hook exists for a compliance purpose — a redaction step, a classification-based routing restriction, a data-residency check.
threats.attackVector: Not primarily an attacker action: it is a control that does not hold. An attacker who can cause a gating hook to fail — resource exhaustion, a malformed document that trips the hook's own error path, revoking the hook's permissions — converts "processing stops" into "processing continues without the gate", with no failed execution to investigate.
threats.impact: A gating extension can be bypassed by making it fail. Compliance-motivated hooks (PII redaction being the reference consumer) may be skipped while the document still produces normal results. Weak repudiation: the error is written into execution state, not surfaced as a failure.
threats.mitigations: `onError: fail` is terminal at every hook point a document reaches. In `patterns/unified/statemachine/workflow.asl.json` each post-step hook state (`PostOcrHook`, `PostClassificationHook`, `PostExtractionHook`, `PostRuleValidationHook`, `PostSummarizationHook`, `PostprocessingHook`) catches `HookFatalError` first and routes it to a terminal failure state (`PostExtractionHookFailed`, or the shared `PostStepHookFailed`); its later `States.ALL` catcher routes forward, so a transient dispatcher fault (timeout, throttle) does not discard an already-processed document. `PreprocessingHook` routes any error to `PreprocessingHookFailed`. The catcher order is asserted by enumerating every hook state from the definition rather than from a list, so a hook point added later is covered. `postOcr`, `postClassification` and `postExtraction` exist only on the Pipeline branch, so a gate placed there does not apply to a BDA-mode document. Hook failures remain visible in CloudWatch and in the execution history. `onError: continue` routes forward by design.
threats.residualRisk: A hook is customer code and a *gate implemented as a hook* is only as reliable as the hook's own availability. Where a control must hold, prefer `preprocessing` (terminal today) and alert on the rate of failed and halted executions rather than inferring success from the absence of errors.

threats.title: Decision Model Answers Set Classification and Confidence Without an Independent Check
threats.description: A configuration that selects a decision model for section classification or extraction confidence takes that function's answer as the result. Under section classification the chosen class becomes the section's class and `probabilities[choice]` its confidence; under extraction confidence a value's confidence is its highest `noul` probability across the pages read, and that number is what thresholds, alerts and human review are decided on. A function that returns a wrong or manipulated answer therefore changes which class schema a section is extracted with and which values reach a reviewer, and does so without any LLM call that could disagree.
threats.attackVector: (a) The decision model function is replaced or redeployed with different code or weights under the same `GENAIIDP-` name, or its model revision is left unpinned and changes on redeploy. (b) A compromised function returns a high probability for every value, so no value falls below its threshold and nothing goes to review. (c) Document content steers the model's answer, as PM.T01 describes for an LLM.
threats.impact: Misclassified sections extracted against the wrong schema; extracted values that should have been reviewed pass as confident; human review suppressed for chosen documents.
threats.likelihood: Low (requires control of a function in the stack's own account and Region, or a hostile configuration)
threats.mitigations: Selecting a decision model and its `endpoint` is a configuration change, which needs the Admin or Author group and is versioned (PM.T06). Every response is parsed into `SystemOneResponse`, and one that does not match the contract raises `DecisionModelUnavailable` rather than being used. A `choice` answer naming no configured class (after `label_map`) is assigned the fallback class instead of being accepted. A field with no answer fails the confidence pass rather than keeping a default. Each value's explainability entry records `confidence_source: decision_model` and a reason naming the model and the page, and each section's classification reason names the model and the probability, so the source of a confidence is visible in the document's details. `low_confidence` can send section answers below `min_confidence` to the fallback class or to the LLM. The function runs under the customer's own role and is a separate trust zone (TB6), as for HOOK.T01 and HOOK.T03.
threats.residualRisk: Probabilities are not range-checked: `NoulAnswer.noul` and `ChoiceAnswer.probabilities` are unconstrained floats, so a function returning a value above 1 clears every confidence threshold (measured: a `noul` of 7.5 parses). The platform cannot tell a correct answer from a manipulated one; evaluation against ground truth (RPT.T04) is the check on accuracy. Recommend pinning the decision model's revision, as `docs/decision-models.md` advises, and restricting who can update a `GENAIIDP-` function in the account.

threats.title: `GENAIIDP-*` Grant Lets Configuration Send Document Content to Any Function So Named
threats.description: The pipeline functions that run the classification, extraction and assessment services — `ClassificationFunction`, `ExtractionFunction`, `ShardRuntimeFunction`, `AssessmentFunction`, and also `OCRFunction` and `SummarizationFunction` for `LambdaHook` inference — may invoke any function in the stack's account and Region whose name starts with `GENAIIDP-`. The grant is a name prefix, not a list of functions this stack owns, so the function a decision model or `LambdaHook` call reaches is whatever the configuration names. Each decision model request carries the section's OCR text or page images and, for confidence, the field names, descriptions and extracted values.
threats.attackVector: An Author points `decision_model.endpoint` (or a `LambdaHook` ARN) at a `GENAIIDP-` function they or someone else deployed — another stack's function, a function that forwards its input elsewhere — and every document processed under that configuration version sends its content there. Alternatively, any principal able to create or update a `GENAIIDP-` function in the account makes it reachable from every stack's pipeline roles.
threats.impact: Document text, page images and extracted values delivered to a function outside this stack's review; that function can then send them anywhere its own role and network allow (HOOK.T02).
threats.likelihood: Low (requires an Admin or Author configuration change, or account-level Lambda write access)
threats.affectedComponents: `ClassificationFunction`, `ExtractionFunction`, `ShardRuntimeFunction`, `AssessmentFunction`, `OCRFunction`, `SummarizationFunction` policies in `patterns/unified/template.yaml`; `idp_common/decision_model/invoker.py`; the configuration's `decision_model.endpoint` and `LambdaHook` fields
threats.mitigations: Each grant is bounded to `arn:${AWS::Partition}:lambda:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:function:GENAIIDP-*` and carries a `lambda:FunctionName` condition on the same prefix, so a function in another account or Region, or one named otherwise, is refused by IAM. The client refuses an endpoint whose function name lacks the prefix (`FUNCTION_NAME_PREFIX`) before calling it, refuses an unimplemented backend, and a configuration that selects a decision model without an endpoint is refused when it is loaded. Changing the endpoint needs the Admin or Author group and is versioned and scope-checked (`updateConfiguration`; PM.T06). The set of functions that must carry the grant is derived from source rather than listed, so the grant follows the services rather than a hand-kept inventory. Images are scaled down before they are sent, which bounds the payload but not what it reveals.
threats.residualRisk: The prefix is shared across every stack and every customer function in the account, so the effective boundary is who may create or update a `GENAIIDP-` function there, which this stack does not control. Recommend restricting `lambda:CreateFunction` and `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` on `GENAIIDP-*` to the principals that deploy decision models and hooks, and reviewing the `endpoint` field in configuration change review.

threats.title: Decision Model Failure or Cost Amplification Stops or Inflates Processing
threats.description: A configuration that selects a decision model uses only that model: a failed call is never converted into an LLM call. Section classification makes one call per section; extraction confidence makes, per section, one call per page read for every batch of up to `max_questions_per_request` values, each a large-memory Lambda execution. A function that is throttled, timing out, crashing or refusing therefore fails the sections or confidence passes that depend on it, and a configuration with high `max_pages` multiplies the calls.
threats.attackVector: The decision model function is deleted, throttled by its reserved concurrency, or returns errors; or an Author raises `max_pages` and `max_concurrency` so that every long section makes many concurrent large-memory invocations.
threats.impact: Sections labelled `unclassified`, failed confidence passes, and Lambda cost that scales with pages × value batches per section.
threats.mitigations: Failures are typed: `DecisionModelRefused` (over the model's window or request limit, too many images, malformed) is never retried, and `DecisionModelUnavailable` covers a call that did not complete. Only throttling, a crashed execution environment and a connection that never opened are retried, with bounded exponential backoff clamped to the calling Lambda's remaining time; a read timeout and a closed connection are not retried because the invocation may still be running and billing. Every terminal failure records `DecisionModelRequestsFailed` once, and an abandoned retry records `DecisionModelRetryAbandonedOutOfTime`. A refused or failed section keeps its boundaries and is labelled `unclassified`, as when an LLM section call fails. `max_concurrency` bounds calls in flight per client across threads, `max_pages` bounds the pages read per section (validated at load), and `timeout_ms` bounds each call. Each request is metered under `{context}/decision_model/{function}`, so the cost appears in the document's cost table.
threats.residualRisk: Cost per document is bounded per section, not per document, so a packet with many long sections still makes many calls. A decision model's own availability is outside the stack; there is no fallback by design.

threats.title: Jobs API Clients Bypass the Cognito Group RBAC Model
threats.description: The Jobs API authenticates against its **own** Cognito user pool (`ApiUserPool`), entirely separate from the Web UI's `UserPool`. Its clients are OAuth `client_credentials` principals with **scopes**, not Cognito **groups**. Consequently none of the authorization machinery this threat model documents for the UI API applies: there are no Admin/Author/Reviewer/Viewer groups, no `allowedConfigVersions` config-version scoping, and no per-operation resolver group checks. A principal holding a `jobs.write` token can submit documents for processing without being any named user, and its submissions are not constrained to a configuration version.
threats.attackVector: An attacker who obtains the client id + secret (from CI configuration, a `.env` file, a build log, or an over-shared secrets store) mints tokens indefinitely and submits arbitrary documents for processing, or reads job status for all jobs via `jobs.read`.
threats.impact: Unauthorized document submission and processing (cost amplification, injection of adversarial documents that reach the models — PM.T01), and disclosure of job metadata. Not bounded by config-version scope, so a compromised client is not limited to one tenant's configuration the way a scoped UI user is.
threats.likelihood: Low (requires the client secret **and** network position inside the VPC)
threats.mitigations: The API is **`EndpointConfiguration: PRIVATE`** with a resource policy that **denies** any invocation whose `aws:SourceVpce` does not match the supplied VPC endpoint — so the endpoint is not reachable from the internet at all, and a leaked secret alone is insufficient without network access. Scopes are **separated by intent** (`jobs.read` vs `jobs.write`), so a read-only integration need not hold write capability. The feature is **off by default** (`EnableJobsApi=false`) and, when enabled, is guarded by a CloudFormation rule requiring VPC parameters. The separate user pool means a Jobs API secret compromise does **not** grant Web UI access or expose human user accounts.
threats.residualRisk: The two-realm design is deliberate and sound, but it must be **documented as such** so operators do not assume UI RBAC covers this path. A single shared client with both scopes is the default shape; recommend (1) issuing separate clients per integration with the narrowest scope, (2) rotating the client secret on a schedule, and (3) noting explicitly in the deployment docs that Jobs API submissions are **not** config-version scoped.

threats.title: Jobs API Is Outside the Automated Authorization Test Harness
threats.description: `make api-test` / `make api-test-static` derive their operation universe from the UI dispatcher (`FIELD_FUNCTION_MAP` ∪ `ddb_direct._HANDLED` ∪ `FIELD_ALIASES`) and drive `POST /op/{field}`. The Jobs API's `/jobs` routes are **not** in that universe, so no automated test asserts their authorization behavior. A regression that widened a Jobs API route's access, or dropped a scope requirement, would not fail the security gate.
threats.attackVector: Not directly attackable — this is a **detection** gap that allows another defect to ship undetected.
threats.impact: An authorization regression on the Jobs API reaches production without a failing test, unlike the equivalent regression on the UI API.
threats.mitigations: The Jobs API surface is **small and static** (a handful of `/jobs` routes vs 168 UI operations), so the review burden is low and drift is unlikely. Authorization is enforced by the API Gateway Cognito authorizer plus scope configuration in the template — declarative IaC rather than per-resolver imperative code, which is the class of defect the UI harness exists to catch (AUTH.T08). The `zapdast` deployment-variant probe and the `stacktest-jobsapi` deploy-variant test exercise the deployed Jobs API stack.
threats.residualRisk: Add a small scope-negative test (a `jobs.read`-only token attempting a write route must be refused, and an unauthenticated request must 401) to the Jobs API stack test. Low cost, closes the gate asymmetry.

threats.title: Static Client Secret with No Rotation Mechanism
threats.description: `ApiAppClient` is created with `GenerateSecret: true`. The client id/secret pair is long-lived, has no built-in rotation or expiry, and is typically stored in a CI system or application configuration to mint tokens. Unlike a human user's credentials, there is no MFA, no password policy, and no global sign-out equivalent.
threats.attackVector: Secret leaks via source control, CI logs, container image layers, or an over-broad secrets-store grant; the holder mints valid tokens until the secret is manually rotated.
threats.impact: Persistent unauthorized access at the granted scopes for as long as the secret remains valid — potentially indefinitely, since nothing forces rotation.
threats.mitigations: Access tokens minted from the secret are themselves short-lived. The PRIVATE endpoint means the secret is unusable without VPC network position (the dominant compensating control — see JOB.T01). Rotation is possible at any time by updating the client. CloudTrail records token issuance and API invocations for detection.
threats.residualRisk: Document a rotation procedure and cadence; prefer sourcing the secret from AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation over embedding it in CI configuration. Consider per-integration clients so one leak has a bounded blast radius and can be revoked independently.

threats.title: Knowledge Base Poisoning
threats.description: The knowledge base indexes everything in the Output bucket. Any document that gets processed contributes its extracted content to the index at the next ingestion, so a misleading document, or one carrying prompt-injection text, contaminates the answers every user receives
threats.attackVector: Upload a document containing misleading information or injection payloads (as an Admin or Author, or as any principal with `s3:PutObject` on the Input bucket), let it be processed, and wait for the next scheduled ingestion
threats.impact: Incorrect or manipulated knowledge-base answers and citations for every user who queries it; document processing itself is not affected, because the pipeline does not query the knowledge base
threats.affectedComponents: S3 Output Bucket, `S3DataSource` and `S3DataSourceScheduler` (`nested/bedrockkb/template.yaml`), Bedrock Knowledge Base, vector store
threats.mitigations: Only Admin and Author can upload documents through the API, which checks the caller's profile scope. The configured Bedrock guardrail is applied to the answer (`guardrailConfiguration` in `get_kb_response`). Every answer carries citations naming the source documents, so a poisoned answer is attributable. Deleting or reprocessing a document changes the bucket, and the next ingestion reflects it
threats.residualRisk: There is no review step between processing and ingestion and no version history of the index; a direct writer to the Input bucket is bounded only by the IAM policy on that writer. The knowledge base can be turned off with `DocumentKnowledgeBase=DISABLED`.

threats.title: RAG Context Injection
threats.description: Retrieved chunks are inserted into the answer model's prompt by `RetrieveAndGenerate`. If indexed content carries prompt-injection text, it can steer the answer, and the answer and snippets are rendered in the user's browser
threats.attackVector: Get a document holding injection instructions or markup processed, so that it is retrieved for other users' questions
threats.impact: Manipulated answers for questions where the poisoned chunk is retrieved; markup in a snippet or answer reaching the page
threats.mitigations: The configured Bedrock guardrail (`BedrockGuardrailId`) is applied through `generationConfiguration.guardrailConfiguration` on `RetrieveAndGenerate`. `markdown_response` HTML-escapes each snippet and document title and URL-encodes each document id before building the citation markup. The web UI renders the result through `SafeMarkdown`, which loads images only from the app's own origins and drops embedded styles. The answer model has no tools, so an injected instruction cannot call anything
threats.residualRisk: The prompt that frames retrieved content is Bedrock's default `RetrieveAndGenerate` template; this solution adds no instruction isolating retrieved text, and the guardrail applies only when `BedrockGuardrailId` is set.

threats.title: Vector Store Data Exposure
threats.description: The vector store holds embeddings and the text chunks of every processed document. Misconfigured access policies, or credentials with access to the store, could expose that content outside the query resolver
threats.attackVector: Overly permissive vector-store access policies, or compromised credentials with S3 Vectors or OpenSearch Serverless data access
threats.impact: Exposure of processed document content stored as embeddings and chunks
threats.affectedComponents: `S3VectorBucketAndIndex` and the S3 vector manager role, or `OSSCollection` with `OSSEncryptionPolicy`, `OSSNetworkPolicy` and `OSSDataAccessPolicy`; `KnowledgeBaseServiceRole`
threats.mitigations: With S3 Vectors (the default), the vector bucket and the knowledge base use the stack's customer-managed key, the vector manager's grants name exactly the bucket and index it creates in this account and Region, and it can pass only the knowledge base's own service role, only to Bedrock (`S3VectorManagerPassRolePolicy`). With OpenSearch Serverless, the data access policy grants collection and index permissions to `KnowledgeBaseServiceRole` alone, so every data-plane request needs that role's IAM-signed credentials. Under `TenantIsolationMode=Strict` or an external `TenantGrantSource`, knowledge-base queries are Admin-only (`_refuse_non_admin_when_unscoped_is_denied`), because retrieval cannot be confined to one tenant (TEN.T01)
threats.residualRisk: The OpenSearch Serverless collection's network policy sets `AllowFromPublic: true` for the collection and its dashboard, and its encryption policy uses an AWS-owned key rather than the stack key, so the data access policy and IAM are the only boundary. The service role's own S3 read reaches the whole Output bucket.

threats.title: Excessive RAG Retrieval
threats.description: A query retrieves from every processed document in the deployment. The resolver applies no configuration-profile scope (`allowedConfigVersions`) and no group check of its own, so outside tenant isolation a user can retrieve content from documents in profiles outside their scope; repeated queries also bill Bedrock inference
threats.attackVector: A signed-in user in any group, including a profile-scoped user, asks questions designed to retrieve content from documents they cannot otherwise see, or submits many queries
threats.impact: Exposure of processed document content across profile scopes, in synthesised and cited form; increased Bedrock and vector-store costs
threats.mitigations: The API dispatcher admits `queryKnowledgeBase` only for a caller in some group (`ANY_GROUP` in `scripts/api_rbac_expectations.yaml`). Under `TenantIsolationMode=Strict` or an external `TenantGrantSource` the resolver refuses every non-Admin caller. `RetrieveAndGenerate` returns the service's default number of retrieved results per query. The resolver truncates the query and response in its logs (`sanitize_event_for_logging`). The REST API is covered by API Gateway stage throttling and, when enabled, the WAF
threats.residualRisk: Profile scope does not bound knowledge-base results (stated in the RBAC page's Known Limitations), and the resolver has no group check of its own (`GAP-02`); a deployment that relies on `allowedConfigVersions` to separate users should disable the knowledge base or use tenant isolation. The resolver sets no relevance threshold or result count of its own, and passes the caller-supplied `sessionId` to `RetrieveAndGenerate` without binding it to the caller.

threats.title: Data Exfiltration via MCP Tools
threats.description: MCP moves document data across the deployment boundary in both directions. The IDP MCP server returns extracted values, classifications and analytics answers to MCP clients, and an External MCP agent sends a chat query, and whatever the orchestrator puts in it, to an external MCP server
threats.attackVector: An MCP caller reads documents outside its configuration scope or tenant; or prompt injection in a chat conversation causes an External MCP agent to pass document data to an external server as tool parameters
threats.impact: Disclosure of customer confidential data, PII, or processing results to an unauthorized caller or external service
threats.affectedComponents: `McpIdentityInterceptorFunction`, `AgentCoreMCPHandlerFunction` and its tools (`src/lambda/agentcore_mcp_handler/tools/`), `idp_common.mcp_access`, `idp_common.mcp_credentials`, External MCP agents (`idp_common.agents.external_mcp`), the chat processors
threats.mitigations: **Inbound:** each caller is resolved by the interceptor (`resolve_caller` in `idp_common.mcp_access`): a signed-in user's token groups and `allowedConfigVersions` (read with `AdminGetUser`, which also refuses a disabled user or a token whose `sub` does not match), or a service credential's role and profiles from its registry row. The handler refuses a call whose signed caller block it cannot verify (`verify_caller`, keyed by `McpCallerSigningSecret` and bound to the gateway request id). `status` and `get_results` return only documents inside the caller's scope (`document_keys_in_scope`), `process` and `reprocess` refuse a document or destination profile outside it, and `search`, which reads reporting tables spanning every profile, is refused to any scoped caller, so under `TenantIsolationMode=Strict` or an external `TenantGrantSource` it is Admin-only (TEN.T01). **Outbound:** External MCP agents are off unless the conversation opts in, and once a data agent (Analytics, Error Analyzer) has returned a result in a session no opt-in agent is built into, or answers in, that session (`select_orchestrator_agent_ids`, `SessionAgentGate`); an opt-in request on such a session moves to a new session with no memory. The handler logs each call's sanitized event to its own log group. **Residual:** an External MCP server is whatever URL the secret names, and there is no egress control on what an opted-in agent sends to it

threats.title: Malicious Tool Injection
threats.description: Tool definitions an agent or MCP client treats as legitimate capabilities could be added or altered. The IDP MCP server's tool set is fixed in code; an External MCP agent's tool set and descriptions come from the external server at run time
threats.attackVector: A caller invokes a tool name the server does not define, or forwards a tool argument the schema does not declare; or an external MCP server (or whoever controls it) publishes tools or descriptions that steer the agent
threats.impact: Agent executes unintended operations; unauthorized system access
threats.mitigations: The IDP MCP server's tool schema is `IDP_TOOLS_SCHEMA` in the gateway manager's source, applied to the gateway target by the `AgentCoreGateway` custom resource on each deploy, and is not configurable at run time. `MCP_TOOL_POLICY` in `idp_common.mcp_access` lists exactly the tools `IDP_TOOLS_SCHEMA` defines; any other tool name is refused for every caller, including Admin, by the interceptor and again by the handler, and `tools/list` and the gateway search tool's results are filtered to what the caller may call. A client-supplied `_caller` argument is replaced by the interceptor and unsigned blocks are refused. External MCP agents are registered only from entries in `ExternalMCPAgentsSecret`, which an AWS principal with write access to that secret edits (no application role can), and each is marked opt-in when registered. **Residual:** the external server's tool list and tool names are taken as returned (`list_tools_sync`) and the names are placed in the agent's system prompt; nothing allowlists or validates them

threats.title: MCP Response Injection
threats.description: Text in a tool result reaches a model as context, enabling indirect prompt injection. IDP MCP server results carry document-derived text to the MCP client's model, and External MCP agent results carry external-server text into the chat orchestrator
threats.attackVector: A processed document contains instructions that an MCP client's model reads in a `get_results`, `status` or `search` result; or an external MCP server returns a prompt injection payload as tool output
threats.impact: Model behavior manipulation via tool result content, cascading to further tool calls or data disclosure
threats.affectedComponents: `AgentCoreMCPHandlerFunction`, `idp_common.mcp_access` (`with_provenance`), the MCP Connector (`idp_mcp_connector.connector`), External MCP agents, the chat orchestrator
threats.mitigations: `get_results`, `status` and `search` results carry a `provenance` field naming the fields that hold document-derived text (`DOCUMENT_DERIVED_FIELDS`) with a notice to treat that text as data, not instructions; the MCP Connector passes that notice to its client's model (`provenance_of`, `notice_text`). For External MCP agents, the opt-in per conversation and the rule that no opt-in agent runs in a conversation holding Analytics or Error Analyzer results bound what an injected result can steer the orchestrator towards. **Residual:** the provenance notice is advisory to the client's model; External MCP tool output is not sanitized or size-limited, and the External MCP agent's system prompt does not mark it untrusted

threats.title: Unauthorized External Service Access
threats.description: An External MCP agent connects to its server with the credentials stored for it in `ExternalMCPAgentsSecret` (a Cognito user pool, client, username and password per server), not with the chat user's own identity. Any chat user whose conversation opts in reaches that external system with the stored identity and whatever tools it exposes
threats.attackVector: A chat user, or prompt injection in their conversation, has the agent call external tools with model-chosen parameters that act beyond what that user should be able to do on the external system
threats.impact: Unauthorized operations on external systems, unintended data modifications
threats.affectedComponents: External MCP agents (`idp_common.agents.external_mcp`), `ExternalMCPAgentsSecret`, the chat processors
threats.mitigations: The secret is encrypted with the stack's customer-managed key and read only by the chat functions granted it; its entries are edited through AWS, not through any application role. External MCP agents are off unless a conversation opts in, and the configuration is validated for its required fields and transport (`_validate_mcp_config`). Least privilege for the stored identity on the external system is the operator's responsibility. **Residual:** every opted-in user shares the stored identity; there is no per-user mapping and no per-tool allowlist on the IDP side

threats.title: External MCP Client Abuse
threats.description: MCP clients connecting to the IDP MCP server could submit excessive requests or attempt operations their role does not allow
threats.attackVector: A client sends high-volume requests or crafted tool calls, or keeps using a credential after it should have stopped working
threats.impact: Resource exhaustion, cost escalation, unauthorized data access
threats.mitigations: No MCP server exists unless `EnableMCP=true`. Cognito authentication is required; the gateway admits only the user-authentication client and registered client-credentials apps (`update_allowed_clients` in `idp_common.mcp_gateway`), and a client with no rule in `resolve_caller` is refused. Per-tool role checks in the interceptor and the handler match each tool's REST equivalent (`mcp_tools:` in `scripts/api_rbac_expectations.yaml`, checked by `make api-test-static` and driven live by `make api-test`): `process`/`reprocess` need Admin or Author, `status`/`get_results` any document role, `search` Admin, Author or Viewer with no scope; a user in no stack group is refused. Write tools also need the credential's write-tools setting, which only Admin and Author credentials can hold. Service credentials carry a role, profiles and an expiry (90 days by default), issue one-hour access tokens, and are read on every call, so a disabled, revoked or expired credential is refused on its next request; a daily sweep (`McpCredentialSweepSchedule`) revokes expired ones. **Residual:** there is no per-caller rate limit, no reserved concurrency on the handler, and no MCP-specific usage alarm; volume is bounded only by service quotas and the workflow concurrency controls downstream of `process`

threats.title: AgentCore Gateway Lifecycle Attacks
threats.description: The gateway's configuration (target, tool schema, JWT authorizer, interceptor) is written by several functions. If it is corrupted or the interceptor is removed, MCP availability or the caller checks could be affected, and a function that manages it could be used to escalate privileges
threats.attackVector: An `UpdateGateway` call that omits the interceptor or rewrites the allowed clients; repeated or conflicting gateway updates; IAM permission escalation via a gateway-managing role
threats.impact: MCP tool unavailability, degraded agent functionality, or tool calls reaching the handler without a resolved caller
threats.mitigations: The manager's role holds `bedrock-agentcore:*` for the gateway and target lifecycle, the two delivery deletes, `logs:DeleteLogGroup` on the gateway's vended log-group path only, and `iam:GetRole`/`iam:PassRole` on the single `AgentCoreGatewayExecutionRole`, with no IAM write (`template.yaml`). `McpInterceptorAttachFunction` and `McpCredentialManagerFunction` hold only `GetGateway`/`UpdateGateway` on this account and region's gateways and `PassRole` on the same role. Every gateway update sends the full current configuration (`full_update_request` in `idp_common.mcp_gateway`), the allowed-client update retries on a concurrent change and never leaves the list empty, and the interceptor attachment re-runs on every release, restoring an interceptor removed out of band. Because the handler refuses any call without a verifiable signed caller block, a missing interceptor refuses every tool call rather than admitting an unresolved caller. **Residual:** `AgentCoreGatewayExecutionRole` carries the AWS-managed `CloudWatchLogsFullAccess` policy; there is no alarm on gateway status changes

threats.title: MCP Client Secret Exposure and Credential Mismanagement
threats.description: MCP client secrets grant a role and scope on the MCP server to whoever holds them. A secret that is readable more widely than intended, a credential granted more than its creator holds, or credentials left behind when MCP is switched off would let a holder act through MCP beyond what was meant
threats.attackVector: Reading a client secret from a stack output, log or console; a scoped Admin creating a credential wider than their own scope or an Admin credential; a credential surviving `EnableMCP=false`, a downgrade or a stack delete
threats.impact: Unauthorized MCP access with the credential's role and scope, including cross-tenant access for an unscoped credential
threats.mitigations: Each credential's secret is written to Secrets Manager (`<stack>/mcp/credentials/<clientId>`, encrypted with the stack's customer-managed key), returned once on creation or rotation, and never stored on the registry row or listed; the credential manager's role can create, describe and delete those secrets but not read them. The stack-created clients' secrets are in `McpConnectorClientSecret` and `McpUserClientSecret`, and the stack outputs `MCPConnectorClientSecretArn` and `MCPClientSecretArn` carry only the ARNs. Every credential operation is Admin-only; a scoped Admin can grant only inside their own scope and cannot create an Admin credential (`require_within` in `src/lambda/mcp_credential_manager/index.py`), and `validate_access` refuses a scope spanning more than one tenant, and, wherever tenant isolation or an external grant source applies, an Admin credential or an unscoped one. The stack-created client is registered as "Default (stack-created)" and starts disabled under Strict isolation or `IdpClaim`/`Api` grants. Rotation overlap is at most seven days, and `McpCredentialsCleanup` revokes every credential when the registry is removed (stack delete, `EnableMCP=false`, or a downgrade). **Residual:** any AWS principal with `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on those secrets and `kms:Decrypt` on the stack key reads them; `idp-cli mcp credentials` acts with the caller's AWS credentials and is not subject to the scoped-Admin narrowing (SDK.T09)

threats.title: Un-Redacted Document Content Reaches the Detection Model
threats.description: The redaction step uses a **Bedrock model to detect** the PII it will remove. The document must therefore be sent to Bedrock **un-redacted** for that single detection call. An operator who deploys this feature believing "no PII ever reaches a model" is mistaken: PII does transit that one call.
threats.attackVector: Not an attack so much as a **misunderstood control boundary** — an operator or auditor assumes an end-to-end guarantee the feature does not provide. It becomes a real exposure if the detection model is configured to a vendor/region that the deployment's data-residency policy excludes (see PM.T08).
threats.impact: PII is disclosed to the detection model endpoint. Where the configured model is an OpenAI GPT-5.x variant on `bedrock-mantle`, that is a **different model family** from the Anthropic/Nova default — a distinction that matters for vendor-approval and residency compliance.
threats.likelihood: High (it is the designed behavior on every document)
threats.severity: Medium (exposure is to an AWS-managed AI service inside TB4, not to a third party outside the account)
threats.mitigations: This limitation is **explicitly documented** in the feature docs and CHANGELOG rather than glossed over ("the redaction step itself uses a Bedrock model to *detect* the PII, so PII does transit that single detection call"). Exposure is to Bedrock within the customer's own AWS account boundary under TLS and IAM, with no training use. Crucially, the reduction is real for the **rest** of the pipeline: classification, extraction, assessment, and summarization — including their prompts, logs, and *stored results* — operate only on de-identified content, so the number of places PII is persisted drops substantially.

threats.title: Redaction Loop / Re-Entrancy via Input-Bucket Writeback
threats.description: The hook writes the redacted copy **back into the Input bucket**, beside the original. Since input-bucket writes are exactly what triggers processing (EventBridge → Queue Sender → Step Functions), a naive implementation would re-process the redacted copy, redact it again, write another copy, and loop indefinitely.
threats.attackVector: Occurs spontaneously without a guard; an attacker could also attempt to defeat the guard by crafting filenames that mimic or evade the marker.
threats.impact: Unbounded recursive processing — Bedrock cost amplification, queue saturation, and Lambda concurrency exhaustion starving legitimate documents.
threats.affectedComponents: `PiiAnonymizerHookFunction`, S3 Input Bucket, EventBridge, Queue Sender
threats.mitigations: The redacted copy carries a `(REDACTED)` marker in its name and the hook implements an explicit **re-entrancy guard** against redaction loops. The host's concurrency counter (DynamoDB) and SQS bound total in-flight executions even if a loop began, and CloudWatch alarms surface abnormal execution rates. Trailing-slash pseudo-objects are skipped by the Queue Sender.
threats.residualRisk: The guard is **name-based**, which is inherently weaker than a metadata/tag-based check (a user-uploaded file legitimately containing `(REDACTED)` in its name would be treated as already-processed and skipped — a false negative that silently leaves a document un-redacted). Prefer an S3 object tag or metadata key as the authoritative marker, with the filename as a human-readable hint only.

threats.title: Redaction Bypass — Un-Redacted Document Processed on Hook Failure
threats.description: If the preprocessing hook errors, times out, or is silently skipped, the pipeline could proceed to process the **original, un-redacted** document — defeating the entire control while appearing to succeed. This is the classic fail-open failure mode for an inline security control.
