threats.attackVector: An attacker submits a document crafted to crash or time out the hook (e.g. a pathological PDF, or one large enough to exceed the hook's Lambda budget), causing the pipeline to fall through to processing the raw original.
threats.impact: PII flows into classification/extraction prompts, logs, and stored results — precisely the outcome the feature exists to prevent — while the run reports success.
threats.affectedComponents: Pipeline hooks dispatcher, `PiiAnonymizerHookFunction`, workflow state machine
threats.mitigations: **The design is fail-closed**: `onError: fail` is **terminal** — a failed hook stops the execution rather than falling through to processing the un-preprocessed original. This is the correct posture and is the key control for this threat. The hook is provisioned with a deliberately heavy timeout/memory allocation because vision/LLM detection over a multi-page document is expensive, reducing spurious timeouts. `PREPROCESSING` is a distinct, visible document status (abortable like other in-flight statuses), so a stuck document is observable rather than silent. In *redact copy and stop* mode the original is deleted, so there is no un-redacted copy left to process.
threats.residualRisk: Fail-closed behavior depends on the hook being configured with `onError: fail`; an operator who sets a permissive `onError` re-opens this. Recommend documenting `onError: fail` as **mandatory** for redaction use cases (as opposed to optional enrichment hooks) and, ideally, validating it at config-import time when the registered hook is the PII feature.

threats.title: Redaction Mapping Table as a Re-Identification Oracle
threats.description: When the opt-in mapping is enabled, the `RedactionMappingTable` stores the **original → synthetic** PII correspondence. This table is a **re-identification oracle**: anyone who can read it can reverse the de-identification for every document processed, making it strictly more sensitive than any single document. It is the highest-value data store the feature creates.
threats.attackVector: A user without access to the original document's configuration version attempts to read the mapping via the feature API; or an attacker reaches the table directly through a compromised role, a DynamoDB export/backup, or the host's `getFileContents` presigned-read gadget (UI.T06).
threats.impact: Complete reversal of PII redaction across all processed documents — the worst-case confidentiality outcome for this feature.
threats.mitigations: Storage is **opt-in**, not default. The table is **feature-owned** (in the feature's own stack, not a host table), with `SSESpecification` encryption and PITR. Access is **RBAC-gated to users whose `allowedConfigVersions` include the *original* document's config version** — the hook deliberately records the original's config version so the report can make that decision. Critically, the scope lookup **fails closed on both halves of the decision**: each lookup key is read from its own claim and nothing else — the immutable Cognito `sub` for the `SUB#<sub>` pointer item, the `email` claim for the `EmailIndex` GSI — so neither is ever substituted for the other and a claims set carrying neither denies instead of resolving to an identifier that matches no `UsersTable` row (an empty page means "unrestricted", so a substituted identifier would have made an unresolvable caller an unrestricted one); and `_caller_allowed_versions` raises `ScopeLookupError` on a missing `UsersTable`, a caller with neither key, a `sub` that no pointer records when there is no email to fall back to, or any DynamoDB error on either key space, with both the mapping and report routes denying rather than treating a transient failure as "unrestricted". Resolving the `sub` first is what keeps the gate applied to a caller whose address has diverged from their row, which on this route would otherwise hand out a re-identification key. All three `/report*` routes answer the same 403 for that condition, so a failed lookup cannot be mistaken for a truthful empty report on what is an audit view. This is the same contract the host now enforces through `idp_common.config_scope` (AUTH.T07); the rule is restated here rather than imported because this extension ships as its own stack with no `idp_common` layer, and `scripts/tests/test_scope_lookup_fail_closed.py` covers this file for key provenance and failure handling — it has no rule about the *matcher*, so the glob-matching restatement beside it is behaviourally identical today with nothing mechanical holding it there. Both single-record routes resolve the caller's **scope before the record**, so a caller whose scope cannot be evaluated receives the same 403 body whatever `documentId` they name; the ordering is the control, and reversing it would restore a one-bit-per-probe oracle over the audit table's contents. **Residual:** the `sub` join applies only to a host `UsersTable` row that records a `sub` — a row the host's back-fill has not reached still resolves on email alone (see AUTH.T07 residual 1) — and none of this has been exercised against a live deployment. The mapping is reachable **only** through that gated route: it is stored in DynamoDB rather than S3 specifically so that the host's object-read path — `getFileContents`, `getFilePresignedUrl` and `getFilePresignedUrls` — **cannot** be used to bypass the gate. ⚠️ **Three server-side controls stand in front of an Output-bucket key, and not one of them is the decision this threat needs.** The `ANY_GROUP` floor is satisfied by every group, so it bounds who may ask and nothing else. The bucket allow-list bounds which bucket, not which object in it. And `document_scope` matches the **owning document's** `ConfigVersion` against the caller's `allowedConfigVersions`, which differs from the decision here in two ways: it is a deliberate no-op for a caller whose scope is unset, which is a host `UsersTable` row's default state because scoping is opt-in per user; and where it does apply it authorizes against the profile of the document that owns the key, whereas re-identification has to be authorized against the **original** document's config version — the value this hook records for precisely that reason, and the one an artifact of the redacted copy need not carry. A presigned URL is additionally a bearer capability for the life of its signature, while the report route re-evaluates the caller's scope on every request. Keeping the oracle out of any host-proxyable location is therefore still what makes this safe (UI.T06). The Redaction Report default view is metadata-only with no PII.

threats.title: Companion Config-Version Pairing Misconfiguration
threats.description: In *redact copy and continue* mode, the original and the redacted copy coexist as separate documents, separated **only** by `allowedConfigVersions` RBAC on their respective config versions. If the pairing is misconfigured — the redacted copy tagged to the wrong version, or a user granted both versions — a user intended to see only de-identified content can read the original.
threats.attackVector: An Admin misconfigures the Config Pairing wizard, or grants a user access to both paired versions; the user reads the original document's results.
threats.impact: PII disclosure to users the deployment intended to restrict to de-identified content.
threats.affectedComponents: Config Pairing wizard, host config APIs, `allowedConfigVersions`
threats.mitigations: The **Config Pairing wizard** clones an existing version into the matched pair via host config APIs rather than requiring manual construction, which removes the most likely source of hand-configuration error. The redacted copy is tagged to re-process under the **companion** version automatically. `allowedConfigVersions` enforcement is server-side and regression-gated (AUTH.T07). Choosing *redact copy and stop* eliminates this threat entirely — the original is deleted.
threats.residualRisk: Correctness depends on the operator's group/scope assignments, which the feature cannot validate. Recommend *redact copy and stop* as the default for deployments whose goal is that PII never be readable, reserving *continue* for cases needing the original retained. Note this threat inherits UI.T06: a scoped user can still read out-of-scope **object bytes** via `getFilePresignedUrl`, which bypasses `allowedConfigVersions` — so config-version pairing is **not** a complete boundary until UI.T06 is closed.

threats.title: Prompt Injection via Document Content
threats.description: Adversarial content embedded in documents (text, metadata, hidden layers) could manipulate Bedrock model behavior during classification, extraction, or assessment
threats.attackVector: Upload document containing prompt injection payloads in visible or hidden text
threats.impact: Misclassification, incorrect extraction, bypassed assessment criteria, data exfiltration via model output
threats.affectedComponents: Classification Lambda, Extraction Lambda, Assessment Lambda
threats.mitigations: The default prompt templates place document content inside delimiting tags, and prompt comments are removed from the template before document text is substituted, so a document cannot use `{# ... #}` to remove prompt text. Model output is parsed against the extraction schema (PM.T03). An optional Bedrock Guardrail (`BedrockGuardrailId` / `BedrockGuardrailVersion`, passed as `GUARDRAIL_ID_AND_VERSION`) is applied to the model calls of the Extraction function (including agentic extraction), the Advanced-extraction shard runtime, Summarization, rule validation, Chat with Document, discovery and Z3 rule translation. Confidence assessment, when `confidence.mode` is `separate` or `integrated`, gives a second per-field signal that drives thresholds and human review.
threats.residualRisk: The guardrail is not applied to the Classification, OCR or Assessment functions, each excluded with its own recorded reason in `GUARDRAIL_ENV_EXEMPT` (`scripts/tests/test_model_call_guardrail.py`), and it is not sent to OpenAI GPT-5.x models on the `bedrock-mantle` Responses route, which logs a warning instead. Prompt injection against an LLM cannot be fully prevented by prompt structure; human review of low-confidence values is the backstop.

threats.title: OCR Manipulation / Adversarial Documents
threats.description: Specially crafted documents designed to produce incorrect OCR output from Textract, leading to downstream processing errors
threats.attackVector: Documents with adversarial fonts, overlapping text, steganographic content, or layout manipulation
threats.impact: Incorrect text extraction leading to misclassification, wrong data extraction, failed validation
threats.mitigations: Document format validation, image quality checks, confidence score thresholds, multi-pass OCR comparison

threats.title: Model Output Manipulation
threats.description: Bedrock model responses could contain unexpected content, hallucinated data, or leak information from training data
threats.attackVector: Crafted prompts or document content that causes model to generate unexpected outputs
threats.impact: Incorrect business decisions based on hallucinated data, false confidence scores
threats.affectedComponents: Classification Lambda, Extraction Lambda, Assessment Lambda
threats.mitigations: Output schema validation (JSON Schema), confidence thresholds, evaluation against ground truth, human review for high-value documents

threats.title: Cross-Step Data Poisoning
threats.description: Compromised output from one pipeline step could poison subsequent steps. For example, incorrect OCR output could cause the extraction step to produce malicious structured data
threats.attackVector: Exploit S3 intermediate storage or Lambda compromise to modify inter-step data
threats.impact: Cascading errors through entire pipeline, corrupted final output
threats.affectedComponents: S3 intermediate outputs, all pipeline Lambdas
threats.mitigations: S3 versioning, server-side encryption, IAM role separation per Lambda, Step Functions state validation

threats.title: Textract Service Dependency
threats.description: Amazon Textract service throttling or outage impacts all document processing in Pipeline mode
threats.attackVector: Volume-based attacks exceeding Textract API limits, or AWS service disruption
threats.impact: Complete processing pipeline stoppage
threats.mitigations: Retry logic with exponential backoff, SQS dead letter queue, CloudWatch alarms on Textract errors, capacity planning with service quotas

threats.title: Configuration Tampering
threats.description: Malicious modification of pipeline configuration (prompts, schemas, model IDs) could alter processing behavior for all subsequent documents
threats.attackVector: Compromised admin account modifies configuration via UI or API
threats.impact: All documents processed with malicious prompts, data extraction to attacker-controlled schemas, use of unauthorized models
threats.affectedComponents: Configuration S3 bucket, DynamoDB config table, configuration resolver Lambdas (REST API)
threats.mitigations: RBAC (only Admin/Author can modify config), configuration versioning, JSON Schema validation, audit logging, configuration change alerts
threats.residualRisk: A `{# ... #}` span in a prompt is documentation and is not sent, so text placed in a comment by an Author does not reach the model while still appearing in the stored configuration; Prompt Preview shows both the sent and the as-written prompt. On upgrade to a release with prompt comments, text between an existing `{#` and a later `#}` in a stored prompt stops being sent without any edit to the configuration.

threats.title: Few-Shot Example Poisoning
threats.description: Malicious few-shot examples uploaded to S3 could systematically bias classification and extraction behavior
threats.attackVector: Upload poisoned example documents that cause model to misclassify or misextract targeted document types
threats.impact: Systematic misprocessing of specific document types
threats.affectedComponents: Few-shot examples S3 storage, Classification Lambda, Extraction Lambda
threats.mitigations: RBAC on example management (Admin/Author only), example validation, evaluation framework to detect accuracy degradation

threats.title: Document Content Sent to a Non-Anthropic Model Family (OpenAI via `bedrock-mantle`)
threats.description: Since v0.6.1 the configured model for OCR, classification, extraction, assessment, summarization, evaluation, and Chat-with-Document may be an **OpenAI GPT-5.x** variant (`openai.gpt-5.6-sol` / `-terra` / `-luna`, plus GPT-5.4/5.5) served on the `bedrock-mantle` OpenAI Responses API. Full document text — including any PII the pipeline has not redacted — is then sent to a **different model family** than the Anthropic/Nova default that earlier versions of this threat model assumed. Deployments operating under a vendor-approval list, a model-provider restriction, or a data-residency policy may be out of compliance without any configuration change appearing security-relevant: selecting a model is an ordinary config edit made by an Admin/Author in the UI.
threats.attackVector: Not primarily adversarial: an Author selects a GPT-5.x model from the config dropdown for cost or quality reasons, unaware of a vendor/residency constraint. Adversarially, a config-tampering attacker (PM.T06) could switch the model to change where document content egresses.
threats.impact: Document content and PII processed by a model family the deployment may not have approved; potential compliance/residency violation. Region exposure also changes: GPT-5.6 is **US-only** (Sol in `us-east-1`/`us-east-2`; Terra/Luna add `us-west-2`), with no EU/global profiles and **no GovCloud** — so selecting one in an EU-oriented deployment moves inference to US regions.
threats.affectedComponents: `idp_common/bedrock/openai_responses.py`, model config enums, config UI model dropdowns, pricing/limits tables
threats.mitigations: All traffic stays **within Amazon Bedrock in the customer's own account** — this is a Bedrock-served model, not a call out to OpenAI's own API, so it does not leave the AWS trust boundary (TB4) and is covered by the same TLS/IAM controls and no-training posture. Model selection requires the **Admin/Author** group and is config-versioned and audit-logged, so a change is attributable and reversible (PM.T06 controls apply). Bedrock model access must be explicitly requested/enabled per model in the account, giving a second account-level gate outside the application. Region availability is enforced by Bedrock itself — an unavailable model fails loudly rather than silently rerouting. GovCloud deployments **cannot** select GPT-5.6 at all. Agentic extraction, Discovery, and Policy Discovery reject these models at `config-validate` and at runtime, and `idp-cli config-validate` and `config-upload` check every model ID in a configuration against `config_library/pricing.yaml`. A configured Bedrock Guardrail is not sent on the `bedrock-mantle` Responses route, and a warning is logged when one is configured (PM.T01).
threats.residualRisk: The application does not implement an allow-list restricting *which* Bedrock models a deployment may select — any model in the enum is choosable by an Author. Deployments with vendor constraints should (1) restrict model access at the **Bedrock account level** (the effective control), and (2) treat the model fields in a config version as security-relevant in change review. Consider a stack parameter constraining the selectable model set for regulated deployments.

threats.title: Weaponized Document Exploits a File Parser on the Processing Path
threats.stride: Elevation of Privilege, Denial of Service
threats.description: PM.T01 and PM.T02 concern what a document *says*. This concerns what its *file structure* does to the code that opens it. Uploaded PDFs, images and Office documents are decoded inside the stack's own Lambdas — page rendering and image conversion (`pypdfium2`, Pillow) in OCR, classification, extraction, assessment and discovery, the PII Anonymizer's preprocessing hook, and `.zip` extraction in the batch pre-processor — with each function's execution role. A malformed or malicious file that triggers a decoder vulnerability runs with that role's grants (document buckets, tracking table, the stack key), and one that triggers pathological decoding exhausts the function's memory or time. Bedrock Guardrails inspect model text and cannot see a file-structure payload. The exposure is a function of the dependency set: Pillow 13.0.0, adopted in this release, closed seven advisories on this path including one CRITICAL heap overflow in JPEG decoding.
threats.attackVector: Anyone able to place a file in the Input bucket — a UI or SDK upload, a Jobs API client, a direct S3 writer or replication rule — submits a crafted document.
threats.impact: Code execution inside a processing Lambda with that function's role, or denial of service for that document's run.
threats.affectedComponents: OCR, Classification, Extraction, Assessment and Discovery Lambdas, `BatchPreProcessor`, the PII Anonymizer hook, `idp_common` image and PDF utilities
threats.mitigations: **Optional ingest gate** on GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 (`MalwareScanning` = `GATE_ONLY` or `CREATE_PLAN`, default `DISABLED`): the queue sender records an upload as `MALWARE_SCANNING` and does not enqueue it until GuardDuty's verdict arrives through EventBridge; `THREATS_FOUND` becomes `QUARANTINED` and every other verdict, including an unknown one, becomes `MALWARE_SCAN_FAILED` unless both the configuration and the `AllowUnscannableDocuments` stack ceiling admit unscannable files. Neither refused status starts a workflow, and reprocess is refused for all three gate statuses in the resolver and the SDK, failing closed when the status cannot be read. Alarms cover a detection, a run of unscannable refusals, an undeliverable verdict, a verdict not applied, and documents held with no verdict for an hour. Independently of the gate: dependencies are pinned and `make dep-audit` gates HIGH-and-above advisories in both CI systems; each Lambda has its own execution role; and Lambda memory and timeout limits bound a decoding run.
threats.residualRisk: The gate is **off by default**, and with it on the scan is signature, YARA and ML based with no behavioural analysis, so a novel exploit is reported clean. It is asynchronous: the object sits in the Input bucket, presignable, between upload and verdict. The plan protects the **Input** bucket only, so a `.zip` in the Staging bucket is opened by the batch pre-processor unscanned — its extracted members do pass the gate when written to the Input bucket, but the archive decoder itself is outside it. `make dep-audit` does not read the six `feature-platform/*/feature-ui` lockfiles. Enabling the gate is the recommendation for any deployment that accepts documents from outside its own organisation.

threats.title: Reporting Data Tampering
threats.description: Parquet files in the reporting S3 bucket could be modified or deleted, altering historical processing records and analytics. The bucket holds raw `metering` and `document_sections_*` data, and the four rollup tables derived from it (`metering_hourly`, `metering_daily`, `metering_docs_hourly`, `metering_docs_daily`) that the dashboard's cost widgets and the analytics agent read
threats.attackVector: Direct S3 access with compromised credentials, or a Lambda bug that deletes or overwrites existing reporting data
threats.impact: Corrupted analytics and cost reporting, unreliable evaluation metrics, loss of audit trail
threats.mitigations: The stack-created `ReportingBucket` has versioning enabled, so an overwritten or deleted object's prior version is recoverable; it is encrypted with the stack's customer-managed key, blocks public access and writes server access logs to the logging bucket. Scheduled rollups are append-only: each partition is written once, and the handler probes for an existing partition and skips the `INSERT` rather than rewriting it. Delete permissions are prefix-scoped: `DataMartRollupFunction` holds `s3:DeleteObject` only on the four rollup prefixes, used only by the migration state machine's `InitialPurge` task, so it cannot delete raw `metering/` or `document_sections_*/` data; `MeteringHourMigrationFunction` holds it only on `metering/*`, for its copy-then-delete partition move. The rollups are derived data and can be rebuilt from raw `metering`
threats.residualRisk: No S3 Object Lock is configured, and a bucket supplied through `ReportingBucketName` takes whatever versioning its owner set. A rollup migration (a stack update that changes `MigrationVersion`, such as the one that adds `n_runs` to the doc-grain rollups) purges and rebuilds **all four** rollup tables over the replay window, so the cost rollups, the dashboard cost widgets and the analytics agent read low until it finishes; raw `metering` is unaffected, and partitions older than the window keep `n_runs` empty

threats.title: Athena Query Data Exposure
threats.description: Athena queries over reporting data expose all processed document information. Query results stored in Athena output location could be accessed by unauthorized users
threats.attackVector: Access Athena query results S3 bucket, or submit queries that extract sensitive fields from processed documents
threats.impact: Exposure of all processed document data including extracted PII and business-sensitive information
threats.affectedComponents: Amazon Athena, S3 query results, Glue Data Catalog
threats.mitigations: Athena workgroup with restricted query result location, S3 lifecycle policies on query results (auto-delete), IAM restrictions on Athena access (Admin/Author only), Athena query logging

threats.title: Glue Catalog Manipulation
threats.description: The Glue Data Catalog defines table schemas and S3 data locations. If modified, Athena queries could read wrong data, miss data, or expose additional S3 paths
threats.attackVector: Modify Glue table definitions to point to different S3 locations, or alter column definitions to expose additional data
threats.impact: Athena queries return wrong data, or expose data from other S3 paths
threats.affectedComponents: AWS Glue Data Catalog, Glue Crawler
threats.mitigations: IAM restrictions on Glue API operations, Glue Catalog resource policies, CloudTrail logging of Glue operations, periodic catalog validation

threats.title: Evaluation Data Manipulation
threats.description: Ground truth data and evaluation results could be tampered with to hide accuracy degradation or mask the impact of attacks on processing quality
threats.attackVector: Modify ground truth files in S3 to match incorrect extraction results, or tamper with evaluation metrics
threats.impact: False confidence in processing accuracy, masked detection of prompt injection or processing attacks
threats.affectedComponents: S3 (ground truth and evaluation data), Evaluation Lambda
threats.mitigations: RBAC (Admin-only ground truth management), S3 versioning on ground truth data, evaluation result integrity checks, separate evaluation metrics storage

threats.title: Discovery Feature — Prompt Injection via Sample Documents
threats.description: The Discovery feature analyzes sample documents to auto-generate processing configurations. Adversarial sample documents could manipulate the AI into generating malicious configurations
threats.attackVector: Upload crafted sample documents that contain prompt injection causing Discovery to generate configurations with malicious prompts, extraction schemas, or class definitions
threats.impact: Auto-generated configurations that systematically misprocess or exfiltrate data when used for production processing
threats.affectedComponents: Discovery Lambda, Amazon Bedrock, Configuration S3
threats.mitigations: Discovery generates draft configs that require human review before activation, configuration schema validation, RBAC (Admin/Author required), evaluation testing before production use

threats.title: Test Studio — Uncontrolled Processing Costs
threats.description: Test Studio allows interactive document testing that invokes the full processing pipeline. Excessive testing could consume Bedrock tokens, Textract calls, and Lambda execution time
threats.attackVector: Repeatedly submit documents through Test Studio to generate excessive processing costs
threats.impact: Cost escalation, processing resource exhaustion affecting production workloads
threats.affectedComponents: Test Studio, processing pipeline, Bedrock, Textract
threats.mitigations: RBAC (Admin/Author required for Test Studio), rate limiting on test submissions, separate test processing tracking, CloudWatch alarms on processing costs

threats.title: Ground-Truth Tampering via the Test Set Visual Editor
threats.description: Test Studio's **Edit Ground Truth** visual editor (v0.6.2) writes directly back to a test set's `baseline/.../result.json`. Ground truth is the measuring instrument for accuracy: an attacker who edits baselines to match current (possibly degraded or malicious) model output makes evaluation report high accuracy regardless of real quality — silently disabling the control that RPT.T04 and PM.T03/PM.T07 rely on to detect misprocessing and example poisoning. Because the harm is to *future* measurements rather than to visible data, it is unlikely to be noticed.
threats.attackVector: An Author (or a compromised Author/Admin session — including via a feature UI bundle, FEAT.T01) edits baseline `inference_result` values so a poisoned configuration or biased few-shot set still scores as accurate.
threats.impact: Loss of trust in all accuracy metrics; conceals systematic misprocessing, prompt injection effects, and few-shot poisoning; corrupted evaluation history.
threats.affectedComponents: `test_set_resolver` (`getTestSetDocuments`), test-set baseline objects in TestSetBucket, evaluation framework
threats.mitigations: Edits require the **Admin/Author** group, enforced server-side (`getTestSetDocuments` is Admin/Author; other roles are read-only in the editor). Every save writes an **`_editHistory` provenance entry** to the baseline, so a modification is attributable and reviewable rather than anonymous — the key anti-repudiation control here. TestSetBucket CORS permits only GET/HEAD + ranged reads for the browser's presigned fetches, so the browser cannot write objects directly; writes go through the resolver. S3 versioning on the bucket retains prior baseline bytes for recovery.
threats.residualRisk: `_editHistory` records that a change happened but nothing *alerts* on baseline mutation, and an Author is legitimately allowed to edit ground truth (that is the feature's purpose), so policy cannot distinguish correction from sabotage. Recommend (1) alerting/reporting on baseline edits for high-value test sets, and (2) treating unexplained accuracy improvements as a signal to diff `_editHistory`.

threats.title: Extended Data Retention via Document Version History
threats.description: Document Versions (v0.6.0) retains **every** successful processing run as an immutable snapshot of pinned S3 object versions, where previously re-processing the same S3 key overwrote prior results. Content an operator believes was superseded — or removed by re-uploading a redacted replacement — remains readable through version history until `DataRetentionInDays` expires. This changes the deployment's data-retention profile in a way that matters for privacy/erasure obligations.
threats.attackVector: A user with access to version history reads a prior run's results for content that was intentionally replaced (e.g. re-uploading a redacted document over an un-redacted one, expecting the original to be gone). Object bytes are fetched with an explicit `versionId` through `getFilePresignedUrl`.
threats.impact: Disclosure of superseded document content and extracted data, including data an operator intended to remove; retention beyond what a naive "delete and re-upload" workflow implies.
threats.affectedComponents: `document_versions_resolver`, versioned S3 output objects, run manifests, `getFilePresignedUrl`
threats.mitigations: Snapshots are bounded by **`DataRetentionInDays`**, so retention is finite and operator-configurable rather than indefinite. `deleteDocumentVersion` is **Admin-only** (server-side enforced), giving an explicit purge path for a specific run. The feature is documented, and the UI surfaces a Version History panel so retained versions are **visible** rather than hidden state.
threats.residualRisk: `listDocumentVersions` requires an **assigned group** (`ANY_GROUP`), so the enumerable index of object keys *and* version ids is not reachable by a caller in no group — but every group reaches all of it, which is the axis that still matters here. Reading the bytes now requires an API operation: `CognitoAuthorizedRole` grants **nothing** on the Output bucket, and **no** `s3:GetObjectVersion` on any bucket, so a `?versionId=` fetch goes through `getFilePresignedUrl` or `getFilePresignedUrls`, where the group floor, the bucket allow-list and `document_scope` apply. `document_scope` matches the owning document's `ConfigVersion` against the caller's `allowedConfigVersions`, which refuses a **scoped** caller another profile's version history — a narrowing this entry did not previously have. It refuses an **unscoped** caller nothing, scoping being opt-in per user, so for the default user row version history still widens the practical impact of UI.T06 and the group floor does not narrow that. Recommend scoping `listDocumentVersions` per document rather than per group, which needs the same document-ownership attribute UI.T06's residual asks for — the group floor is the wrong axis for "may this caller see this document's history", and no setting of it supplies one. For redaction workflows, prefer the PII feature's *redact copy and stop* mode (which deletes the original) over manual replace-and-reupload.

threats.title: Credential Exposure on Developer Machines
threats.description: The SDK and CLI run with the caller's AWS credentials, which reach the stack's resources directly with no application-role check. Those credentials, and secrets the CLI prints (an MCP client secret on creation or rotation), could be exposed through credential files, environment variables, shell history, terminal scrollback or process memory
threats.attackVector: Long-lived access keys in `~/.aws/credentials`, environment variable leakage, a printed client secret captured in a terminal log, or a memory dump of a running SDK process
threats.impact: Unauthorized access to the deployment with the victim's IAM permissions, which for a deploying principal can be broad
threats.mitigations: The SDK takes credentials from the standard boto3 chain, so short-lived credentials (IAM Identity Center, assumed roles) work unchanged and nothing is stored by the SDK itself. `idp-cli mcp credentials create` and `rotate` print the client secret once, as JSON on stdout, say on stderr that it will not be shown again, and never list it afterwards; the secret is also in Secrets Manager. `tenancy verify` logs and returns no token. **Residual:** the protection of the credentials themselves is the operator's machine and practice

threats.title: Insecure Automation Pipelines
threats.description: SDK used in CI/CD pipelines or automation scripts may have credentials hardcoded or stored insecurely in pipeline configurations, or write secrets into pipeline logs
threats.attackVector: AWS keys in CI/CD configuration files, pipeline logs capturing a printed MCP client secret, shared pipeline roles with excessive permissions
threats.impact: Pipeline compromise leads to access to the deployment with the pipeline role's IAM permissions, potentially administrative
threats.mitigations: Use the CI platform's OIDC federation or secret store rather than stored keys; give read-only pipelines an IAM role limited to the read actions they use; send `idp-cli mcp credentials` output to a secret store rather than the log, or read the secret from Secrets Manager later. For a non-human MCP caller, an MCP service credential carries its own role, profiles and expiry rather than a shared user (MCP.T07). **Residual:** these are operator practices; nothing in the SDK enforces them

threats.title: SDK Supply Chain Attack
threats.description: The SDK and CLI are installed as Python packages. If a package or a dependency is compromised, or a same-named package is fetched from a public index, malicious code runs with the operator's credentials
threats.attackVector: Compromised dependency in the dependency chain, or a bare `pip install` of a first-party package name, which on public PyPI belongs to an unrelated party
threats.impact: Arbitrary code execution on developer machines with access to AWS credentials
threats.mitigations: First-party packages are installed from the local checkout (`make setup`), never by bare name (`docs/dependency-confusion.md`); `scripts/check_first_party_deps.py` confirms each first-party package resolves from source in this tree; pinned dependencies are audited against OSV by `make dep-audit` in both CI systems

threats.title: Batch Processing Abuse
threats.description: SDK enables batch document upload and processing. Malicious or misconfigured batch operations could flood the processing pipeline, exhausting Lambda concurrency, SQS capacity, or Bedrock quotas
threats.attackVector: Script using SDK uploads a massive number of documents at once, overwhelming processing capacity
threats.impact: Processing pipeline saturation, legitimate document processing delayed or blocked, cost escalation
threats.affectedComponents: Document queue, Queue Processor Lambda, Step Functions, Lambda concurrency, Bedrock quotas
threats.mitigations: Uploads enter the same queue as every other ingest path; the Queue Processor starts workflows only within `MaxConcurrentWorkflows`, tracked in `ConcurrencyTable`, so a burst waits in the queue rather than running at once. CloudWatch alarms cover workflow errors, timeouts, a stalled document queue, dead-letter queues and concurrency-counter drift (`template.yaml`). Uploading at all requires IAM write access to the input bucket. **Residual:** there is no per-caller rate limit; a caller with that access is bounded only by the global concurrency limit and cost

threats.title: Deployment Service Role Is Broad by Design
threats.description: The accelerator ships an optional CloudFormation **service role** (`iam-roles/cloudformation-management/IDP-Cloudformation-Service-Role.yaml`) so that operators can deploy the stack without holding administrator rights themselves. It is a deployment role, not a least-privilege role: it holds `cloudformation:*` and wildcards on the services the stack uses, with `Resource: "*"`, so whoever can pass it to CloudFormation can change any resource of those services in the account. It appears here with the SDK/CLI because `idp-cli deploy` is its most common consumer
threats.attackVector: A principal permitted to pass this role to a stack operation uses a template to change resources the role can reach, or to try to grant itself IAM privileges through roles the role creates
threats.impact: Changes to any resource of the services the role covers; IAM escalation is contained by the controls below
threats.likelihood: Low (requires an existing principal able to pass the role)
threats.mitigations: The role is optional: a deployment may use any role or an administrator directly. Every IAM role it creates or re-permissions must carry the boundary named by `CreatedRolePermissionsBoundaryArn` (`CreateOrChangeRolesOnlyWithBoundary`); stripping any permissions boundary, editing the boundary policy, modifying the service role or its PassRole policy, and creating IAM users, access keys or identity providers are explicitly denied; IAM writes and `iam:PassRole` are confined to names starting with `ManagedStackNamePrefix`. The trust policy admits only the CloudFormation service principal for stacks in this account (`StringEqualsIfExists`/`ArnLikeIfExists` on `aws:SourceAccount`/`aws:SourceArn`), and the role may carry its own boundary (`ServiceRolePermissionsBoundaryArn`). `scripts/sdlc/validate_service_role_permissions.py` runs in both CI systems and checks the shipped role covers what the stack needs and has no hardening findings; every use is a CloudTrail event attributable to the passing principal. **Residual:** the service wildcards remain broad; treat `iam:PassRole` on this role as authority over every resource of those services in the account, and set the IDP stack's `PermissionsBoundaryArn` to the same value as `CreatedRolePermissionsBoundaryArn`
threats.residualRisk: A CloudFormation service role for a stack this broad will always be substantial — it creates IAM roles, KMS keys, buckets and Lambda functions. The goal it meets is that it cannot escalate IAM beyond the created-role boundary, not that it be small; `iam-roles/cloudformation-management/README.md` explains per service why each wildcard stays broad

threats.title: Terraform Working Directory and State Disclosure
threats.description: `idp-cli deploy --terraform` keeps the deployment's Terraform state and configuration in a working directory (default `./idp-terraform/<stack-name>`) with no backend configured. The state records account IDs, ARNs and sensitive values — every parameter passed, and secrets the module creates, such as the MCP client secrets — and the directory is the only record Terraform has of the deployment. The migration command reads an old deployment's state and writes state backups
threats.attackVector: Another local user, a backup, a shared volume or an accidental commit exposes `terraform.tfstate`, `terraform.tfvars` or a migration backup; or the directory is altered or lost, so a later `apply` or `destroy` acts on the wrong resources or cannot run
threats.impact: Disclosure of deployment secrets and parameters; loss of the ability to update or delete the deployment
threats.mitigations: `terraform.tfvars` and the remembered-parameters file are created owner-only (`0600`) from the start, and an existing wider file is narrowed before it is written (`write_private`); the migration's plan, configuration backup and state backups are written the same way. The saved plan file is deleted after apply. `idp-terraform/` is in the repository's `.gitignore`. `write_root_config` refuses a `main.tf` or `terraform.tfvars` idp-cli did not write, and a directory that holds another deployment's stack name. `docs/terraform.md` directs operators to plan the state's location before the first apply and recommends an encrypted, locked remote backend. **Residual:** `terraform.tfstate` itself is written by Terraform with Terraform's own file mode and, without a backend, is unencrypted on local disk

threats.title: Terraform Module Integrity
threats.description: `idp-cli deploy --terraform` applies a module fetched from a URL with the deploying principal's credentials (or an assumed role). A substituted or altered module would create whatever resources and IAM it declares with those privileges
threats.attackVector: Write access to the artifact bucket or pointer, a module URL pointing at an attacker-controlled location, or a module changed between the SDK's check and Terraform's download
threats.impact: Arbitrary resource and IAM changes in the deploying account
threats.affectedComponents: `idp_sdk._core.terraform_deploy` (`fetch_url`, `load_module_manifest`, `terraform_module_source`, `check_assume_role_arn`), `idp-cli deploy --terraform`, the published module zip and pointer
threats.mitigations: Each published module has a SHA-256 checksum beside it and in the `idp-terraform-latest.json` pointer, and the SDK refuses a module whose digest differs from the pointer's. S3 module URLs are read through the S3 API and written for Terraform's signed `s3::` getter, so a private bucket works and no public object is needed; any other URL must be HTTPS. `--terraform-assume-role-arn` must be an IAM role ARN and is written into both providers. A name already used by a CloudFormation stack is refused. **Residual:** the checksum is checked on the SDK's own fetch, which supplies the module manifest; Terraform downloads the module again with no checksum pinned in `source`, and a module URL given directly (`--terraform-module-url`) carries no checksum at all. The pointer travels the same channel as the module, so it detects corruption, not substitution by someone who can write both

threats.title: Destructive Terraform Plan or Migration
threats.description: A Terraform apply, a module upgrade or the `genai-idp-terraform` migration could delete or replace a resource that holds documents, configuration or users — buckets, tables, the KMS key, the Cognito user pool — losing its data
threats.attackVector: A plan that replaces a stateful resource after a module or parameter change, an adoption that imports the wrong resource, or an old deployment's destroy that still manages an adopted resource
threats.impact: Loss of documents, configuration, users or the key that decrypts them
threats.mitigations: `deploy --terraform` saves a plan, refuses it when it would delete or replace any address the installed or new module lists as retained or stateful, and applies exactly that saved plan; only `--terraform-allow-replace-stateful` overrides the refusal. Every migration phase that changes something is a dry run unless given `--apply`; the plan refuses an old-state resource of a stateful type it has no verdict for, `check_apply_plan` requires every adopted resource to be imported with none replaced or destroyed, `check_destroy` requires that the old deployment's destroy plan deletes nothing adopted, and state and configuration are backed up before they are changed. **Residual:** `--terraform-allow-replace-stateful` applies such a plan, by design

threats.title: MCP Credentials Managed with AWS Credentials
threats.description: `idp-cli mcp credentials` and `IDPClient.mcp` create, change, rotate and revoke MCP service credentials by calling `idp_common.mcp_credentials` directly with the caller's AWS credentials, not through the Admin-only REST operations behind the MCP Configuration page. The page's narrowing of a scoped Admin to their own scope is in the credential manager Lambda and does not apply on this path
threats.attackVector: An AWS principal with access to the stack's user pool, credential table, secrets and gateway creates an unscoped or Admin MCP credential without holding any application role
threats.impact: An MCP credential with any role and scope the deployment's tenancy settings allow
threats.mitigations: The SDK reads the deployment's tenancy mode from the credential manager function's own environment, not the local machine's, and calls the same `validate_access` the page does, so an Admin or unscoped credential is still refused under tenant isolation or an external grant source and a scope spanning tenants is always refused. The actor recorded on the credential is the caller's STS ARN. Reaching this path requires IAM permissions on Cognito, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager and Bedrock AgentCore that already confer comparable control over the deployment. **Residual:** application roles do not gate this path; IAM does

threats.title: Service Deployed Into an Account That Does Not Own the Product
threats.description: `SearchAgreements(PartyType=Proposer)` answers only for the account that **owns** the product. Deployed into any other account — a dev account, a different seller account of the same organisation — it returns an **empty list rather than an error**, so every activation is refused.
threats.attackVector: Not an attack: operator error. But the failure is the worst shape available — silent, remote, and only visible to paying customers. The service comes up healthy, CloudWatch shows 200s on the API, and the extension simply stops working for everyone.
threats.impact: Total outage of the paid extension for every customer, with nothing in the seller's logs explaining why.
threats.likelihood: Medium (a seller almost always has several accounts, and credentials are easy to confuse)
threats.severity: High (complete loss of function for all paying customers)
threats.mitigations: `idp-feature-cli seller-service deploy` runs a **preflight** that refuses to deploy unless the caller's account owns every registered product, verified with `marketplace-catalog:ListEntities`. The check is **ownership-based, not identity-based** — comparing an account id would pass for any seller, including one that does not sell this product. `AccessDenied` on `ListEntities` also **fails** (it nearly always means these are not seller credentials) with `--skip-ownership-check` as a documented, loudly-warned escape hatch. Passing a product *code* where the `prod-…` entity id is required is rejected before any AWS call. 12 unit tests cover the refusal paths; verified live against a real seller account (passes) and a buyer account (refused, exit 1).

threats.title: Spoofed Buyer Identity in the Request Body
threats.description: The service decides entitlement from *which account is asking*. If that account came from the request body, any AWS principal could claim to be a subscribed account and be issued a valid token for a product they never bought.
threats.attackVector: `POST /activate {"productId": "...", "buyerAccountId": "<a subscribed account>"}` from any AWS account. Subscribed account ids are guessable/discoverable in some contexts, and an attacker can simply try their own partners' accounts.
threats.impact: Complete bypass of the commercial gate, and the resulting token is cryptographically valid — indistinguishable from a legitimate one to the extension.
threats.likelihood: High if the flaw existed (it is the first thing an attacker would try)
threats.mitigations: The account is read **only** from `requestContext.identity`, which API Gateway populates from the **verified SigV4 signature** before invoking the Lambda; the body is never consulted for identity. `AWS_IAM` authorization means an unsigned request is rejected at the edge with 403. A missing verified identity returns 401 and mints nothing, rather than falling back to anything. Guarded by a dedicated unit test that passes a *conflicting* `buyerAccountId` in the body and asserts the verified value wins, a static template test asserting `DefaultAuthorizer: AWS_IAM` and no `Authorization: NONE`, and a live test asserting an unsigned request is refused.

threats.title: Resource-Policy Over-Exposure (`Principal: '*'`)
threats.description: The API resource policy admits **any** AWS principal, because the seller cannot know buyer account ids in advance. If the policy's `Resource` were wildcarded, that openness would extend to every route the API ever gains — including an administrative one.
threats.attackVector: A future `/admin` or `/meter` route added to the same API inherits `Principal: '*'` if the resource is `execute-api:/*/*`.
threats.impact: Depends on the added route; for a metering or admin endpoint it would be severe.
threats.likelihood: Low today (one route), rising with every route added
threats.mitigations: The policy is pinned to `execute-api:/*/POST/activate`. A static test asserts exactly one statement, that it names `POST/activate`, and that it does **not** end in a wildcard path — so adding a route does not silently publish it. Note `Principal: '*'` here means "any *authenticated* AWS caller may attempt activation", not anonymous access: an unsigned request never reaches the Lambda.

threats.title: Cost and Quota Exhaustion by an Arbitrary AWS Account
threats.description: Anyone with an AWS account can call the endpoint. Each request consumes a Marketplace `SearchAgreements` call (a **service quota shared across the seller account**), a Lambda invocation, and — when entitled — a KMS `Sign`. API Gateway throttling is **aggregate at the stage**, not per-caller, so a single attacker sustaining the limit consumes the whole allowance.
threats.attackVector: Sustained signed requests from one or many attacker-controlled AWS accounts. Per-caller throttling is not expressible in a resource policy, and usage-plan API keys cannot be issued to buyers the seller has never met.
threats.impact: Legitimate activations throttled → extensions fall back to their grace period and then stop working. Secondary: Marketplace API throttling could affect other seller-side tooling; modest KMS/Lambda cost.
threats.likelihood: Low (requires deliberate abuse and an AWS account traceable to the attacker)
threats.severity: Medium (degradation, bounded by the buyer-side grace period; no data or key compromise)
threats.mitigations: Stage throttling (25 rps / 50 burst) **and a Lambda concurrency reservation** cap blast radius — the reservation matters independently, because without it a flood would consume the seller account's entire Lambda pool and take unrelated seller-side functions down with it — activation is a once-per-TTL-per-install call, so this is generous for legitimate traffic. Every attempt is attributed to a **verified AWS account** in the access log and roster, so abuse is identifiable and actionable (AWS abuse report / block by account). `NotEntitledActivations` and `ActivationAttempt{Outcome=refused}` metrics make a probing pattern visible. The buyer-side **grace period on the last-known-good token** is the control that keeps paying customers working through an outage. Body size is capped at 4 KB before parsing.

threats.title: Signing-Key Compromise or Trust Re-Pointing
threats.description: The token signing key is the root of trust for every deployed extension. Whoever can sign with it can mint valid entitlement for any account; whoever can change the key or its policy can re-point that trust.
threats.attackVector: Compromise of the `ActivateFunction` role (e.g. via a dependency or a future code-injection flaw) and use of its KMS grant beyond signing; or destruction of the key, which invalidates all issued tokens.
threats.impact: Forged entitlement (revenue loss) or an outage that cannot be repaired by redeploying, since previously-issued tokens become unverifiable.
threats.mitigations: **Asymmetric** key (`RSA_2048`, `SIGN_VERIFY`): verifiers hold only the public key, so the ability to *verify* is not the ability to *mint* — this is what makes it safe to embed the public key in public-read extension artifacts. The function's grant is **`kms:Sign` only** on that one key — no `PutKeyPolicy`, no `ScheduleKeyDeletion`, and deliberately not even `GetPublicKey` (the operator fetches that with their own credentials). The key policy grants no wildcard principal. `DeletionPolicy: Retain` + `UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain` so a stack delete cannot silently destroy the root of trust. Tokens carry a **`kid`**, so a compromised key can be rotated by standing up a second key and trusting both during the overlap. Static tests assert the key spec, the sign-only grant, the absence of a wildcard principal, and the retain policies.

threats.title: Token Misuse — Replay, Sharing, and Verifier Weakness
threats.description: The token is a detached signature over base64 JSON claims. Its security depends on the **verifier** (code in the buyer's account, written by the extension author) checking the right things. Three ways that goes wrong: (a) verifying a *re-serialised* copy of the claims rather than the exact signed bytes; (b) trusting the `signingAlgorithm` field from the response instead of pinning it — the JWT `alg:none` class of bug; (c) not checking `buyerAccountId` and `exp`, making a token portable between customers or usable forever.
threats.attackVector: A customer extracts a valid token from their own deployment and shares it, or an attacker supplies a crafted response to a lax verifier.
threats.impact: Entitlement shared beyond the subscribing account, or accepted from an attacker.
threats.likelihood: Medium — this is an integration hazard, and the extension author is the one who has to get it right
threats.mitigations: Claims bind the token to `productId` + `buyerAccountId` and carry `iat`/`exp` with a short TTL, so a shared token is both account-scoped and short-lived. The README's integration contract states explicitly: verify over the **exact base64-decoded bytes**, **pin** `RSASSA_PSS_SHA_256` rather than reading it from the response, and check `buyerAccountId` against the running account and `exp` against the clock. The live test asserts account binding, `kid` presence, a future `exp`, and a real signature verification against the published public key.

threats.title: Product-Existence Oracle
threats.description: If an unknown `productId` answered differently from an unentitled one, any AWS account could enumerate which products the seller has registered. That matters most for a listing in **Limited** state, whose `productId` is not public — it would confirm an unreleased product exists.
threats.attackVector: Probe `POST /activate` with candidate product ids and compare responses.
threats.impact: Disclosure of unreleased or private product identifiers; competitive/roadmap leakage.
threats.mitigations: An unknown product returns **the same status and byte-identical body** as "not entitled". The distinction is preserved only in the seller-side log, where it still helps diagnose a legitimate integrator's typo. A unit test compares both responses for equality, and the live test does the same against the deployed stage.

threats.title: Unavailability of the Activation Service Locks Out Paying Customers
threats.description: The service becomes a hard dependency of every deployed paid extension. It **fails closed** on its own errors — an `AccessDenied` or throttle from the Marketplace API is reported as *not entitled*, not as *unknown* — so a seller-side fault would refuse legitimate customers.
threats.attackVector: Seller-side outage, expired/broken IAM, regional Marketplace API issue, or the throttling in SELL.T04.
threats.impact: Paying customers lose function through no fault of their own.
threats.mitigations: The fail-closed choice is deliberate and is *paired* with a compensating control on the other side: the buyer-side integration is **required** to cache the last-known-good token and apply a **grace period longer than the TTL**, so a seller-side outage is absorbed rather than fatal. This asymmetry is stated in the README as a table (host = advisory allow, this service = deny, extension = grace period) precisely so the three are not "simplified" into agreement. Roster writes are **fail-open** — bookkeeping never causes a refusal.

threats.title: Customer Roster Disclosure
threats.description: The activation roster is a list of the seller's customers — AWS account ids, which products they activated, when, and caller role ARNs — retained indefinitely by design. Read access to it discloses the seller's commercial position; write access could fabricate or erase activation history.
threats.attackVector: Compromise of the `ActivateFunction` role, or over-broad IAM in the seller account.
threats.impact: Competitive intelligence (who your customers are); repudiation risk if history can be altered.
threats.mitigations: The function holds **`dynamodb:UpdateItem` only** — it cannot read the roster (so a compromised function is not a way to enumerate the customer list) and cannot delete it. Reads happen out-of-band via `idp-feature-cli seller-service activations` using the operator's own credentials. SSE at rest, point-in-time recovery, and `DeletionPolicy: Retain`. Free-text fields from upstream errors are truncated to 512 bytes. Static tests assert the update-only grant, SSE, PITR and Retain.

threats.title: Allow-List Bypass Left Enabled in Production
threats.description: `AllowedAccounts` issues a token **without any subscription check**, for testing the paid path. Every entry is an account receiving the full paid product for free. Left populated after testing, it is a permanent revenue hole — and it is a plaintext CloudFormation parameter, so it is not obvious in review.
threats.attackVector: Operator forgets to clear it; or an insider adds an account.
threats.impact: Direct revenue loss, undetectable from the buyer side.
threats.mitigations: Documented in the parameter description, the README, and the code comment as "every entry here is an account getting your paid product for free — keep it empty in production". Use of the path logs at INFO with the account id and is recorded in the roster with `lastDetail = "allow-listed account"`, so it is visible in `seller-service activations` output rather than invisible. Default is empty.

threats.title: Cross-Tenant Access in a Shared Stack
threats.description: Isolation between tenants is enforced by the application. Every processing Lambda, table and bucket is shared, and IAM does not separate one tenant's documents from another's inside the stack. A non-Admin user therefore sees another tenant's documents, profiles or results in any of four cases: when their scope admits that tenant, when they have no scope in a mode that reads that as unrestricted, when an operation reads documents without applying scope, or when the surface they use cannot be scoped at all.
threats.attackVector: (1) With `TenantIsolationMode=Off` and `TenantGrantSource=Manual`, the defaults, a non-Admin user row with no `allowedConfigVersions` is unrestricted. (2) A new or changed operation reads documents without a scope check. (3) Agent Chat, agent queries, Knowledge Base queries and the MCP `search` tool read across every profile and cannot be confined to one tenant. (4) An Annotator's `allowedTestSets` names a test set built from another tenant's documents.
threats.impact: Disclosure of another tenant's documents, extraction results and configuration, and operations on them (review, reprocess, delete).
threats.affectedComponents: `idp_common/config_scope.py`, `idp_common/config/tenants.py`, every scope-checked resolver, `queue_sender`, the chat, agent, Knowledge Base and MCP handlers, `mcp_identity_interceptor`
threats.mitigations: **Declarations are enforced when written, in both modes.** Once tenants are declared, a scope, mapping or tenant that would cross a tenant is refused, so a scoped user cannot be given two tenants' profiles. **Fail closed when configured to.** `Strict`, or either external grant source, makes an unscoped non-Admin resolve to nothing (`unscoped_is_denied`), refuses a cross-tenant document at ingest, makes the unscopable surfaces (Agent Chat, agent queries, Knowledge Base queries, the MCP `search` tool) Admin-only, and moves the web UI's chat onto the REST path. MCP tools other than `search` apply the caller's scope as the equivalent REST operation does, and a service credential carries a scope of its own that must sit inside one tenant. **Scope on every single-document operation.** Fetch, versions, review, Send to review and bulk Skip All Reviews, delete, abort, copy-to-baseline, discovery, section auto-detection and the test-set and test-run operations apply profile scope in both modes. `scripts/api_rbac_expectations.yaml` declares where each operation applies it, and `make api-test-static` fails when the code does not match the declaration; its check S10 also fails when an operation whose arguments name a profile, a document or a session declares no scope at all. `idp-cli tenancy audit` reports unscoped users and boundary-crossing mappings, and `tenancy verify` and `make stacktest-tenancy` test the boundary on a live stack.
threats.residualRisk: `Off` with `Manual` is the default. Under it, an unscoped non-Admin is unrestricted by design, so a shared stack depends on every non-Admin being scoped; run `tenancy audit` and use `Strict` for a shared stack. Admins are cross-tenant in every mode. The static gate proves that a declared check exists, and S10 that an operation whose argument names a scoped object declares one; an operation that reads documents without naming one in its arguments (a listing, a search) is outside S10, so a new one with no declaration is a cross-tenant read until one is added. Test sets record no tenant, so `allowedTestSets` is not confined to one. The reader binds the record to the account's Cognito `sub` and denies a record naming another `sub` wherever an unscoped caller is denied, and the grant writer gives each account sharing an address a record of its own; the remaining residuals of the join are those AUTH.T07 records.

threats.title: Access-Point Delegation Trusts Every Access Point in the Account
threats.description: Under `Strict`, the Input and Output bucket policies delegate to access points through `DelegateToTenantAccessPoints`, conditioned on `s3:DataAccessPointAccount` equalling the stack's account. The condition admits **any** access point the account owns, not only the generated per-tenant ones. A principal that can create an access point on these buckets, or change an access point's policy, can therefore grant itself bucket access that no tenant boundary confines.
threats.attackVector: A principal in the account holding `s3:CreateAccessPoint` or `s3:PutAccessPointPolicy` creates an access point on the Output bucket, or rewrites a tenant's access point policy, naming itself.
threats.impact: Reads of every tenant's output, or writes into any tenant's Input prefixes, outside the application's scope checks.
threats.mitigations: The statement exists only under `Strict`. On the Input bucket it grants `s3:PutObject` on objects only, so delegation widens nothing for a principal that does not go through an access point. The generated access point policies allow one tenant's principals and add explicit denies for other tenants' principals and for objects and listings outside the tenant's prefixes. An account-root principal is refused, because the deny compares `aws:PrincipalArn` and a root entry would otherwise escape it. `docs/multi-tenancy.md` makes restricting `s3:CreateAccessPoint` and `s3:PutAccessPointPolicy` to the access point deployer a prerequisite of `Strict`, gives an SCP for it, and recommends alarming on the CloudTrail events. `tenancy audit --principals` compares the deployed access points with the declarations.
threats.residualRisk: The template cannot enforce that prerequisite. Whoever can create access points in the account is inside the delegation boundary, and nothing in the stack detects one created outside the tooling until `tenancy audit` is run. Apply the SCP before switching to `Strict`.

threats.title: An External Grant Source Decides Tenancy
threats.description: Under `TenantGrantSource=IdpClaim` the identity provider's group or role claim decides which tenant a user belongs to. Under `Api` an entitlement system decides it, through the Admin-only `setUserTenant` (and `setMcpCredentialTenant` for an MCP service credential) or through the SDK with IAM credentials that can write the UsersTable. Either way, the authority over the tenant boundary moves out of the stack to whoever administers that source.
threats.attackVector: An identity-provider administrator, or a principal able to change a user's group or role assignments there, adds a tenant's **Granted by** value to a user. A principal holding the entitlement system's credentials, or UsersTable write in the account, pushes a tenant. A grant removed at the source is not applied to a live session until its next fresh sign-in.
threats.impact: A user is placed in a tenant they should not belong to, or keeps one they should have lost.
threats.mitigations: The claim is honoured only under the same two checks as the group mapping. The user must be linked to the configured provider, which is read from the Cognito-managed `identities` attribute. The sign-in must be fresh, never a token refresh, since a refresh re-reads a stored attribute the user can write. A grant is exactly one tenant's pattern or the deny marker: values granting several tenants grant none, and so does an unknown value. A grant that cannot be written fails the sign-in or the API call, rather than leaving the previous tenant in place. A grant binds to the account's Cognito `sub`: the writer updates only a record naming that `sub` or naming none (conditioned in the same write), and an address-only push refuses an address more than one record holds, so a grant cannot land on, or be read from, a second account that shares the address. Admin edits of a scope are refused under both sources, so the stack has one writer per mode. Admins are never granted a tenant, and a claim that promotes a user to Admin removes the tenant it granted. `RefreshTokenValidityHours` bounds how long a removed grant can outlive its removal.
threats.residualRisk: Whoever administers the identity provider's roles, or the entitlement system, decides tenancy. Treat those as administrative to the stack. A removal applies at the next fresh sign-in, so a session can keep a revoked tenant for up to `RefreshTokenValidityHours`; shorten that value where revocation latency matters. The reader binds the record to the account's Cognito `sub` and denies a record naming another `sub` wherever an unscoped caller is denied, and the grant writer gives each account sharing an address a record of its own; the remaining residuals of the join are those AUTH.T07 records. An MCP service credential's tenant changes take effect on its next call, because the interceptor reads the credential row on every call.

threats.title: The Sign-In Trigger Holds UsersTable Write Under `IdpClaim`
threats.description: Under `IdpClaim` the pre-token-generation trigger writes users' scopes, so its role holds `dynamodb:GetItem`, `PutItem`, `UpdateItem` and `DeleteItem` on the whole UsersTable with no key condition, `Query` on its email index, `GetItem` on the ConfigurationTable restricted by `dynamodb:LeadingKeys` to `TenantIndex#__index`, and encrypt and decrypt on the stack key. The UsersTable row holds a user's `persona` as well as their scope, and the UsersTable stream syncs a `persona` change into Cognito groups (`UserSyncFunction`). Which rows and attributes the trigger writes is therefore decided by its code, not by IAM.
threats.attackVector: A defect in the trigger, in the `idp_common` layer it imports under `IdpClaim`, or in a dependency of either, writes another user's row or a `persona` attribute.
threats.impact: Changes to any user's scope, or to their role through the stream sync.
threats.mitigations: The grants exist only when `IsTenantGrantFromIdpClaim` holds, and so does the layer. In every other mode the function runs layer-free with no data-plane grant, as it did before tenant grants existed. On an existing row the writer sets only the scope attributes and the row's link to the signing-in account, in one write conditioned on the row recording no account or that one; it never rewrites `persona`, never changes an Admin row, and creates no row for an Admin. A row it creates records the persona the claim maps to and `source: cognito`, so the stream sync does not create a second Cognito account. The trigger runs only on Cognito's invocation, on the fresh-sign-in and linked-provider checks of TEN.T03. Unit tests are in `src/lambda/external_idp_group_mapping/test_index.py`.
threats.residualRisk: IAM cannot express "this user's own row" or "these attributes" for a trigger that runs for every user, so the code is the only bound. A `dynamodb:Attributes` condition limiting `UpdateItem` to the scope attributes would move part of that bound into IAM, and is recommended.

threats.title: Tenant Declarations Are an Authorization Input and a Single Point of Failure
threats.description: The declarations decide where each tenant's documents land and which profiles each tenant may use, and they live in one ConfigurationTable item. Changing them redraws the boundary. Under `Strict` every ingest reads them, so a read failure stops processing for every tenant.
threats.attackVector: A principal with ConfigurationTable write in the account edits the tenant index item directly. Throttling, a missing grant or a deleted item makes the ingest read fail. One tenant's bulk upload uses the workflow concurrency and Bedrock quota every tenant shares.
threats.impact: A boundary redrawn without the write-time checks, or every new document refused until the read recovers.
threats.mitigations: Only an Admin can call the API operations that write the declarations, and they apply the write-time refusals of TEN.T01. The index is size-bounded (`MAX_TENANTS`, prefix and grant caps) so it stays within one item. Under `Strict` a failed read **fails closed**: `queue_sender` emits `TenantIsolationLookupFailed` and raises, so the document is retried rather than admitted unchecked, and `TenantIsolationLookupFailedAlarm` (deployed only under `Strict`) alarms on it. `TenantBoundaryRejected` records each refusal.
threats.residualRisk: A direct table write bypasses the write-time checks. That is the same exposure every ConfigurationTable item carries, so keep table write to the stack's roles. Throughput is shared between tenants, and nothing in the stack meters it per tenant.

threats.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
threats.description: Document processing results displayed in the UI could contain malicious HTML/JavaScript. If results are rendered without proper sanitization, XSS could execute in the user's browser. Document-derived content is inherently attacker-influenced: an uploaded document's text, extracted field values, class names, summaries, and model-generated `confidence_reason` strings all reach the DOM.
threats.attackVector: Upload a document containing XSS payloads in text content; extracted values containing script tags are rendered in the results viewer, section tables, processing-issue popovers, markdown panes, or another user's Inbox, where a message body interpolating the uploaded file name is rendered through `SafeMarkdown` (HITL.T03). Secondary vector: a prompt-injected model response (PM.T01) emits an active payload into a field the UI renders as markdown/HTML.
threats.impact: Session token theft, unauthorized API calls from the user's browser (with their full role), data exfiltration
threats.affectedComponents: Web UI (React), results viewer, configuration editor, markdown/SafeMarkdown renderers, feature UI bundles
threats.mitigations: React JSX auto-escaping is the primary control; document-derived markdown is routed through a `SafeMarkdown` renderer. **CSP is a partial control only** — see the residual risk below. Tokens are held in memory/session storage rather than cookies, so there is no cookie-theft path, but an XSS payload can still call the API as the user. The ZAP DAST probe checks response headers each build.
threats.residualRisk: The shipped CSP is **not** a strong anti-XSS control: `script-src` is `'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/`, so inline script and `eval` still run. `'unsafe-inline'`/`'unsafe-eval'` are retained pending Monaco editor compatibility work. `script-src` names no scheme source; the one cross-origin source is the CDN path `@monaco-editor/react` loads Monaco from at runtime (`cdn.jsdelivr.net`), and self-hosting Monaco out of the Web UI bucket would let that go. `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'none'`, `form-action 'self'`, `frame-ancestors`, and a hostname-restricted `connect-src` (`'self'`, `*.amazonaws.com`, `*.amazoncognito.com`, `*.on.aws`, and `ws://localhost:*` for the local development server) are genuine hardening (they block plugin execution, base-tag hijacking, and `fetch`/`XHR`/WebSocket exfiltration), but the policy does **not** stop inline script from executing. The resource directives name specific sources: `default-src 'self'` is set, `style-src` allows `'self'`, inline styles and the jsDelivr `/npm/` path Monaco's stylesheet comes from, `font-src` is `'self' data:`, `media-src` is `'self'`, `worker-src` is `'self' blob:` (Monaco starts its language workers from same-origin `blob:` URLs, and the pdf.js worker is a same-origin asset), and `img-src`/`frame-src` allow `'self'`, `data:` (plus `blob:` for images) and `https://*.amazonaws.com`, the S3 hosts presigned URLs use. That last source is the whole of `amazonaws.com` rather than this deployment's buckets, so CSP alone does not limit a page load to the deployment's own buckets; rendered markdown is held to them by `SafeMarkdown` (`src/ui/src/components/common/safe-markdown-policy.ts`), which loads an image only from a `data:image/` URL, a `blob:` URL of the page's own origin, the page's own origin, or an S3 URL for one of the deployment's own buckets, shows any other image as a link, removes `<style>` elements with their text, renders no `srcset`, `<picture>` or `<source>`, and keeps a `style` attribute only for layout and typography properties whose value cannot name a resource. Rendered markdown still admits external `http(s)` links, which navigate only when the user follows them; printing a report writes the document name as text. Treat React escaping — not CSP — as the control of record for UI.T01. **See also UI.T07: the same policy is now emitted in `WebUIHosting=APIGateway` mode too.**

threats.title: Presigned Upload URL Abuse
threats.description: S3 presigned URLs for document upload could be shared or reused to upload documents without re-authenticating
threats.attackVector: Intercepted or shared presigned PUT URL used to upload documents outside the normal authentication flow
threats.impact: Unauthorized document upload, processing of malicious documents, storage/processing cost abuse
threats.mitigations: Minting the URL requires the **Admin/Author** group (enforced server-side in `upload_resolver`); short expiration; S3 bucket lifecycle policies; the concurrency counter and SQS bound runaway processing. Trailing-slash pseudo-object keys are skipped by the Queue Sender so console "folder" artifacts don't start executions.

threats.title: UI API Abuse (REST dispatcher)
threats.stride: Tampering, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service
threats.description: The UI API is a **single API Gateway REST route** — `POST /op/{field}` — fronted by a Cognito authorizer that **only authenticates**. Any authenticated user can name *any* routable operation in the path (the list is `operations` in `scripts/api_rbac_expectations.yaml`). The dispatcher applies a field-level group floor from a generated manifest before routing and refuses an undeclared operation (AUTH.T16), so a caller outside an operation's declared groups is refused there; every narrower decision — configuration-profile and test-set scope, ownership, review-queue eligibility — is made inside the resolver, so an operation whose resolver omits one is reachable by every caller its group list admits. Separately, a caller can drive high request volume or expensive operations (bulk list/scan ops, agent invocations) to degrade the API or run up model cost.
threats.attackVector: An authenticated low-privilege user (e.g. Reviewer/Viewer) enumerates operation names from the JS bundle or `schema.graphql` and calls privileged ones directly with `curl`, bypassing UI navigation gating; or floods a costly operation.
threats.impact: Privilege escalation / unauthorized data access where a server-side check is missing; API performance degradation; Bedrock cost amplification
threats.affectedComponents: API Gateway REST API, `http_api_dispatcher`, all resolver Lambdas, `ddb_direct` handlers
threats.mitigations: **The dispatcher's default-deny group floor** plus **per-object checks inside each resolver** (the authorization boundary — see AUTH.T03/T08/T16). Static check S10 of `make api-test-static` fails when an operation whose arguments name a configuration profile, a stored object or a session declares no scope for it. Every 403 carries `errors[0].authzControl`, naming which layer refused, and an unexpected server error answers a generic 500 `InternalError` with a request id while the detail (which can name internal resources) is logged server-side only. **Central input-shape validation** in the dispatcher rejects unknown/missing/wrong-typed/out-of-enum arguments with HTTP 400 before routing (AUTH.T12). **Automated authorization testing is the primary regression control**: `make api-test-static` fails on op↔schema↔expectations drift or a missing enforcement pattern, and `make api-test` drives the live op×role matrix with per-role Cognito users plus unauthenticated/tampered-token calls. Optional WAFv2 IP allow-list (default-Block WebACL) on the stage; `ApiGatewayVisibility=PRIVATE` restricts invocation to a VPC endpoint. API Gateway stage throttling and Lambda reserved concurrency bound volume.

threats.title: Hosting Origin Misconfiguration
threats.description: A misconfigured UI origin could expose S3 bucket contents beyond the SPA, serve stale/cached sensitive data, or allow cache poisoning. Applies to both hosting modes: CloudFront (OAC → S3) and the API Gateway S3 proxy.
threats.attackVector: Manipulate cache keys or exploit misconfigured origin access to reach unintended S3 objects; in APIGateway mode, traverse the `{proxy+}` path to a non-UI key in the Web UI bucket
threats.impact: Exposure of S3 bucket contents beyond the UI; cached content served to the wrong user
threats.affectedComponents: CloudFront distribution, API Gateway `GET /` + `GET /{proxy+}` methods, S3 UI bucket, `WebUIProxyRole`
threats.mitigations: CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) with a restrictive S3 bucket policy; in APIGateway mode the proxy integration assumes a dedicated `WebUIProxyRole` scoped to the Web UI bucket, so traversal cannot reach other stack buckets, and a missing key maps to 404.
