The Web UI bucket holds only build artifacts and feature bundles — no customer documents. Feature bundles are served with `Cache-Control: max-age=300` (matching the CloudFront TTL) so a republished hotfix propagates in minutes instead of being pinned for a year.

threats.title: Client-Side Configuration Exposure
threats.description: The React SPA requires configuration values (Cognito pool/client IDs, identity pool ID, REST API endpoint, chat Function URL, bucket names) embedded in client-side code. These could be used to discover and target backend services
threats.attackVector: Extract configuration from browser developer tools or the JS bundle to identify backend endpoints
threats.impact: Knowledge of backend endpoints enables targeted attacks against the REST API, the chat Function URL, Cognito, or S3
threats.affectedComponents: Web UI JavaScript bundle, runtime config
threats.mitigations: All backend services require authentication; client-side config contains only public endpoint identifiers; authorization is enforced server-side. Security does not depend on endpoint obscurity. Note the corollary for UI.T03: because the endpoint and operation names are inherently public, **server-side authorization is the only thing standing between a Viewer and an Admin operation.**

threats.title: Object Reads Carry No Document Ownership Axis
threats.description: `getFileContents`, `getFilePresignedUrl` and `getFilePresignedUrls` accept caller-supplied `s3Uri` values (with an optional `versionId`, per entry on the batch field) and return the bytes, or presigned GET URLs for them. Three server-side controls apply to every request, all of them in `_parse_and_validate_one` — the one function every field and every batch entry passes through before S3 is touched: the dispatcher's field-level group floor (each is declared **`ANY_GROUP`**, so a caller in *no* group is refused), the **bucket** allow-list, and **key** authorization. Key authorization has two halves covering different buckets. For the Configuration and Test Set buckets — the two partitioned **per user** — the key itself is matched against `allowedConfigVersions` / `allowedTestSets`. For the Input and Output buckets the object belongs to a *document*, so `document_scope` resolves the owning document from the tracking table and matches its `ConfigVersion` against the caller's `allowedConfigVersions`. ⚠️ **That is the only per-document axis this deployment records.** There is no document-owner attribute in the product, so "is this document yours" cannot be asked; a tenant is a set of profiles and Input prefixes (TEN.T01), so the profile check is also the tenant check. Because scoping is opt-in per user under the default `TenantIsolationMode=Off` with `TenantGrantSource=Manual`, a caller whose `allowedConfigVersions` is unset — the default, and what self-signup produces — is bounded by the group floor alone and may read any document's bytes by key: another user's document results, evaluation baselines, reporting Parquet, and prior document versions via `versionId`. **Group membership is not per-document authorization**, and no setting of it supplies one.
threats.attackVector: An authenticated user calls `getFilePresignedUrl` (or `getFilePresignedUrls` with a list) for `s3://<output-bucket>/<other-users-doc>/sections/1/result.json`, or enumerates keys through `listDocumentVersions`, `listDocumentsDateHour` or `listDocumentsDateShard` (all `ANY_GROUP`, so that arm needs an assigned group — any one of the five will do), then fetches the bytes. ⚠️ **Every route to the bytes is an API operation.** `CognitoIdentityPoolSetRole` attaches one `authenticated` role with no role mappings, so whatever that role can read is readable by every signed-in user with no resolver in the path; the role accordingly grants **nothing** on the Input and Output buckets, **no** `s3:GetObject`, `s3:GetObjectVersion` or `s3:ListBucket` on any bucket, and **no** KMS action ([#1033](https://github.com/aws-solutions-library-samples/accelerated-intelligent-document-processing-on-aws/issues/1033)). A self-registered caller in no group who runs `cognito-identity get-id` and `get-credentials-for-identity` with their own ID token and assumes that role fails at `s3api get-object`, because the vended credentials can read no bucket. What is left is the presign or inline-read call itself, which needs an assigned group and, for a document outside the caller's profile scope, is refused; see AUTH.T03 residuals (1) and (3).
threats.impact: Cross-user disclosure of document content and extracted data within the deployment, bounded to objects in the stack's own document buckets, and bounded further to callers whose configuration-profile scope is unset — a scoped caller is refused a document outside their profiles.
threats.likelihood: Medium (requires an assigned group, a caller whose `allowedConfigVersions` is unset, and a key. It stays at Medium rather than dropping: an unset scope is the default state of a user row, the key-returning operations are `ANY_GROUP` and so reachable by all five groups, and a group member in that state reads any document through the resolver exactly as `listDocuments` lists it for them)
threats.affectedComponents: `get_file_contents_resolver` (`_parse_and_validate_one`, `_validate_bucket`, `_validate_key_scope`, `_handle_presigned_url`, `_handle_presigned_urls`, `_handle_file_contents`, `key_scope`, `document_scope`, `s3_targets`), the tracking table, `CognitoAuthorizedRole`, S3 input/output/reporting/baseline buckets
threats.mitigations: **The browser holds no S3 grant.** `CognitoAuthorizedRole` carries two inline policies — `lambda:InvokeFunction` on the chat-streaming Function URL and `ssm:GetParameter` on the settings parameter — and no S3 or KMS statement, so there is no bucket a signed-in user's own credentials can read and every document byte the UI displays comes from one of the three operations above. `scripts/tests/test_browser_s3_grants.py` fails if an S3 statement reappears on the role under any policy name. A **bucket allow-list** built from injected env vars prevents the resolver being used as a generic S3-read gadget for arbitrary or third-party buckets, and fails **closed** — an unset allow-list refuses every request rather than skipping validation. Presigned URLs are short-lived; the URI must be `s3://` form, is parsed literally (preserving `#` in keys) and must be in canonical form, so two spellings of one key cannot derive different authorization answers. **Per-user key scope** matches a Configuration-bucket `config_revisions/<profile>/<nnnnnn>.json.gz` against `allowedConfigVersions` and every Test Set bucket key (`<test_set_id>/…`, covering source documents, ground truth and published baseline snapshots) against `allowedTestSets`, through the canonical fail-closed lookups (`idp_common.config_scope`, `idp_common.testset_scope`). **Per-document scope** finds the document owning an Input- or Output-bucket key by walking the key's `/` boundaries longest-first against the tracking table — longest-first because uploads may nest, and prefix-walking rather than a list of known artifact segments because an unrecognised artifact prefix would otherwise read as "not document-scoped" and pass — then applies `allowedConfigVersions` to its `ConfigVersion`. The ordering is strict rather than optimised: trying ancestors followed by a *known* artifact segment first would put a shorter ancestor ahead of the true owner for an artifact prefix it does not know, and authorize a nested document's artifact against its parent. It fails closed on both halves: a scope that cannot be evaluated denies, a key no tracked document owns denies, and a document carrying no `ConfigVersion` denies a scoped caller. Every refusal raises the identical non-disclosing message, naming neither bucket, key, document nor profile, and the object is never read, so a refusal is not an existence oracle; on the batch field a single refusal fails the **whole** request, because per-entry refusals would turn one call into an N-key authorization oracle. The list is capped server-side (`MAX_BATCH_OBJECTS`, refused rather than truncated) and the distinct documents one call may look up more tightly still (`document_scope.MAX_DOCUMENT_LOOKUP_BATCHES`, where one round trip resolves up to 100 candidate document keys), so a caller-supplied list cannot amplify one API call into unbounded DynamoDB reads. Past that cap the caller gets the same opaque refusal rather than a distinguishable "too broad" error, because round-trip count is a function of which candidate documents exist and a different status class would be an existence oracle. Under `TenantIsolationMode=Strict` or an external `TenantGrantSource`, an unscoped non-Admin resolves to a scope no profile matches, so `document_scope` refuses them every document rather than admitting all of them; a shared stack depends on that (TEN.T01). Under the default modes the design assumption is that every authenticated user belongs to one organization's deployment, which is what makes the remaining gap acceptable for most deployments.
threats.residualRisk: **Document ownership is not modelled, so the per-document check can only ask the profile question.** For a **scoped** caller that is a real boundary: a page image or section result stamped with a profile outside their `allowedConfigVersions` is refused before S3 is touched. For an **unscoped** caller — a UsersTable row that sets no scope, or no row at all — under the default modes the check is deliberately a no-op, because scoping is opt-in per user, so a caller in any one of the five groups may still read any document's bytes through the resolver. That is the same reach `listDocuments` already gives them, and it is the whole of the per-document boundary this product can express. Recommend giving documents an ownership or tenancy attribute and deriving the permitted key from it; that is the one change that would close the rest, and it is a data-model change rather than a read-path one. Note also that the broad read sits on `get_file_contents_resolver`'s own role, which makes that function the single component whose compromise yields every document. Coverage: the out-of-scope-key cases for both per-user axes are offline (`get_file_contents_resolver/test_key_scope.py`), the per-document cases likewise (`test_document_scope.py`), and the browser's grant is pinned in both directions by `scripts/tests/test_browser_s3_grants.py`.

threats.title: Security-Header and CSP Divergence Between Hosting Modes
threats.description: Response security headers are attached by the hosting layer, and the two hosting modes attach them in different places. The `SecurityHeadersPolicy` that carries the **Content-Security-Policy** is a CloudFront `ResponseHeadersPolicy` gated on `Condition: UseCloudFrontHosting`, so in `WebUIHosting=APIGateway` mode (required for `--govcloud`, and used for private/VPC-only deployments) there is no CloudFront, and the SPA's headers come from the API Gateway methods `WebUIRootMethod` and `WebUIProxyMethod`. If the two sets diverge, one mode loses the CSP or part of it.
threats.attackVector: An XSS payload (UI.T01) that the CloudFront CSP's `connect-src` restriction would limit from exfiltrating to an arbitrary origin runs without that restriction in an APIGateway/GovCloud deployment whose methods lack the CSP.
threats.impact: Loss of the plugin/`base-uri` hardening and of the `connect-src` restriction on API-shaped exfiltration precisely in the deployments most likely to be handling regulated data (GovCloud, private VPC). (Neither mode closes image-based exfiltration — see UI.T01's residual risk.)
threats.likelihood: Low (requires a UI.T01 XSS to chain from)
threats.mitigations: Both hosting modes now emit the same CSP: in APIGateway mode it is a static integration-response value on the SPA document and asset methods, held once in `Mappings -> WebUiSecurity -> ContentSecurityPolicy` of the api-resolvers template and pinned against the CloudFront copy by `scripts/tests/test_csp_policies_in_sync.py`. The only intended difference from the CloudFront policy is `frame-ancestors 'none'` instead of `'self'`, matching that mode's stricter `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (a CSP `frame-ancestors` overrides `X-Frame-Options`, so copying `'self'` verbatim would *relax* framing there). `nosniff`, HSTS, `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and `Referrer-Policy` remain set per-method, and on the `/op` Lambda responses and the 4xx/5xx gateway responses. APIGateway mode is also typically deployed PRIVATE (VPC-only) or behind the WAF IP allow-list.
threats.residualRisk: `scripts/tests/test_csp_policies_in_sync.py` asserts the two copies match directive-for-directive (with `frame-ancestors` as the one asserted difference) and that neither `script-src` regains a blanket scheme source, so drift fails the build rather than reaching a GovCloud deployment. All three response codes of both SPA methods (200/404/500) carry the CSP, not just the 200 — a 404 for a missing asset key is still a response from the SPA's own origin. The CSP is deliberately **not** added to the API's `DEFAULT_4XX`/`DEFAULT_5XX` gateway responses or the `/op` JSON responses (non-HTML bodies, already served `nosniff`). The header itself is only observable against a deployed stage (`make stacktest-*`, APIGateway variants).
